en: The *Cakrasaṃvaratantra*, Volume 2:
The Twenty-sixth Chapter on the Examination of Disciples and the Ritual of Vows.
Beyond this, the mantra-word is not found in the three worlds.
Having known the mantra of Śrī Heruka, one should abandon all other mantras. || 1 ||

Now he speaks of the benefits of the mantra, beginning with "ataḥ" (from this): "From this" refers to the root mantra; "the supreme mantra-word" means that the address to Vidyutā Vajravārāhī is present therein.
Or it is the explanation of "it does not exist.
"Mantra" refers to the root mantra and so forth.
Having realized this, one should abandon all mantras;
for even the mantra of Śrī Heruka is Śrī Heruka himself, due to the non-duality of the two. || 1 ||
The Yoginīs are established in both direct and reverse order;
bestowing success eternally above and below, they are all-pervading as one's own messenger.
He describes the sequential placement (*kramanyāsa*) of the Yoginīs, such as Mahāvīrā and others, mentioned in the fourth chapter—beginning with the words "anuloma" and so forth.
"Anuloma" refers to the reverse order (*viloma*), that is, a non-sequential arrangement; by that [reverse order], the Yoginīs were previously established and shown.
Now, showing that they are to be placed in the direct order (*anuloma*), he says: "below and above."
The meaning is that the action [should be performed] downward and upward.
The intention is that one should place those well-known goddesses, such as Pracaṇḍā and the others, upward in the *cittacakra* and so forth. Why is that?
He says: "They grant success eternally.
The meaning is that when they are meditated upon in such a manner, they become accomplished. Therefore, he says:
"But the self-messenger (ātmadūtī) is all-pervading."

The self (*ātman*) means the mind (*citta*), that is to say, the wheel of the mind (*cittacakra*). "Beginning with that self" is the meaning. They pertain to all three wheels; they are present throughout the three wheels.
The word "ārabhya" (beginning with) is elided.

The messenger (dūtī), however, bestows the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings; her sight and touch, as well as her kissing and embracing, are constant, and especially so is the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha). || 3 ||
The word *dūtīm* is the nominative plural and the accusative singular; *tu* is used for emphasis; that messenger (*dūtī*) [is for] the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding "bestowing success":
"them" refers to those female messengers (dūtīs).
To the question "how?", he says: "by sight and likewise by touch."
"Vision" means apprehension, that is to say, direct realization;
"touching" means the mind of cultivation.
If these two were to exist, then...
The meaning is "bestowing all accomplishments.
Regarding the passage beginning with "cumbana" (kissing) and so forth:
they are called *cumbanāḥ* because they are kissed (*cumbyante*).
They are called *gūhanāḥ* because they conceal (*guhyante*); the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The *yogapīṭha* consists of the seats of the *yoginīs* and so forth.
"Specifically" means the particular types of embraces and so forth prescribed in the treatises on erotics (kāmaśāstra). || 3 ||
As many as there are assemblies of yogas, they are all remembered as effecting every accomplishment;
one should give everything that truly exists, and never otherwise.
"As many as there are" means those situated on all the seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth without exception.
To the question "By whom?", he says: "The assemblies of yoga" (*yogasaṅghātā*); the meaning is "the multitudes of *yoginīs*."
To the question "What do they do?", he says: "They are remembered as effecting all accomplishments" (*sarvasiddhikaraṃ smṛtam*).
They are remembered as effectors of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhikarāḥ*). The neuter gender and the singular ending are used because of the sense of the whole.

Alternatively, by virtue of the rule of etymology (*nairukta*), there is the shortening and elision of the vowel *ā*, the bindu, and the single letter [of the suffix], due to their being in the nominative plural;
thus, "to be given" (*deyam*) means "that which is to be bestowed as the totality of all existence. In every respect:

"By this, their true being (*sadbhāva*) comes into existence"—thus, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), food, and so forth, should be given to them as characterized by that [state]. Then they achieve success; therefore he says: "But never otherwise.
The word "but" (*tu*) is for emphasis. || 4 ||
Whether she be a mother, a sister, a daughter, or indeed a wife, whoever stands as a messenger and constantly imparts the mantra—this is indeed recorded as the prescribed rule for him. || 5 ||
He says that by this [means], the yoginīs will be affectionate like one's mother and so forth: "The mother, sister, daughter, or wife—these indeed abide as messengers.
By "wife" is meant a woman with whom one shares a single husband.

"For it is traditionally taught that this is the rule for him to whom one would constantly give the mantra. This means that the Yoginī should bestow the mantra—which is her very self—upon whichever yogin she chooses, and having received it, he should accomplish the siddhi.
Thus she should offer it.
The procedure for the mantra-system (mantranaya) is prescribed for him, because that [system] has that as its purpose;
or "mantra" means conversation. || 5 ||
I shall now declare a certain samaya that is difficult to find within the Yoga Tantras:
whether it be a man or a woman who walks on the left side, they attain accomplishment and reach their desired goals.
"I shall speak of one of the *samayas*": here, *samaya* is a form resulting from the elision of the dual plural ending;
*anyatvam* refers to [one among] the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth.

And [there is] unity within multiplicity. Even in the reading "I shall explain another convention," it is exactly the same; that is, another convention (*samaya*). [This refers to] the case-ending (*vibhakti*)—

However, in the case of elision, there is the elision of the vowel *a* in the word *atha*. Alternatively, there is a neuter designation as *samayāni*. He states the convention (*samaya*): "on the left"—
"Neti," and so forth. "Naraḥ" means a man.
Having stationed either a man or a woman on the left, another man or woman who proceeds is known to be a yogin or a yoginī in the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara.
And for this reason, the desired accomplishment proceeds and becomes certain. || 6 ||
It is known that even if he is situated far away, in another house or field, the Ācārya who is devoted to Śrī Heruka and the Mothers of Yoga [are perceived]. (7)
Therefore, he says: "It is known even at a great distance.
Even when the previously mentioned characteristics are not visible, the messenger or female messenger is recognized by their movement in a counter-clockwise direction.
He states where the messenger is by means of the words "in the house," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the supreme yoga of Śrī Heruka":
it is that in which Śrī Heruka is supreme, that is, most excellent.
Śrī Heruka would not be supreme in that way, and that [mere] yoga would not exist at all; rather,
the meaning is that the yoga which is supreme Śrī Heruka is indeed true yoga.
By this method, it should be understood that the preceptor and the mothers of yoga, the yoginīs, are supreme. || 7 ||
In this tantra, practitioners and virtuous people alike must not be despised, nor should they be reviled; rather, they should be honored according to one's ability.
He asks "Why? and says: "In this tantra, the practitioners are indeed virtuous.
Regarding the word "in this" (*asmin*), it refers to the abiding in the essential nature of the letter *na*.

The substitution of *nā* for the nominative plural of the word *sādhu* occurs within the *khaṇḍa*; the meaning is that those who are exceedingly accomplished in the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara Tantras* are indeed *sādhus*. Therefore, they are not to be disregarded on account of their small number.
They are to be understood,
nor should they be reviled;
therefore, they should be honored according to one's ability.
The meaning is "according to one's means. || 8 ||
Indeed, these eight, beginning with Kākāsyā, increase devotion and faith;
they are the eternal cause of the supernatural powers (siddhis) and the preservation of the rules of conduct (samayas).
To explain how devotion itself arises toward them for one who has been born [there], he says "Kākā" and so forth.
The eight goddesses, Kākāsyā and the others, serve to increase devotion and faith.
And these are the causes of the supernatural powers (*siddhi*);
those forms such as Kākāsyā and the others are the causes of the powers.
He states what those eight are: "of the pledges" (*samayānām*), and so forth.
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis. [The first is] the preservation of the pledges (*samayapālana*).
First. || 9 ||
Free from association with other deities and undeluded by desire,
he practiced the conduct and activities of the samaya in non-dual and unimpeded fashion.
"One who has desisted from eating [meat] due to association with another deity should not eat it.
To the question "In what state should he be?", he says: "one who is free from desire..."
Regarding the word "deluded" (*mohita*): the sense object is desire; the meaning is that, due to delusion regarding it, one first engages [with it], and subsequently desists.
That desisting is the second [stage].
Where duality—that is, conceptual construction—does not exist, that is non-duality (*advaita*);
the state of being free from conceptual construction is the third. [The word "and" (*ca*)] indicates their conjunction.
"Obstructed" means resistance; "unobstructed" means the increase of one's own accepted and certain tenets,
which is the fourth [perfection], namely, firm resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
The conduct (*ācāra*) of the *samayas* and *yoginīs* consists of the service of desire (*kāma-sevā*) and so forth;
therein lies their activity (*ceṣṭita*).
Activity is the fifth. || 10 ||
The worship of the Sovereign Goddess (Nārīśvarī), celibacy, the maintenance [of vows], freedom from anger, and the movement of the ear—these are the eight rules of conduct (samayācāra). || 11 ||
"By the sovereignty of Nārī, there is the churning.
Sovereignty means *aiśvarya*.
The rule regarding vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) is not mandatory.
That is not a lack of sovereignty; "it does not exist" is *nārīśvaryam*, which is without case endings.
To the question "Where is that?", he says: "in the Samanātha."
The Yoginī is in the expansion of the vajra; therein, sovereignty itself is the sixth. To the question "Where is there no attachment to celibacy?", he says: "In the suchnesses of the foundation."

The seventh [perfection] is non-attachment toward that very arousal and undertaking of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). "Non-anger" (*akrodha*) means the absence of anger; it is intended as a state of turning away [from aversion].

The ears are the sense organs; that in which they move is the "movement," namely the collection of objects. The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis. Furthermore, turning away from attachment to the collection of objects is the eighth cause.
Thus, there are eight causes. Eight.
Devotion arises toward those things in which the causes of accomplishment reside;
they alone are to be worshipped. Why is this so? He says:
"Regarding the 'conduct of the observance' (samayācāra): it is because of the conventional usage of the Yoginīs. || 11 ||
Those who are established in the practice must always be recognized by practitioners as perfected ones;
they are common to all tantras and must not be harmed by those lacking reason.

The practitioners of the means should know that the eight commitments, beginning with the preservation of the *samaya*, are the causes of accomplishment; they are established as accomplished and certain for those abiding in the practice.
This is common to all tantras.
To explain how these serve as the cause for accomplishment, he says: "They are not to be killed, they are not to be slain.
By whom? He says: "By slayers who are without cause."
By means of the instruments of knowledge (pramāṇas), such as direct perception and the rest, which are themselves devoid of [independent] causes. || 12 ||
These are grasped by faith alone, neither by hand nor by eye;
this secret is not to be revealed and must be guarded with great effort. (13)
Since they are grasped by faith alone,
he says: "not with the hand, nor with the eye."
And for this reason, he says it must be kept secret: "It is not to be revealed," and so forth.
This concludes the Octad of Samayas (13).
The wise one should move the little finger; the messengers are stationed there.
They are pure, impure, or mixed—such is the threefold state of the practitioner.
"A man who is devoted, pure, an illuminator, and possessed of virtues.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, titled "The Procedure for Examining Disciples and the Vows. 26.
He describes the method for the messenger’s arousal: "the little finger," and so forth.

One should move—that is, stimulate—the channel at the tip of the mouth of the bird (the *khagamukhā*), which resembles a *bandhūka* flower, by means of the seed-syllable (*kiṃbīja*) resembling a flower, placed within the hollow formed by the tips of the ring and middle fingers. For what purpose?
He said: "O messengers," and so forth.
The arrangement of the messengers (*dūtī*) is their own state, which is the state of flowing with intoxication.
This is the examination of the disciples.
"Pure," and so forth:
"pure" means one whose intention is purified;
"impure" means the opposite; and "mixed" means that which is a combination of both.

There are three kinds of practitioners (*sādhakas*). The *ārādhaka* is one who possesses intense conviction regarding qualities (*guṇas*) and those possessing qualities (*guṇins*) through their connection with the fruits of action.
Pure, pervading that which is taught by the Teacher, and illuminating for those possessed of wisdom;
possessing qualities such as non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion; for this very reason, he is a guide, one who knows the right method. (14–15)
"Disciples" (śiṣya) refers to those who are instructed and established in their own teaching;
the "examination" (parīkṣā) of them is a thorough inspection, an observation from all sides regarding both their virtues and their faults— this is the examination of disciples.
"Restraint" (saṃvara) is the commitment (samaya). That by which it is prescribed is the "chapter" (paṭala); thus, it is [called] that [chapter].
The twenty-sixth.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛtti*. 26.
The twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for Conduct, Vows, Worship, and Offerings.
Now, the hero’s vow of conduct (*vīracaryāvrata*): by knowing the distinctions of characteristics, the practitioner of all *yoginīs* proceeds toward swift accomplishment.

The word "atha" (now) should be understood as follows: immediately after the power of the mantras and the characteristics of the Yoginīs—which are the signs for accomplishing the observance of the pledge (*samaya*) and so forth—the vow of conduct (*caryā-vrata*) occurs.
Conduct (*caryā*) refers to the practice of yoga; it is called a "vow" (*vrata*) because one engages in it with single-minded devotion.
And as for what one should do with that, or by whom it is to be practiced, he says "O Hero," and so forth.
The particle *tu* is used for emphasis.
Only by knowing the distinctions of the characteristics of the yoginīs does a hero become a practitioner of all yoginīs.
Why? For what reason? He says: "Swift accomplishment proceeds. (1)
Traveling from village to village, he beheld his two female messengers;
those two messengers were like the edge of a sword, yet pure and increasers of merit.
Regarding the phrase "going from village to village":
in every multitude of people, the movement of that yogin is like a thunderbolt; from that, the messengers proceed—this is how it should be understood.
The meaning is that they become manifest.
To the question "How are they to be known?", he says: "It is a characteristic mark."
Form alone is the defining characteristic and the cause of cognition;
and that has been stated previously:
"The two messengers and the edge of the sword."
The two messengers and the sword-edge vow—this pair is pure;
therefore, it increases merit.
For one who holds that sword-edge vow in high regard...
It is called "pure" because it is undertaken with that pure intention;
having placed a freshly sharpened sword between the two, lying upon a bed with a beautiful woman is the "sword-edge vow."
Alternatively, courtesans and the edge of a sword are both equal because they are difficult to master.
Moreover, the sight of courtesans is exceedingly pure, increasing merit, while the edge of a sword accomplishes one’s aims.
It occurs. And (ca) signifies conjunction. || 2 ||
Through contact with such female messengers (dūtīs), the practitioner attains accomplishment;
likewise, they themselves achieve success without delay, even without recitation, meditation, or ritual worship.
Therefore, he says: "He attains accomplishment through contact.
Through contact such as the sight of the *dūtī* and so forth, the practitioner attains accomplishment. To the question "Why?", he says: "The *dūtīs*, etc."
For a yogin who has become such, even the *dūtīs* are accomplished and appear before him through his vision and other means;
for, even without external recitation, meditation, and worship, in a very short time— [even] in the space of incalculable eons— ...
Because of the negation of [all] extremes. Alternatively,

this is a hyperbolic praise of such a yogin, meaning that even without mantra-recitation, the maṇḍala-circle, meditative cultivation, the fivefold offerings, or the worship of deities, the messengers (*dūtīs*) are accomplished.
Regarding the term "messengers" (*dūtayaḥ*): through contact with the female messengers (*dūtīs*), one attains accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Even without recitation (*japa*) and so forth, practitioners (*sādhakas*) achieve success simply by means of non-discrimination (*avicāra*).
Some say that the greatness of contact with a messenger (dūtī) has thus been explained. || 3 ||
Worships proceed, as do mantras, mudrās, and practitioners;
there is no worship higher than this—such is the certainty of the scripture. (4)
Practitioners who are intent on accomplishment should always delight in the path of the messenger (dūtī).
Endowed with the knowledge of mantra and vidyā, the practitioner, being well-composed, should constantly partake of the sacrificial pap (caru) and offer it to others.
He says, "And the worship, etc.," because worship and the other rites proceed from the mere sight of the messenger (dūtī).
"Mantras and mudrās" refers to the mantras and mudrās.
"This" refers to the seeing of the messenger (*dūtī*) and so forth. "Of the scripture" refers to that known as the *Śrīsaṃvara*, the [scripture] of the Yoginīs.
Of the tantra. For this very reason, practitioners (*sādhakas*) become devoted to the path of the female messenger (*dūtī*) and established in the instructions of the *yoginīs*.
They are constantly and at all times intent upon and dedicated to that accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Regarding the phrase "the practitioners intent on accomplishment for those devoted to the path of the messenger" (*dūtīmārgaratānāṃ tu sādhakāḥ siddhitatparāḥ*), according to the alternative reading:
because [of this], the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
Among those devoted to the path of the messenger, whoever is intent on accomplishment is a practitioner of that [path].
It occurs. He states the specific manner of propitiation with the words "and the *caru*," and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the acts of propitiation.
The *caru* [is to be prepared] in one place—
One should always provide food with respect and without interruption for a long period of time by means of the yoginīs.
"Endowed with mantra and vidyā" means being engaged in the recitation of mantras and so forth.
"The practitioner is well-composed" means that he is one by whom yoga is placed (āhita) within the perfectly even Śrī Heruka.
In the alternative reading "sarvayogapravṛttasya," the genitive case is used in the sense of the nominative;
for [it refers to] one who is engaged in the yoga of emptiness with respect to the stable, the moving, and so forth.
Because one who is negligent lacks the qualification [for this practice], "well-concentrated" (susamāhita) constitutes another meaning [of the term]. (4–5)
One should act for the sake of all castes and should not discriminate regarding what is fit to be eaten;
in reality, his two messengers are indivisible in the practice of accomplishment.
"One should act toward all castes" means that one should eat together with people of all castes in one place;
this applies both to what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit to be eaten.
"It is not differentiated as 'this' or 'that. Why, then, would he perform anything as a whole? To this he says: "In reality, it is indivisible for him.
For that practitioner of yoga (*caryā-yogin*), the whole is indivisible in reality, that is, by virtue of its single nature.
The messengers are also indivisible because of the indivisibility of all things;
therefore, he says: "the messengers" and "the two means."
There are two types of non-conceptuality regarding the means of accomplishment, as well as the female messengers. || 6 ||
One should accomplish it in two ways, for the messenger is indeed one alone;
however, the accomplishments (siddhis) are impelled through proximity to the means of accomplishment.
And he says that there are two things to be accomplished: "The means of accomplishment is indeed twofold:
mundane happiness, which is accompanied by affliction, and supramundane [happiness], which is free from affliction. For the portion consisting of the means is indeed one."
The word *hira* signifies absolute certainty.
To the question "What is this?", he says: "the female messengers" (*dūtayaḥ*).
The meaning is that for the sake of accomplishing both [goals], the female messengers alone are sufficient, and nothing else.
Since non-conceptuality will be accomplished through their grace, he asks, "Whence comes their grace? and replies, "Being impelled.
Their grace is as previously described; such is their intention.
They have been brought face-to-face by means of the sādhana for the purpose of being present during the accomplishment of both types of siddhi.
At that time, the reality (tattva) belonging to him is indivisible.
Reality is its very nature, which is indivisible; its messengers are also two,
meaning there are two means of accomplishment.
The equipment of merit and the yoginīs belong to one who is practicing and accomplishing the two types of siddhi.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "for the messengers are indeed one": the messengers constitute a single means (*sādhana*).
This is because, according to an alternative reading, they are the cause for bringing about proximity to those [goddesses] who are the accomplishments (*siddhi*). And here:
There is an addition in the text: "The sites of the fields are perfected, and the ḍākinīs are assembled there;
staying in that place, one should perform recitation, and in one spot, one should obtain the sacrificial pap (caru)."
“They play there” —
this passage is to be introduced as follows:
he says “made in the heart,” referring to the words beginning with “field” (*kṣetra*).
He should take food; he should eat. || 7 ||
One who has been consecrated on a festival day of the Guru, who is well-equipped with the ritual instruments,
who has correctly instructed the messengers, and who is habituated to the application of mudrās.
He says that one who has indeed received initiation is "dear to the Yoginīs," beginning with the words "guru" and so forth.
"Guru-parva" refers to the specific rites such as the water-consecration and others, which have arrived in succession through the lineage transmitted from teacher to teacher.
"By them, [he was] consecrated.

"Consecrated" means the act of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). That which possesses appropriate and fitting [implements] such as the preceptor's seat and so forth, for which the consecration has been performed, is described in that way.
"Śaiṣyaka" refers to one who is worthy of respect;
"suyantrita" means well-restrained;
"susaṃvara" means well-guarded.
In the reading *sumantritam*, it means the mantra has been recited;
and in the alternative reading *samanvitam*, it means that the tradition has been properly obtained. Thus, it is said that the messengers have been correctly instructed.
The messengers have spoken well:
"By means of the disciple's own nature, the disciple [is known] through the specific qualities of his character."
Because there is no difference between these two;
and thus, such a yogi is beloved by the Yoginīs—this is the intended meaning. Why is this so? He says: "and one whose habit is the union with the Mudrās."
Because the knowledge of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) has been attained through the union with the *mudrā*, it is to be enjoyed by him;
therefore, the letter *ca* (and) is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*). || 8 ||
Here [in this world], the body of complete knowledge is complete; there [in the state of liberation], that which is born of the body is complete.
Having risen in the morning, the one whose self is consciousness should make the body whole once again.
In this context, Śrī Heruka is the embodiment of complete gnosis; one who knows that becomes [Heruka].
"Complete" refers to those born from the body therein. This is without case endings.
And there is protracted pronunciation.
He explains the sequence of meditation for the sake of becoming Śrī Heruka, beginning with "In the morning" and so forth;
"prātaḥ" means at dawn.
Having arisen from his bed, he becomes one whose self is mind (*cittātmā*).
That is to say, he is one whose very self or essential nature (*svarūpa*) is nothing but mind (*cittamātra*). Why?
Having said "having done thus," he says:
"having shattered the body.
By means of the weapon of wisdom, [one shatters] the body consisting of the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth.
The intended meaning is that one should meditate on emptiness by dividing [the object] into parts. || 9 ||
One should practice the "anointing" scriptures situated within the body;
having thus purified the body, one should then utter the pervasive mantra.

To explain what precedes this, he says: "One should practice the anointings and the scriptures residing within the body. Scriptures (*śāstrāṇi*) are so called because sentient beings (*sattvāḥ*) are taught (*śiṣyante*) by them; thus, they are the Tathāgatas.
One should understand that those [senses] such as the eye, which reside within the body,
are established as being ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Alternatively, there are six auxiliary sciences of the Vedas (*vedāṅga*): phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), etymology (*nirukta*), metrics (*chandovicitis*), and astronomy (*jyotiṣa*).
He has transcended these.
The meaning is that those [limbs] do not become accessible to it. Regarding "pavitrī" and so forth:
following the purification of the aggregates and so on, by means of emptiness...
He is indeed purified.
One should utter the mantra: "Om, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature. One should recite it. He refers to the yogi.
It is "stretched" (*tata*) and "widely stretched" (*vitata*) because it is taught in various tantras. || 10 ||
One established in yoga should demonstrate the stages of yoga and must not transgress the scriptures;
the practitioner should not revile others, nor should he overstep those who are engaged in the practice.

The "stations of yoga" (yogasthānāni) mean the stations of meditative absorption (samādhisthānāni), that is, the stations of the two armor-mantras (kavacadvayasthānāni). "One should show" means that one should preside over them with their respective mantras or with the deities born from them.
And thus, only a mere indication of the method of cultivation has been shown. One should not transgress the scriptures;
one should not transgress the yoginīs.
Alternatively, some say that these are the symbols of the deities (*devatācihna*).
The intention is that a practitioner of yoga (*caryāyogin*), for the sake of play, might even maintain the meaning of the Vedas through occasional jesting;
however, the initiate (*samayin*) must not revile them.

Regarding the word "nara" (man): the meaning is that the initiate (*samayin*) and the practitioner of yoga (*caryāyogin*) should not revile [others] but should generate a [virtuous] thought. "One should not transgress against those who are devoted" refers to those devoted to the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara*. || 11 ||
One who seeks liberation and desires that goal should enjoy happiness with them and practice the conduct of the *samaya*, even if confusion should arise. (12)
"By them" means by the *yoginīs*. "Bliss" refers to the bliss of sexual union and so forth. "Seeking liberation" means seeking that [bliss] for the sake of liberation.
And seeking pleasure, having performed the gestures described in the treatises on love (*kāmaśāstra*), he should sleep together with them; such is the connection [of the sentence]. *Vaibhramam*.
"Born of dalliance" (*vilāsasaṃbhūtam*).
It is called "fitting" (*yujyate*) because it is appropriate;
the meaning is that one should perform whatever action is intended.
And if they long for such activity, then it shall be so—meaning, until that time. || 12 ||
And at night he should always remain naked, and he should always be smeared with black and red [pigments]. His clothing should consist of animal parts, as well as a necklace and bracelets. (13)
Adorned with earrings, a sacred thread, and a garland of skulls,
he has a necklace upon his neck and a girdle that makes a jingling sound.

Adorned with a crown of matted locks and a headband, falsely decorated with hair and other ornaments, [he holds] a vajra and a lotus, and makes the sound of the *khaṭvāṅga* and the *ḍamaru* with the syllable *HŪṂ*. (15)
"During the night," and so forth.
"Black and red" means the black fortnight and the red [fortnight].
The necklace and other ornaments are fashioned from human hair, as is the crest-lock (*cūḍā*).
A collection of bracelets,
a sacred thread, and a girdle fashioned from hair;
with her jingling sounds, such as those of the *ghurghurā* and anklets.
The meaning is that one should wear a necklace and so forth. "Jaṭāmakuṭa" refers to a crown of matted hair.
"Aṅkapaṭṭa" refers to a hero's sash.
"Adorned with false hair and so forth" means fashioned from the hair, yak-tail whisks, and other materials of others. [This refers to] the verse marked by the *vajra*.
He is so called because he abides together with the skull-cup, the vajra-lotus, the vajra-khaṭvāṅga, the sound of the ḍamaru drum, and the utterance of the syllable HŪṂ. (13–15)
One who desires happiness should move about happily, adorned with the three armors of all the heroes and yoginīs, clothed in garments made of animal skins. 16.

The "all-heroic" (*sarvavīra*) refers to the three wheels (*cakratraya*) wherein all heroes reside; the *yoginīs* of that [system] are Pracaṇḍā and the others. The meaning is that these [deities] are to be meditated upon by that practitioner (*yogin*).
For this very reason, he is adorned with the three armors (*kavacatraya*).
The three wheel-turning goddesses constitute the triple armor because they repel the weapons of Māra;
the intention is that [the practitioner] is endowed with the nature of the thirty-six deities. [This applies to] the limbs of living beings—
"Vāsasāvāsam" means:
it should be understood that one should make one's dwelling with a garment of hide. "Vāsas" refers to clothing or a covering.
This is the meaning.
The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
He provides the instruction for one who "should experience pleasure together with them": "and one who seeks pleasure... [the rest of the verse follows].
But it is happiness. || 16 ||
Having completely cast off the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), the practitioner intent on accomplishment should maintain purity as established by Śrī Heruka, bound by the five mudrās. (17)
Adorned with a necklace, bracelets, earrings, and a crest-jewel,
he always wears the sacred thread and ashes.
At night, one should always practice openly, but during the day, one should act in secret;
thus, with well-guarded ritual action and knowledge, and free from weariness, one becomes truly tranquil.

And purity should be known as threefold, established within one's own stream [of being], free from the distinctions of caste and non-caste, and devoid of the binding of tufts of hair, crests, and the like. (20)
"And having completely abandoned the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta), [one attains] purity as established in Śrī Heruka.

The particle *ca* is used for the purpose of inclusion (*samuccaya*) of what has not been explicitly mentioned. The intended meaning is that one abandons the purity produced by the sacrificial thread and other such items prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and instead abides in the purity established through the yoga of Śrī Heruka.
The practitioner, intent upon attaining accomplishment, should be bound by the five mudrās and adorned with a necklace,
bracelets, earrings, and a crest-jewel.
"The sacred thread and the ashes are to be worn at all times;
however, one should always wear them openly at night, and keep them concealed during the day."
"Action and knowledge well-guarded, free from agitation and exhaustion,
and the threefold purity should be known as established within one's own stream. Thus ends the additional text.
This is its meaning: the intention is that the activity is bound to the families of Vajra, Ratna, Padma, Karma, and Tathāgata. At night, it emerges manifestly, bound to the five families.
*Tu* has the sense of "exceedingly."
One should cause it to be well-concealed during the day; or rather, this is for the sake of a restrictive rule,
so that there may be no fault regarding the rejection of sentient beings.
Through ritual action and service, one attains knowledge and the knowledge of innate bliss, which is well-guarded;
one becomes tranquil, compassionate, and free from weariness.

And his purity is threefold, which consists in the non-restraint of the arising of passion and so forth; or else, it is that which will be described hereafter, beginning with "the role of the messenger" (*dūtya*). Therefore:
"Established in one's own stream, which is one's own mind.
"Varṇas" refers to the Brāhmaṇas and so forth; "avarṇas" refers to the outcastes (antya-jas). "Mukham" (the mouth).
The primary [is the main point]; that which is implied is the secondary.
"Tuft" (śikhā) means a crest; by the word "etcetera," the girdle of muñja grass, ashes, matted hair, and so forth are included. "Devoid of their binding" means devoid of their wearing. || 17-20 ||
First, the office of the messenger; second, the Soma sacrifice is desired;
and third, the consumption [of the Soma] in one place is called purification. || 21 ||
From the diligent maintenance of this purity, the purification of purity arises;
and for the yogi who has attained it through gradual stages, what accomplishment would not come to pass? (22)
He states another form of purification: "But the female messenger," and so forth.
*Dūtyaṃ* means "the female messenger" (*dūtī*);
there is the elision of one *bindu*. [The word] *somaṃ* [is used].
Soma is the *bodhicitta*.
That which is consumed in one place is the meaning of "caru" (*carum*). Thus, it is called *caru*.
If even a single drop is omitted,
that constitutes the third impurity. By the gradual attainment of purity through the maintenance of this purification, for whom would success not be achieved?

"It is born. By the thorough observance of these purifications, having attained purity through purification, for whom would the accomplishment of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā-siddhi) not arise? || 21-22 ||
That which was stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* has been likewise stated in the *Cakrasaṃvara*,
fully explained in the *Guhyatantra*, and similarly in the *Paramādya* and the *Mahāvajrabhairava*, bestowing the accomplishments of recitation, vows, and so forth.
The mantra practitioner shall accomplish this very thing in an instant through meditation alone. || 24 ||
"Saṃvara" refers to the *Saṃvarottara*. "Guhyatantra" refers to the *Guhyakośa* and other such works.
"Tathā" means "without restraint. "Eva" is used for emphasis. The particle "ca" serves to aggregate [the preceding] conduct.

The vow (*vrata*) and the recitation (*japa*) constitute the observance (*niyama*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the restraint of the senses (*indriyanigraha*) and other such practices are included; thus, she who bestows success through these means is the deity who grants success in the vow, recitation, and other rites.
The collective meaning is that in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other such works, accomplishment is attained through recitation and so forth;
however, here in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*, this very meditation on Śrī Heruka alone is the great [accomplishment].
The intention is that it accomplishes the siddhi of the mudrās; for this very reason, the yogi shall accomplish [it] in an instant. (23–24)
But for those devoted to the path of yoga, this is the purification they should practice;
the merit of such purifications cannot be described by even one person. (25)
Praising purity itself, he says: "By yoga," and so forth.
Yoga is the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in mind-only (*cittamātra*).
That alone is perfect awakening (*saṃbodhi*).
Among the paths for those devoted to that [practice], one should perform this Śrī Heruka yoga, which is the purification previously described.
He states the purpose of purification with the words beginning "of purifications," and so forth.
The female messengers and others are called "purifications" because they are the causes of purification.
The merit derived from them cannot be expressed by a single mouth. || 25 ||
The practitioner is the expansion of qualities; his face consists of many hundreds of thousands of mouths.
He is the purification of the great wisdom of Śrī Heruka, the means for accomplishing all characteristics. || 26 ||
He asks "Why? and says: "Because the practitioner is extensive in virtues.
Since the practitioner is one who is expanded by the quality of purity (*śauca*), he asks "By what means is it possible? and says: "But the mouth is manifold."
He says that when there are many mouths, then it is possible;
[the word] "mouth" is used in the singular by way of genus (*jāti*).
He states that even duality and so forth possess multiplicity by saying "thousand-faced" (*sahasrānanam*).
A thousand-counted face is "thousand-faced," meaning there are a thousand faces.
To the question, "Why is the practitioner such [as this]? he says:
"Śrī," and so forth. Śrī Heruka himself is great gnosis (*mahājñāna*), which is pure and free from afflictions (*niṣkleśa*).
That in which all the characteristics of qualities such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) reside is "possessing all characteristics" (*sarvalakṣaṇa*).
The meaning is that the conjunction with that [object] is likewise of such a nature. || 26 ||
And for the practitioner, the drinking of the water of bliss and non-duality itself;
by that, the self of non-dual yoga becomes pure and a destroyer of sins.
Regarding the phrase "and for the practitioner":
Because: "The water of bliss of the practitioner is the *bodhicitta*; in its consumption..."—this should be construed as:
"one whose self is the yoga of non-duality through the consumption of the water of bliss, being liberated from all sins. Why?
Thus he says: "It is pure and destroys sin. The meaning is that the water of bliss is of such a nature. || 27 ||
Freed from all sins by the mere touch or even by the speech [of this mantra], that best of men conducts himself with a pure body, free from disease. (28)
With a self purified of all evil, one shall obtain the glory of the Tathāgatas;
likewise, through successive births, one is born into the families of the Tathāgatas. (29)
"From touching or even from conversing" means with the practitioner.
"All sins," such as the five crimes of immediate retribution and so forth.
"A purified body" means free from affliction.
It should be understood that it is called the "pure body" because it is free from affliction;
that "a person practices the water of bliss" is easily understood.
In birth after birth, he is born into the family of the Tathāgata. || 28-29 ||
Having thus always performed worship, one should devotedly offer the bali-oblation;
the yogi then performs his actions according to his own will and becomes a righteous king.
"Thus, 'worship' means that one should worship the yoginīs and offer a bali; as for when that should be offered, he says:"
"It should be given.
This refers to the performance of the bali offering.
"Svecchāni" means one's own desired rites, such as those for pacification (śāntika) and so forth. || 30 ||

And the bali offering as well as the worship should be given according to the prescribed rule, on whichever tenth lunar day (daśamī) occurs during either the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight. (31)
These Vajra goddesses are to be worshipped with great effort by means of intoxicants and even meats.
When they are worshipped by a person of devotion who has attained delight in Śrī Heruka, they become satisfied in mind and grant boons, for the boons are held in their hands. (32)
At night, the observer of the vow, with hair loose and naked, should offer the bali-oblation;
through yoga, being the very self of Śrī Heruka, he propitiates the Mothers. (33)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Offering and Bali of the Conduct Vow," in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
The procedure here is as stated in another tantra; it specifies the particular times for worship with the words "on the black [fortnight]," and so forth.
By the word "or," the ninth and fourteenth days are also included.
The word "tu" has the sense of specification or the sense of conjunction;
alternatively, there is a variant reading: "on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, but on [the fourteenth] of the bright fortnight."
The word "tu" (but/and) includes both the tenth and the ninth days.
Regarding the phrase "the remainder which": it refers to whichever day is the tenth or the ninth.
Thus, worship should be performed on the fourteenth day, as well as on the tenth and the ninth.
What else? He says:
"In these [states], the Vajra goddesses are to be worshipped with effort by means of intoxicants and even meats.
When they are worshipped by a person possessed of devotion who has attained delight in Śrī Heruka..."

"Those whose minds are contented become givers of boons, for then boons are held in their hands. Thus, on these lunar days (tithis), one should exert effort in worship; "held in their hands" means that the desired boons (*varāḥ*) are within reach. The rest is easily understood. (31–34)
That [chapter] in which the conduct, vows, worship, and offerings are prescribed is thus [described];
it is the twenty-seventh,
the twenty-seventh.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛtti*. || 27 ||
The twenty-eighth chapter, on the procedure for the unity of the colors of the internal fire-oblation;
thereafter,
the practitioner whose self is thoroughly purified should worship the supreme Self.
Nirvāṇa is the one who has emerged as the Hero, worshipped by all the Buddhas and others. || 1 ||
He speaks the chapter on Equanimity (Samatāpaṭala), beginning with "Then, worship" (tataḥ pūjā) and so forth.
The word *tataḥ* should also be understood here in the sense of "thereupon"; alternatively, the change to *u* [in *tato*] is due to its being an archaic (ārṣa) form.
Since perfect enlightenment cannot occur without equanimity (*samatā*), the meaning is that one should worship oneself.
One whose self (*ātman*) is purified by means of external and secret worship is "one of perfectly pure self" (*suviśuddhātman*).
What kind of self?
He said: "Nirvāṇa is the departed hero.
Nirvāṇa is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*), because external objects of the intellect are no longer perceived;
immediately after that, one has gone with certainty.
"One should worship him while remaining [in that state]" means that through the worship of practice, one worships the self—the mind—abiding in innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
Alternatively, "gone" means having attained innate bliss by way of its incomparability; the self has gone, that is, it has realized.

Those of unrefined intellect mock him who, without [receiving] instruction, points to the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*) as being prior to innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*), failing to understand that joy of cessation.
For they, perceiving the "cessation" to be the emission of the *bodhicitta*, deceive themselves. By them, in this world...
Innate bliss is not perceived;
however, for the sake of guarding one's own mind, one should remain vigilant.
What would happen then?
To this he says: "All," and so forth.
The meaning is that all the Buddhas and others become worshipped when [he] is worshipped.
"All the Buddhas and others" means...
Due to the elision of the nominative plural ending,
when the vowel *ā* in the word "pūjita" is shortened,
[it becomes] "buddha-sahajānandajñānam."
Thus, it is established that he is called "Buddha" because he has awakened within his own self.
Regarding the reading "worshipped by all Buddhas and others," it follows that he is worshipped by the entire assembly of Buddhas and so forth. || 1 ||
The yoginīs of Sarvavīra—both the stationary and the moving, as well as the brothers and attendants established in the union with Soma—one should worship. (2)
Furthermore, he says "all indeed is Buddha," beginning with the word "sarva.
Regarding the phrase "of the All-Hero" (*sarvavīrasya*), it is the first plural form.
This is the state of being (*bhāva*). The immobile consists of trees and so forth;
the mobile consists of humans and so forth.
This is the worship of reality (*tattvapūjā*).
"One should honor the brothers and their followers"— here, "but" (*tu*) is used as a conjunction; the "brothers" are those together with the disciples (*śrāvaka*).

They are called "wanderers" (*cāra*) because they move while remaining established in their own tradition (*svāgama*). They are "established in union with the moon" (*somasaṅgamasaṃsthitāḥ*); "union" (*saṅgama*) refers to yoga with the moon, which is the *bodhicitta*, and they abide therein with equanimity.
The nominative case is used here in the sense of the locative.
The meaning is that one should worship them as well. || 2 ||
Together with one's brother or son, regarding the arising of pleasure and pain,
one should not reveal knowledge there, nor likewise mantra and mudrā.
"Regarding the arising of happiness and suffering together with one's brothers and sons, one should not reveal the knowledge there"—
the connection is that one should not reveal the knowledge to those brothers.
It is equal to that of his brothers, sons, and certain friends, along with their knowledge; moreover,
since this knowledge arises together with pleasure and pain as "this" and "that," it remains nevertheless unstained by those two, for it is the essence of happiness.
Because it is a constituent part of suffering as presented here;
and although it is common [to all], it is uncommon because it is perceivable only by those who are skillful.
This is the ultimate truth—
It is "non-illumination" because it is impossible to illuminate [the truth].
It is "interpolation" because even they insert their own compositions into the scriptures (*āgama*).
It is "corrupter of all" because it defiles the fruits of all actions and so forth.

The sense is that one should not reveal this even to these two. Because of excessive association with them, because of their opposition to one's true nature (*prakṛti*), and because of showing them contempt, they go to hell;
therefore, they do not even deserve the status of disciples.
Thus it should be understood.
Another meaning is stated: the brother is Ānanda, because he is the conventional designation for the Dharma;
the son is Paramānanda.
The one-and-a-half [joy] is the sound of cessation (*viramānanda*).
It is so called because its arising and abiding consist in the equanimity of pleasure and pain;
this is innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
In that regard, innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*) does not manifest as an agent,
because of the absence of manifestation;
nor does it manifest itself.
One should rest [in that state], because of the contradiction of action within one's own self.

The discernment that "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done" is the act of casting [the mind) away. The meaning is that the mass of afflictions such as passion, which corrupts everything, and all things such as the body do not exist therein; thus, it is characterized by innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
This very point is stated again and again,
because this alone is the means for accomplishing the supreme goal of human life.
One who has performed the conduct of the observance (samayācāra) should always consume the sacrificial offering (caru);
one should not give the mantra to anyone, nor should one destroy the oral instruction.
One should give instruction according to the truth to those who abide by the samaya;
however, one should not, deluded by passion, abandon the dūtī and go to another.
"Caru, and so forth" refers to the five purifying nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
To the question "What is the purpose of consuming them?", he replies: "It is for the sake of performing the conduct of the pledge (*samayācāra*)."
Thus [it is said]. The convention (*samaya*) is characterized by the "chewing of the cow" (*gokudana*).
By what reason? He says: "always" (*sada*). "Always" (*sat*) means abiding (*sadana*); from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of cause (*hetau*).
For the power of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs is indeed inconceivable.
"Mantra" refers to the mantra and so forth.
"Of someone" refers to a king or similar person.
"One should not destroy the instruction" means that one who has been requested even once should not [act] out of greed.
One should give the initiation and so forth;
however, one should give the instruction according to the actual meaning.
Therefore, the word "tu" (however) indicates a distinction.
The messenger (dūtī) is one who observes the pledges (samayinī).
The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction, while "tu" (but/then) is for emphasis.
Deluded by desire, would this man not go to some particular woman? || 4-5 ||
The protection of the messenger always leads to liberation; even if she has transgressed, one should feed her.
One should not show her disrespect, even if she remains one of low birth.
"Protection of the messenger is always liberation":
protection (*rakṣā*) of the messenger (*dūtī*), that is, the external woman (*bāhyāṅganā*), consists of her armor (*kavaca*).
By means of her, all [obstacles] are seized.
Tranquility. Alternatively, through subjugation, the messenger must be made incapable of going elsewhere; this is the protection of the messenger.
Then follows liberation through the constant pursuit of reality.
Some say this is because of the scriptural injunction: "One should not eat what has been left over by others.
Others maintain that for the female messengers (dūtīs) born of the Tathāgata family, their protection consists in public service.
"One should also feed [her] even after passing [others]" means that since the female messengers (dūtīs) are held in high esteem,
one should not show such respect toward them during sexual union.
One should provide her with the pleasure of sexual union even by means of seizing her hair and so forth;
therefore, it says: "One should certainly not show formal respect."

"Having overcome them by force, one should enjoy [them]; those are not meals taken with formal hospitality"—from this statement, it follows that even one of low birth may be enjoyed for pleasure. || 6 ||
If a mother, sister, daughter, or wife stand as messengers,
one's austerity will certainly diminish, or else the obstacles and the supernatural powers will become crooked.
He states when success (*siddhi*) occurs: "When [they are] like a mother," and so forth.
The meaning is that when they become affectionate like a mother and others, then there is success.
However, he says that when they become crooked, then even the successes are crooked: "Austerity," and so forth. [This refers to] beginningless...
Austerity performed over time goes to ruin. Why? He says: "Or crookedly" (*vakram vā*). "Vā" means "because."
Since the heart of the messenger (dūtī) is crooked, likewise the accomplishments (siddhis) also become crooked; that is to say, they turn away. || 7 ||

One should attract [the deity] together with the supreme [consort]; such is the certainty regarding the ritual substance. In this world, one who follows the left-hand path (vāmācāra) should always step forward with the left foot first.
Regarding such a messenger, he says "one should attract" and so forth.
That which is the supreme *bodhicitta* accompanied by *rajas* (the seminal essence);
therefore, it is "more than half."
Thus, "the determination of the substance" means that the substance is the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), and its faultless grasping is the determination.
In this world, one who follows the Vāmācāra path should always step forward with the left foot first; this is easily understood. || 8 ||
Turning with the left hand, honoring with the left raised;
merely taking with the left, as well as satisfying and consuming with the left. || 9 ||

"Turning with the left hand" means turning the body while remaining steady with the left hand. "Worshippers of the upward-left" means that by the word "upward" (*ūrdhva*), the *vajra* is intended; thus, the yogins are those who worship according to the intention of the yoginīs. "Left," and so forth.
This is easily understood. || 9 ||

One who does not destroy his vows, who is perfected in his observances, a practitioner intent on what has been done, and who eats the sacrificial porridge (caru) together with those of his own lineage according to the Kula tradition and the rules of conduct—[he is a true initiate]. || 10 ||

"One who does not destroy his vows, one whose vows are fulfilled": non-vows (*avrata*) refer to the vows of the Brahmins and others; these are the rules of conduct established by convention and so forth once [the path] has been undertaken.
He is devoted to the meditation on the deities and so forth, having made that his primary focus.
The *samayas* are the *yoginīs*, and the *kulācāra* is the practice. In a certain single location, he is one who partakes of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*). || 10 ||
The practice of the five castes is proclaimed as the four castes;
the practice of the single caste is the worshiper who has attained perfection in yoga.

One who practices and partakes among the five castes is called "one who practices among the five castes" (*pañcavarṇasamācāra*). Why? Because it is proclaimed that he is "not of the four castes" (*acaturvarṇa*).
He for whom the four castes do not exist is such a yogi;
this is because they are merely conceptual constructs in the world.
One who has become thus is celebrated and described as being in the midst of the yoginīs.
Alternatively, he is "of four castes" (caturvarṇa) because he possesses the four castes; this refers to his state as the yogin of the four-faced Śrī Heruka.
The substitution of *u* for *o* occurs due to Vedic archaism (*ārṣatva*).

To the question "From what [source] does the state of having no four castes arise?", he says: "One whose conduct and determination regarding the castes are of a single nature is 'one whose conduct regarding the castes is unified' (ekavarṇasamācāra).
Even while being a practitioner of Śrī Heruka, [he remains so] by virtue of that unity."
The meaning is that through the purity of conduct regarding the [four] castes, one attains the state of being the mouth of the four castes. || 11 ||
Using cow flesh, horse flesh, dog flesh, and that of variegated animals, one should construct a triangular mandala; by this, even a Buddha will certainly perish.
He describes the expansion of ritual action for the purpose of destroying those who harm the Three Jewels and others, out of fear [of them]: "With beef," and so forth.
The sacrificial pit and other requirements should be prepared according to the prescribed method suitable for the fire offering (*homa*).

Having kindled a fire with pungent oils and other materials used for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), one should visualize Khaṇḍarohā entering within through the right nostril and emerging via the path of excretion; then, by means of her—
bearing the marks of the vajra-hook and the knife— one [should seize] the naked and agitated [sādhya].

Having drawn him in with that very [mantra] and visualized him as being cut into pieces, one who forms the mental impression that "this meat is beef" and so forth kills him by releasing [the mantra] with great wrath and ego-inflation.
One should perform the oblation with the root mantra using variegated chickens and the like. || 12 ||
The meal of the heroes, accompanied by mantra and mudrā, is likewise the emanation of Śrī Heruka; it is an offering devoid of [worldly] treatises. (13)

One should constantly perform the retention [of the mantra] and provide protection through every action; one should practice yoga as non-dual knowledge, and the mind should remain fixed on the single point. || 14 ||
An external woman consists of mudrā and mantra; it is said that eating together with her is praised for those heroes—beginning with the words "mantra" and so forth.
This means being endowed with both mantra and mudrā, and being endowed with equality through mantra.
In that regard, during the meal, one should perform the ritual service (*upacāra*) of Śrī Heruka’s emanation within oneself and of the goddesses toward the yoginīs;
and this is [taught] in all the Yoginī Tantras.

He says "the desired [subject] to be spoken" with the words beginning "Śrīheruka," and so forth. Furthermore, he says "the maintenance," and so forth, to indicate that at other times as well, one must constantly maintain the yoga of Śrī Heruka.
"Yogam" means of yoga; "yoga" is a qualifier of *dhāraṇā*, meaning that which possesses yoga. "Advayajñāna" [means non-dual knowledge].
Because one knows the non-duality of Śrī Heruka, it is "tattva" (reality); and because it is "cetas" (mind), there is thus the state of being a single word [tattvacetaḥ]. || 13-14 ||
So that he may achieve success without obstacles, no one else is as renowned in this matter as his divine female messenger (dūtī), who is excellent, diligent, and accompanied by her retinue. (15)

He says "nirvighna" and so forth, [meaning]: no other means is perceived for the sake of accomplishment than this which is free from obstacles. And her messenger (*dūtī*)—the most excellent and supreme one who is of such a nature—is divine and fit for accomplishment;
she is endowed with patience. (15)
One who is unattached [attains] the state of separation from the substances of yoga through the union of passion;
one who is devoted to the teacher’s instruction is equal to Kubera, the giver of wealth, for that purpose. 16.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, the procedure for the unity of colors in the internal fire offering, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
"Unattached through union with passion":
having encountered external union with passion, the yogi should always remain unattached—that is, dispassionate.

Yoga is *samādhi* (meditative absorption), and *bhakṣya* is the substance to be consumed; he is so called because he possesses a distinction between those two, namely yoga and the consumption [of the substance].
Its state is to be understood as the differentiation of the substance of yoga;
or alternatively, it is the differentiation of the substance born of yoga, which is the bodhicitta.

The meaning of "vibhāgatā" (the state of being divided) is that one possesses a share in enjoyment together with wisdom (*prajñā*). It is "vibhāga" because its portion (*bhāga*) is in a particular state; the abstract state of that is "vibhāgatā. He says "guru... and so forth, [meaning] that yogins who are devoted to the teacher’s instruction may come into being.
The intention is that they may become passionately devoted to the instruction on the yoga of Śrī Heruka given by the gurus;
therefore, because they seek that [instruction], they are "tadarthāḥ" (those who have that as their purpose).
Furthermore, "wealth" refers to faith and the other [perfections].
Thus it is said: "The wealth of faith, the wealth of wisdom, the wealth of learning, the wealth of vigor, the wealth of joy, the wealth of meditative concentration, and the wealth of mindfulness.
He gives these to those who possess desire by invariably accomplishing their aims; therefore, Śrī Heruka is the "Giver of Wealth," and those equal to him are likewise so called. (16)

Because it prescribes the internal fire-sacrifice (*adhyātmahoma*), its exclusion from worldly fire-sacrifices, and the unity of the castes (*varṇaikatva*), this chapter is designated as such; thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, the "Chapter on the Internal Fire-Sacrifice, the Unity of Castes," in the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 28.
The twenty-ninth chapter: The Procedure for the Characteristics, Powers, and States of the Female Messengers (Dūtī).
Now, furthermore, the knowledge of the characteristics of the female messengers is fully explained, by which one correctly recognizes the Ḍākinīs who abide by the sacred pledge (samaya).
Since there is no conduct (*caryā*) without the practice of "heat" (*ūṣmakriyā*), he speaks this chapter in order to explain its meaning, beginning with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth.
"Now" means immediately after the explanation of the internal fire-oblation (*adhyātmika-homa*) and other such practices.
"Other" (*apara*) refers to another accomplishment (*niṣpādana*).
He asks, "What is that? and replies: "It has been enumerated. The meaning is that another enumeration has been made.

To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "By knowing the characteristics of the messenger (dūtī). This is for the sake of knowing those characteristics, by which one correctly understands that the ḍākinīs abide by the pledge (samaya).
The nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
In an instant, she sees her brother, her father, or even her husband—she who has a thick tongue, tawny eyes, a harsh voice, and reddish-brown hair. (2)
He beholds his brother, the hero, his father, the Lord Śrī Heruka; for him, the Lord himself [bestows] lordship, in an instant, through the power of mantra. "Sthūla" and so forth.
She whose eyes are tawny is thus [described];
she is rough to the touch; she whose hair—meaning her locks—is tawny is thus [described]. || 2 ||
She is common to all accomplishments, always devoted to recitation and vows;
she is endowed with mindfulness and possesses the status of a messenger and so forth.
He says that it is common to all accomplishments: "It is general for all siddhis.
Recollection is *cintā*; being joined with that is "continuous application" (*samanuyoga*).
To whose thought [does this belong]? He says: "By the messenger," and so forth.
"Endowed with words" means, by implication, the preservation of the *samaya*.
"Step" means knowledge; endowed with that and joined with recollection—by this it is stated by one intent on the *samaya* that the meditation upon the *dūtī* must be performed. || 3 ||
The twenty-four supreme ḍākinīs bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
one who seeks to accomplish all desires and aims should constantly recite the root mantra. (4)
And from this, the mantra is born, which bestows the fruit of the play of yoga, pacifies all Māras, and [pervades] the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving. || 5 ||
Regarding how many such messengers (dūtīs) there are, he says: "The twenty-four supreme Ḍākinīs bestow the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
By way of illustration, this refers to the twenty-four Ḍākinīs beginning with Pracaṇḍā;
however, here it should be understood that the twelve are also included.
He states for what purpose they are to be cultivated: enjoyment (*bhukti*) consists of heaven and so forth;
liberation (*mukti*) is the removal of the bonds such as the afflictions (*kleśa*). These are the two fruits.
They are so called because they bestow [attainments] pre-eminently.

Regarding them—those residing within the mandala of the Lord Śrī Heruka—it is said that one should recite the root mantra through their meditative cultivation; thus he says "the root," and so forth, which is easy to understand.
The three worlds are conquered and brought under control;
for this very reason, they bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 4-5 ||
The practitioner who is devoted to accomplishment and endowed with both mantra and mudrā attains success;
for embodied beings, a mantra devoid of mudrā does not bring about the presence [of the deity]. (6)
To the question "Why is it so?", he says: "Mantra," and so forth.
Mantra is speech that impels the reality (tattva);
mudrā is the deity; [the state arises] from these two.
One who is endowed with the goal to be accomplished and is intent upon its attainment becomes a practitioner (*sādhaka*).
To the question, "Why is the mantra alone not recited?
he says: "The mudrā," and so forth.
The presence and direct realization described as belonging to the divine state do not occur—
that is, they are not attained—
by the embodied practitioner (yogin) merely through connection with a particular body. || 6 ||
It must be understood through diligent application, just as the practice of "heat" (ūṣman) occurs within oneself;
[this applies] to those who hate Mahāyoga, which accomplishes all desires and goals.
Having passed through a hundred births as a dog, one is even born among the Caṇḍālas;
just as someone seeking butter might, out of faith, churn water.
Yet ghee is not produced; there is only physical exhaustion.
Otherwise, the wearing of auspicious ornaments and even worship would be in vain.
Because it is the cause of the means of livelihood, it is resorted to by those engaged in other practices;
or it is the land of Mahāyoga where the heroes dwell.
Even among beings who are Caṇḍālas or Mlecchas, one should designate that place as [one's own];
there I shall always abide for the sake of favoring those beings. (11)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the female messengers (*dūtī*), their powers, and their states, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

And that proximity to the mantra is to be understood and attained through *abhiyoga*—that is, through practice that is respectful, uninterrupted, and long-lasting. To explain what that very thing is, he says: "Just as in the nature of the *ūṣma-kriyā* [heat-stage]";
[referring to] the *sattva* for the purpose of the *vajra* in the context of pacification (*śāntika*).
Auspicious rites (*pauṣṭika*), malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), and so forth constitute its "heat" (*ūṣman*); their accomplishment is its "activity.
Just as that [activity] occurs within oneself, so too is there "capacity"; that is to say, it is precisely that capacity.
Against those who harm the Three Jewels, one's efficacy should be demonstrated by inflicting suffering and other penalties right here in this world.
Furthermore, he says "those who... and so forth, to show that the power of mantra exists even in the next world.
"Mahāyoga" refers to the yoga of Śrī Heruka. The remainder is easily understood.
He states "Just as... and so forth to show that there is no other means for accomplishing perfect enlightenment than Mahāyoga. Faith—

The meaning is that by means of such firm conviction, there is no result whatsoever from the practice of other forms of yoga. "Retention" refers to holding [the mind] because another form of yoga is a cause of welfare;
or alternatively, it is like "worship," meaning it is indeed worship.
For example, he says "another yoga" to indicate that the practice of other yogas does not lead to the welfare of the next world;
furthermore, even the dwelling place of the glorious Heruka-yogins generates merit.
Thus he said: "Those who uphold the Great Yoga," and so forth.
Even a region such as that of the Caṇḍālas, if it is inhabited by heroes, one should consider even that region to be a truly auspicious land.
"For him"—that is, for the sake of favoring those sentient beings belonging to that land presided over by the illustrious Śrī Heruka, I remain forever. (7–11)

*Śakti* is the power of mantra. *Avasthā* (state) refers to abiding for the sake of sentient beings in a region inhabited by those fit for Śrī Heruka; it is the state of the power characterized by the *dūtī*. That which establishes these for the sake of knowledge is the *paṭala*, and thus it is so called. *Ūna-*...
The thirtieth [is] the twenty-ninth.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 29.
The thirtieth chapter: The Ritual for Extracting the Mantras of the Wall-Binding.
Now I shall describe another [method], the prastāra which is very difficult to obtain;
by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner swiftly achieves success.
Now, immediately after the arrangement for extracting the root mantra, I shall describe another arrangement (*prastāra*).
The phonemes (or *mātrās*) are spread out therein.
That which is spread out upon this is the *prastāra*; it consists of a continuous series of forty-nine grid-lines. Describing what kind of thing this is, he says: "extremely difficult to obtain."
Since the four-faced mantra is extracted from this [source], it is therefore called "that" (tathā).
To the question, "What is the specific distinction of the mantra itself that is to be extracted?", he says: "By which," and so forth.
"By which" means by the mantra.
"He who accomplishes swift success" means that by him there is the pacification of obstacles. || 1 ||
On a level and delightful plot of ground, having smeared it with sandalwood paste, which is fragrant with sweet scents and strewn with heaps of flowers; || 2 ||
In a place strewn with garlands of lamps and delightful with the fragrance of incense,
one should perform the ritual of self-protection (sakalīkaraṇa) and then carry out the binding of the directions (diśābandha).
Then, having formed a circular *murajabandha* with nine lines,
one who is well-composed should draw the individual letters and syllables and spread them out.
He asks, "Where should one spread [the seat]? and replies with the words beginning with "on the ground" (*bhūmi*).
By "sandalwood" and "the five nectars" (*pañcāmṛta*), what is intended is that which brings delight to one who knows its true nature.

"Sugandhagandha" refers to sandalwood and the like; the meaning is that the ground should be smeared with fragrant substances mixed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). "Puṣpasugandha" refers to flowers such as the *campaka* and others.
Incense refers to *piṇḍadhūpa* and the like.

In such a place, having meditated upon emptiness within the void, one should first perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) and so forth, and then spread out, that is, lay down, the mere syllables.
The phonemes (*varṇa*) are those beginning with *a* and those beginning with *ka*; "phonemes alone" means merely the phonemes.
Having done what? He says: "having inscribed."
Having superimposed [the letters] in the order of the vowels beginning with *a* and the consonants beginning with *ka* by means of equanimity,
he asks what must precede the very act of writing, and says: "muraja," etc.
A *prastāra* (metrical grid) whose arrangement of forms has a binding like that of a *muraja* (drum) is so described.
Then, due to the grasping of vowels and consonants in both forward and reverse order, there is a similarity to a drum (muraja) by virtue of its facing in all directions. || 2-4 ||
The practitioner should extract the Hero situated therein, which accomplishes all desires and goals;
he should [extract] the vowels and consonants in both direct and reverse order.
The hero is the mantra.
"The accomplisher of all desired aims" is an epithet of the mantra.
Why? Because from that [mantra], one should extract the hero—
He says: "The practitioner [should recite] the vowels and consonants in direct and reverse order. The vowels are *a* and so forth;
the consonants are *ka* and so forth, because they have the nature of sound (*dhvani*).
For one should rescue them from that. || 5 ||
One should cause this merit, included within this number, to belong to the Sage;
having gathered it in thirty-two compartments, it is then divided by the fifth.
"Included within this number" means that one should extract it in such a way that it falls within the number of the grid cells (*koṣṭhaka*).
Anticipating the question "By whose statement is this [stated]?", he says: "of the Sage" (*muneḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "having grasped the thirty-second cell":
the word *koṣṭha* is used here without a case ending. Starting from the cell presided over by the letter *ka*, one takes the thirty-second cell, which is presided over by the letter *sa*.
By counting starting from the letter *ka*, the letter *sa* itself is to be understood;
in all such cases, by the mention of a square (*koṣṭhaka*), the syllable situated within that square is to be taken.
This is because of its very utility.
Regarding the reading "the third of the chest" (koṣṭhatṛtīya), starting from that which is presided over by the palatal *śa*, the third [consonant] presided over by the dental *sa* is understood.
"But it is pierced by the fifth" means it is distinguished by the letter *u*. || 6 ||
Having taken half of half of one hundred (fifty), divided by twenty-four;
[this is] the thirty-sixth square, divided by three squares.
"Having taken up half of half of a hundred" means that,
starting from the square presided over by the letter *ka* and counting sequentially, one reaches the letter *ma*. Thus, it is "divided twenty-four times."
Likewise, the meaning is "beginning with that which is presided over by the letter *ka*. It is "divided twenty-fourfold," meaning the twenty-fourth [letter], which is *bha*.
By that, the lower portion is divided by half of a hundred [i.e., fifty].
The thirty-sixth cell is divided by three cells.
Starting from the one presided over by the letter *a*, the thirty-sixth is that which is presided over by the letter *na*.
The third consists of three compartments. Beginning with the compartment presided over by the letter *a*, it is divided by the letter *i*. (7)
Then, having taken thirty-two, it is divided by five;
then, having taken twenty-five, one should join them with twenty-four. (8)
"Then, having taken the thirty-second, it is pierced by the fifth cell.
"Then" (*tataḥ*) means starting from that which is presided over by the letter *ka*; "tu" (*then*) has the sense of "indeed" (*eva*) or is used as a conjunction (*samuccaye*).
In the same way, in the preceding case as well, one should take the twenty-fifth and join it with the twenty-fourth.
The "twenty-fifth" refers to the twenty-fifth [letter] presided over by the letter *ma*. "From that" means from the one presided over by the letter *ka*.
"Twenty-fourth" means the twenty-fourth letter, which is *bha*, and it is in the third case (instrumental).
The meaning is that one should join the letter *ma* at the lower part with the letter *bha*. || 8 ||
Taking thirty-three and adding fifteen to the storehouse,
when joined with the fifth, it is considered a most excellent and beautiful [arrangement].
"Having taken the thirty-three, it is honored by fifteen storehouses.
The word "thence" (*tataḥ*) is understood from the context.
[It is] presided over by the letter *ka*.
Beginning from the thirty-third [letter], which is presided over by *ha*;
beginning from the fifteenth, which is presided over by the *anusvāra* and presided over by *a*;
joined with the fifth—it is considered beautiful and supreme.

Its status as the fifth begins with its being empowered by the letter *a*. This seed-syllable is beautiful because of its efficacy in accomplishing all aims by means of the fifth [vowel], *u*. || 9 ||
"Taking all of this—namely, that which is joined with twenty-two and that which is twenty-seven—the first step is thus declared. (10)
"Endowed with the twenty-second, and likewise the twenty-seventh.
"The twenty-second" refers to the twenty-second [letter], which is presided over by the syllable *pha*.
Taking the twenty-seventh [consonant] presided over by the letter *a*, which is presided over by the letter *ṭa*—
having taken all of this,
it is the first word.
The first word is so called because the first mantra-sentence is uttered therein. || 10 ||
The nineteenth letter from the grid, conjoined with the son of fire (Ra),
and divided by three grids, becomes the syllable [Sa].
The eighth seed-syllable from the *ya*-group, joined with the thirty-sixth cell, and likewise the word [formed] in this manner, is the accomplisher of all desires and goals. (12)
"The nineteenth cell from the one presided over by Fire’s son, divided by the three cells of the fire. This means:
from the cell presided over by the letter *a*, the nineteenth is that presided over by the letter *ga*.
"Fire's son" refers to the letter *ra* (repha), as he has fire (*agni*) as his son. [The letter *a*...]
It is presided over by the letter *i* which is distinguished by three treasuries (*koṣṭha*),
and it is the thirty-sixth seed-syllable from the *ya*-group.
"Furthermore, the word is thus joined.
The letter *ya* and its class (*varga*) constitute the *ya*-class; from that, the eighth seed-syllable is *ha*.
Regarding "the thirty-sixth cell," this refers to the thirty-sixth cell starting from the one presided over by the vowel *a*, which is the cell presided over by the letter *na*. Furthermore—
Such is the word *pada*.
The particle *ca* (and) is used for conjunction (*samuccaya*) and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). || 11-12 ||
Then, taking the self-existent (Svayambhū) from the fifth chest [of consonants], adorned above with the bindu. || 13 ||
The second step is said to be named "Accomplisher of All Aims" (Sarvārthasādhaka);
it consists of nineteen squares and is divided by the twenty-seventh [line].
But when joined with the third [digit], it is auspicious and supremely beneficial when combined with the twenty-second [digit] and the second [digit] of the thirty-three-fold collection. || 15 ||
"Then, having taken the *svayambhū*": *svayambhū* is the letter *ha*. "From there" means from the word *gṛhṇa gṛhṇa*, that is, from the square (*koṣṭha*).
"Joined with the fifth" means that which is presided over by the letter *u*, which is the fifth [vowel] from the letter *a* (the first), and is adorned above by the *bindu*.
"Thus" [means]: here, it is not the case that there is a half-moon (ardhacandra) everywhere, because it is adorned with a mere dot (bindu).
