"The name which accomplishes all desires and aims" means it is well-known by this designation.
The syllable *phaṭ* is to be followed by the letter preceded by *bindu* (the nasal *m*) joined above;

from this [series], one takes the twenty-second and likewise the eleventh. According to a certain reading, these refer to the twenty-second letter presided over by *ka* (which is *pha*), and the eleventh letter presided over by *ṭa* (which is *ṭha*).
Thus, the syllable *phaṭ* is easily understood.
This is the second word.
Furthermore, the nineteen squares are divided by the twenty-seventh [syllable].
"Joined with the third" means:
the nineteenth [consonant], presided over by the letter *ga*, following that which is presided over by the letter *a*.
The particle *tu* is used for conjunction.
The twenty-seventh [letter], presided over by the letter *ra*,
having taken the thirty-third [letter] and joined it with the twentieth [letter] of the second cell, is the most excellent and supreme.

Regarding "beneficial" (*hitam*): from the thirty-third [letter] presided over by *ka*, [take] the second [letter] presided over by *a*, which is presided over by *ā*. From the one presided over by *ka*, [take] the twentieth, which is presided over by *na*. (13–15)
One should extract, with a well-concentrated mind, that which consists of twenty-one squares, joined with twenty-six, and likewise contains the position of double repetition.
"Likewise, [the mantra] consists of twenty-one squares and is joined with the twenty-sixth.
This means that the letter *pa* is to be taken from the position presided over by the twenty-first letter, *ka*.

The word *tu* signifies a conjunction (*samuccaya*). "In that manner" means [the letter] presided over by *ya*, which is the twenty-sixth [letter] following that which is presided over by *ka*. And the phrase "the term of double repetition" is likewise.
The second [type] is such a state in proximity; the meaning is "even by necessity. || 16 ||
Then, taking from the first square in reverse order,
it is joined with the end of the fourth [square], and likewise honored as the fifteenth.
Then, taking from the first square in reverse order,

it is joined with that which ends in the fourth [letter], thus being honored as the fifteenth. Then, by way of inversion, having first taken the letter *ha* itself from the first square of the grid which is presided over by *ha*.

The connection is that "the third word is spoken. From that which is presided over by the letter *a*, [comes] the fourth, which is presided over by the letter *ī*; its end is presided over by the letter *u*.
The rest is easily understood. || 17 ||
For those desiring dharma, artha, and mokṣa, the third word is said;
it is the second seed from the square, from the thirty-sixth square. (18)
The third word is "the word of Dharma and so forth"; another word must be supplied [to complete the phrase]. Here too, the syllable *phaṭ* should be carried over.
Thus ends the third word.
"The second seed from the *koṣṭha*," that is,
from that which is presided over by the letter *a*,
[one takes] that which is presided over by the letter *ā*.
The second seed-syllable belongs to the deities. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. [It is derived] from the thirty-six squares.

The meaning is that, starting from the square presided over by the letter *a* which is the thirty-sixth square, one should take the letter *na* itself from among those squares presided over by the letter *na*. || 18 ||
Likewise, the twenty-sixth is indeed called the fourth quarter;
taking the thirty-third, it is honored in the thirteenth square. (19)
It should be understood that the fourth word is spoken by taking the letter *na* [from the first word]; the remainder is easily understood. Thus it is the thirty-third.
The letter *ha*: "the thirteenth from the chest" means from that which is presided over by the vowel *a*. || 19 ||
The practitioner should take the tenth from the square [presided over by the letter *a*], moving in reverse order,
and likewise the nineteenth from that same square.
From the cell presided over by the letter *ka*, from the twenty-third cell;
it is joined with the second cell and adorned above with a *bindu*. (21)
Then, having likewise taken the eighth [syllable], which is the earthly element,
the wise one should cause it to be pierced by fire, joined with the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* at the end.
"The practitioner [is found] by reversing from the tenth square," meaning that from the one presided over by the letter *ha*,
the tenth is the one presided over by the letter *bha*.
The nineteenth from the square [beginning] with the letter *a*—
that is, from that which is presided over by the letter *a*—
is the letter *ga*.
Presided over by *rā*.
"From the twenty-third square" means from the twenty-third square starting from the one presided over by *ka*, which is the square of *ba*.
The meaning is that, being presided over [by the vowel], the letter *va* (or *ba*) alone is to be grasped;
from that which is presided over by the letter *a*, the second [letter] is presided over by the letter *ā*.
"Adorned above by the bindu" means that the mere dot is the *bindu*.
The seed-syllable *va* is the earthly element (*pārthiva*). From that...
From the *prastāra*. The eighth [letter] from that which is presided over by the letter *ka*.
"By Agni," and so forth, is easy to understand.
Here too, there is the syllable *phaṭ*.
It should be applied. Regarding the phrase "joined at the end with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*":
it means that *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are joined at its end; thus, [the mantra] is "joined with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*."
"Joined with *niṣṭhā*" means that the word ending in the *niṣṭhā* suffix is placed last;
it is a word without a case-ending.
And there is also protracted pronunciation. || 20-22 ||
This mantra named Trailokyavijaya is adorned with four words;
all [the syllables] are illuminated by the syllable *oṃ* and joined at the end with *huṃ phaṭ*. (23)
The phrase "etad" refers to the mantra-utterance, which is the *samaya*.
It is called *Trailokyavijaya* because it conquers the three worlds— namely Hari, Hara, and Harinyagarbha— completely and without remainder.
The remainder is easily understood.
"Oṃ" and so forth: these four mantra-words are illuminated by the *praṇava* (Oṃ).
Next, the nature of the *praṇava* is stated:
those mantras to which the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are joined— *hūṃ* at the beginning and *phaṭ* at the end— are described as such.
Then this mantra: oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ | oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ | oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ | oṃ ānaya hoḥ ||
The Blessed One: Vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ. || 23 ||
This mantra of the Vidyārāja-Cakravartin has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again, within the Tattvasaṃgraha, the Paramādya, the Saṃvara, or the Vajrabhairava. || 24 ||
For the protection of that [maṇḍala], especially against all evil beings, there is a maṇḍala joined with the four wrathful deities and endowed with the eight forms. (25)
By merely obtaining this, one indeed dies through lack of discernment;
yet, by reciting it through the yoga of the wheel, the fruit of all accomplishments arises. (26)
Regarding the term *vidyārājacakravartin*:
they are called *vidyārājas* because they shine (*rājante*) by means of the *vidyās*, which are the deities;
[of these] *vidyārājas*—
This mantra is for the protection of that maṇḍala which, among many others, appears in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other works. This very point is stated:
"In the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the *Paramādya*, the *Saṃvara*, and the *Vajrabhairava*..."
Endowed with the four wrathful deities and possessed of the eight forms.
"The mandala is for his protection, especially against all malevolent beings. Thus, the eight forms are the eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*).
Regarding "all malevolent beings":
For the sake of protecting the maṇḍala from all malevolent beings. "By this" refers to the mantra; "malevolent" refers to anyone who dies [by its power].
"From the application of the wheel" means:
From one's own self into wisdom, and then from that into the self—by reciting [the mantra] in this manner, the fruit of all accomplishments arises. (24–26)
Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavān vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ || 27 ||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, the procedure for extracting the *murajabandha* mantra, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
It is said that there are four mantra-words; thus he states the collection of mantras beginning with *oṃ*.
Here, two further *huṃ* and *phaṭ* syllables are concealed. That which prescribes the extraction of the *muraja-bandha* mantra, and which is also a chapter (*paṭala*), is thus [described].
The thirtieth is the thirtieth.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. || 30 ||
The thirty-first chapter on the rules for the consumption of food, fire-offerings, ritual oblations, and hand-gestures;
thereafter,
the destruction of all [obstacles] by means of "great flesh" (mahāmāṃsa) is known as the Vajra-born.
It is likewise a destroyer of all cruel things and is itself formidable.
In this same manner, the consumption of dog and pig meat, as well as that of cocks,
should be performed for the purposes of food, fire-offerings, and ritual oblations without hesitation.
The twenty-seventh [chapter] taught the worship and the ritual of offerings (balikriyā);
in the twenty-eighth, the ritual of fire-offerings (homakriyā). To explain that, he now states the chapter beginning with "tataḥ" (then).
"From the fire offering (homa).
Of all [beings]" refers to the gurus, buddhas, bodhisattvas, and so forth.
For those who perform [the rite], that which is born of the vajra refers to the body, faces, and so forth.
It is also stated in the *Śrīsamāja*: "The destruction of all [obstacles] by means of 'great meat' is known as that which is born of the vajra."
Or [it is] "born from the indestructible gnosis" (vajraja). Why is this so?
He says: "This," and so forth.
"This" means "this very one."
And since that flesh-oblation is the destroyer of all cruel things and is likewise terrible,
the meaning is that it was performed with that "great flesh" (mahāmāṃsa).
The excellence [of this rite] over other homas has been stated;

for according to the statement, "Gentleness is not appropriate toward those who are exceedingly cruel and fierce," its purpose is to prevent their falling into states of ruin. Therefore, they must be pacified by means of this.
Thus:
the destroyer is cruel;
[the word] "paśvādi" (beginning with cattle)—
There is also the oblation of meat.
"Having eaten" refers to eating for the purpose of worship;
the meaning is that the rites of worship and so forth should be performed with the meat of those very [beings].
"What might be intended by this?"—such is conceptual deliberation (*vikalpavicāra*); its opposite is non-deliberation (*avicāra*). (1.2)
The entire kingdom, without exception or remainder, is accomplished and fully realized;
for conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and pearls, there are three origins based on specific causes. || 3 ||
By whom can the skull of those whose bodies are the knowledge of the Dharma be defiled—the Hero who wears a garland of skulls and is adorned with the crescent moon? (4)
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "It is accomplished," and so forth.
"Entirely" means all the lower accomplishments such as the sword (*khaḍga*) and others; "the rest" refers to the subsequent ones; "without remainder" refers to Buddhahood.

The entire kingdom and the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*)—these are to be seized by him personally without being killed. Furthermore, he states that the skull-bowl alone must be used as a vessel for the practice of the yogin: "Conch," and so forth. "Pearls" refers to a specific type of creature that produces pearls.
Even its specific bone is called by the word "pearl.

Just as conch shells and other such items are purifiers for the Vaidikas, so too is the skull; [the author says this] to show that there is no difference [between them], because both are specific parts of a living being.
"Three arise from causes.
The causes are karma, the afflictions, and the aggregates (skandhas) and so forth.
These three are the conch-shell and the others.
[They] arise from a cause;
man is likewise [so].
Therefore, how could one who proclaims the Vedas disparage the skull? [Is it not so?]

If, through its application in medicines and the like, [purity] is attributed to conch shells and such things, why was no other purpose for other people seen? Even by the Blessed One, no utility was perceived from a skull.
For a jewel is not a common property for all people by its very nature.
[The word] "knowledge" [is used]. To which [objects] does the refutation apply? He says: "of those whose body is the knowledge of phenomena. This means:

phenomena (*dharma*) such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth; the knowledge or awakening of these [phenomena] by way of their emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth—that very [knowledge] is the "body," that is, the essential nature (*svarūpa*), of those [yogins]; they are thus described. Of such yogins [the refutation applies].
In these cases, the genitive case is used in the sense of the locative.
For this very reason, he says "kapāla," etc., [asking] by what could one defile even Śrī Heruka, who possesses that?
To "melt" the skull-cup...

"Kapālamālī" means one whose nature (*śīla*) is [to wear] a garland of skulls; or, because it belongs to the *śikhādi* group, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is applied to mean "one who possesses a garland of skulls," as he wears a garland of five skulls upon his head.
He is a hero because of his detachment (*niḥsaṅgatva*).
He is one for whom the ornament consisting of the crescent moon itself has been fashioned and refined; thus, he is "one whose ornament is the fashioned crescent moon" (*candrārdhakṛtabhūṣaṇaḥ*).
The holding of the half-moon [occurs] through the purity of grasping the stainless emanation-body. || 3-4 ||
In this very way, that which is born of heroes is known as the hero's [mudrā].
The practitioner should display the secret signs (chommakas) with the left hand. || 5 ||

He is remembered as that from whom even among heroes—those heroes such as Hari, Hara, and others—they are born; who could disparage him, he being so well-known? "One should show the five *chommakas*" refers to the five goddesses mentioned, beginning with Vajravārāhī. [The word] *jaṭā*—
One should show and meditate upon those [five skulls] situated on the crown;
"the practitioner with the left hand" is the connection for the word "should show."
In the specific case of *turvi*, the meaning is that one should offer the *samaya* and so forth held in the left hand. || 5 ||
For this is the abode of heroes and the source of the secret signs (chommaka);
the entire world, the three realms with all that is moving and unmoving, has originated from Vāma.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Of the heroes," and so forth.
"Of the heroes" refers to Vajrasattva and the others.
This left [hand] is their abode.
"Hasta" means "because. Because from which left hand proceeds the activity of the heroes and heroines who are designated by the secret signs (saṃketa) of the Śaumbhakas.
He says "by that [one] is purified as this" with the words beginning with *vāmā*.
*Vāmā* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). From empty phenomena...
Because of the statement, "Empty phenomena alone are produced," *vāmā* is *prajñā*, and the entire world arising from that—

consisting of the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth— is [the result]. For it is not by means of *upāya* alone that the three worlds possess any causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and thus it is likewise [understood] externally.
He establishes [this]. || 6 ||
Vajrasattva resides in the body, and likewise Vairocana in the creeper;
in this very manner, there shall be the flower-dancer for the Guru.
Established in the *dhārā*, the Hero bestows all accomplishments;
in the *kaniṣṭhā* [finger], he is the imperishable body whose womb is space (*ākāśagarbha*).
And in the nails is Hayagrīva, and likewise Mālaya has been declared;
these are the causes for the arising of the left-hand [practices] among all heroes. || 9 ||
He describes the worship of the hands: "Vajrasattva" means that Vajrasattva is to be meditated upon on the thumb (tanu),
and Vairocana on the forefinger (latā).
Guru is on the middle finger; Padyanartaka and Padyanarteśvara are on the ring finger;
Vīra and Śrī Heruka are on the little finger.
In the little finger is Ākāśagarbha; this is a word without a case ending. He is "tanu," meaning subtle, because his nature is difficult to comprehend.
He is "avyaya," meaning imperishable, because he does not pass away.
Ākāśagarbha is Vajrasūrya;
and Hayagrīva is in all the fingers and nails. The word "and" (ca) is used for conjunction.
He states that these also arise from the left [side] with the words "the ālaya.

That in which the nature of the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) and so forth dissolves—that is, is no longer perceived through investigation—and from which deities such as Vajrasattva are born, is the *ālaya*. "These" refers to...
The nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
Of all these heroes, the hand born from Vāma is the cause. 7–9.
On the palm of the hand, one should show Śrī Heruka eager for union with Vajravārāhī;
on the back, however, all the ḍākinīs—[thus one should show one's own fivefold nature]. (10)
This placement of the limbs (karaṇyāsa) brings about union with all that is dear;
thus, by means of this prescribed ritual, one should worship the supreme Hero.
The earth element is known as Locanā; the water element is remembered as Māmakī;
fire is known as Pāṇḍarā; and wind is proclaimed as Tārā. || 12 ||
"In the palm of the hand" means in the center of the hand.
"Śrī Heruka-Vajravārāhī" refers to Vajravārāhī who has entered into union with Śrī Heruka.
This is the meaning of "hi.
Therefore, he is eager for a meeting.
As for the phrase "on the back, however, all the ḍākinīs": [it refers to the following].
On the sides and so forth are all the Ḍākinīs;
for the word "tu" (but/however) indicates that it includes the back as well.
This is what has been stated: in the center of the hand is an eight-petaled lotus.
In its pericarp is Vajravārāhī, who has entered into union with Śrī Heruka;
on the eastern petal is Ḍākinī, and on the northern petal is Lāmā.
In the west is Khaṇḍarohā;
in the south is Rupiṇī;
in the northeast is Yāminī.
In the southeast is Mohanī; in the southwest, Sañcāriṇī;
and in the northwest, Trāsanī—thus they should be visualized.
This *karanyāsa* (hand-consecration) is "the union with all that is dear. Where the placement of deities upon the hand is performed according to the prescribed ritual procedure, that is *karanyāsa*.
All things that are dear—[are attained through it].
"By means of this one goes," thus it is so;
in this manner, by this sequence, one should worship the Hero.
[This is] another designation for the Ḍākinīs and so forth.
Māha—“Earth,” and so forth. (10–12)
The kissing [seal] is in the void; likewise are the perfections.
In the center is the abode of all heroes; at the back, the wise one should release [the breath]. 13.
*Cumbikā* is another name for Vajravārāhī;
she herself is in the void, in emptiness—
for the sake of the purification of emptiness.
This is the meaning. Therefore, regarding the *pāramitās*:
the *dāna*, *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, and *dhyāna* *pāramitās* are to be known respectively as the *Ḍākinīs* and so forth, ending with Vajravārāhī.
The word "likewise" indicates that the perfection of wisdom is conjoined with the other five perfections;
it is further indicated by the phrase "the abode of all heroes" in the middle [of the text].
It should be understood that one should see the abode and play of all heroes, such as Vajrapada and others, in the center.
The intended meaning is "the middle of the hand" due to the purification of the place of play for all heroes.
"A wise person should project it upon its back"—
this means that all the deities should be seen either on the back of the hand, like reflections in a mirror.
By the word "tu" (but), he indicates the specific meaning that one should contemplate [the deities] both upon the hand and on its back.
Therefore, he alone who is the seer is the wise one. || 13 ||

This secret is not to be disclosed; it must be guarded with great effort. Thus one should initiate a single hero and then undertake the *caru* sacrifice, which is the *Sarvavīrasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. 14.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, concerning the rules for the consumption of food, fire offerings, bali offerings, and hand gestures, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 31.
"One should show the five secret signs (*chommaka*).
It should be understood that the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are also designated by the term *chommaka*. Consequently, this refers to the ritual placement upon the hands (*karanyāsa*).

In that very place, one should accomplish the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) for Pracaṇḍa and the others, produced from the seed-syllables VUṂ ĀṂ JRĪṂ KHAṂ HŪṂ, having the nature of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas], and empowered by the three syllables.

"Oṃ pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ" and "Oṃ khaṇḍakapālin hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ"— having first uttered these names of all [the deities], one should offer twenty-four libations with the ring finger and the thumb joined at the mouth, and then place one [libation] upon the tongue; this is the enjoyment of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
Thus, another meaning should be understood:
from that, worship (pūjā) shall take place.
It should also be understood that one should offer the secret sign (chommaka) preceded by the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa).

And it should be understood that one should likewise taste the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in the skull-cup and other vessels after first performing the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), precisely because the meaning of the tantra is so vast.
"One should kiss the hero" means that one should worship him.

"In that regard, it should be done by one" means that one should consume the *caruka*— which is not to be eaten [ordinarily]— placed in a single vessel, according to this procedure involving the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth.
He states the fruit of enjoying the *caru* (sacrificial oblation): "The Union of All Heroes, the *Saṃvara* of the *Jāla* of *Ḍākinīs*.
The meaning is that one becomes Heruka. || 14 ||
The "Chapter on Food, Fire-offerings, and Bali-rites" is so called because it prescribes other *chommaka* (secret signs) by means of which that chapter is defined.
It is the thirty-first, the thirty-first [chapter].
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 31.
The thirty-second chapter, on the ritual procedure for the generation stage of the accomplishment of animals, spirits, and vetālas;
hereafter is fully explained the gathering of foods and drinks,
by which, through the correct performance, success quickly proceeds.
Now he states the chapter on the ritual substances for the means of worship and so forth, beginning with "After this" (*ataḥ param*).
After the explanation of worship and so forth (*pūjādikathanāt*), that which follows is fully explained (*samākhyātam*) because it is fixed (*niyatam*) as being about to be explained.
He asks, "What is that? and says: "The union of the eatables and the food.
That by which the eating—the enjoyment—of the eatables, such as animals and so forth, comes together is thus [described];
it is the power of mantra. By which...

"By means of the union of food and drink" refers to that [practice] wherein there is a perfectly beautiful arrangement such as the yoga of the deity and so forth, by means of the union of food and drink. "Accomplishment" (siddhi) is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā.
"Swiftly" means in this very life. || 1 ||
The cultivation of animals is also achieved through the previously mentioned sequence;
and those animals are likewise fivefold, consisting of the donkey, human, tortoise, camel, jackal, horse, and so forth. || 2 ||
He states the materials for worship and so forth with the words "of the bound souls" (*paśūnām*), etc.
"Drawing out" (*karṣaṇam*) refers generally to the extraction and separation [of those who are] the most excellent among the accomplished bound souls.
"And indeed" means that only the most excellent animals are to be accepted.
As for what kind of practitioner accomplishes this, he says: "One accomplishes worship by means of animals through the yoga of the deity according to the previously mentioned sequence."
He who has been so described is the practitioner of the previously mentioned sequence.
To the question, "Who are those animals (paśu) to be attracted? he says: "The animals," and so forth.
The word *ca* has the sense of the particle *api*.
The word "tathā" means that they are treated in the same manner as animals;
"khara" refers to a donkey; and "mānuṣa" refers to a human being, which is well known.
Some say "vanamānuṣa" refers to a forest-dweller;
"kūrma" means a tortoise;
"uṣṭra" means a camel with a long neck; and "śṛgāla" means a jackal.
This is well known.
When the nominative plural ending is elided in the expression "donkey, human, tortoise, camel, and jackal," these five are indeed the foremost.
In the phrase "with horses and so forth," the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*).
By the word "etcetera," the dog and the cow are also included. || 2 ||
These are the limbs for the accomplishment of the sacrificial animal (paśu) and indeed the means for attaining success (siddhi).
Among the castes, the Brāhmaṇa is the animal; among quadrupeds, the elephant is said [to be the animal]. (3)
"These are the limbs for the accomplishment of *paśu*":

those whose very nature (*svarūpa*) is excellence (*prakṛṣṭa*) as their limb (*aṅga*), namely their means of accomplishment (*siddhi*), are thus [described]. He states that even ordinary accomplishment is obtained from them: "and they are indeed the means of accomplishing *siddhi*."
The accomplishment of feats such as summoning and the *vetāḍa* is also the completion of the practice;
thus is the meaning of the rule.
The word *ca* (and) serves to collect the various accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Furthermore, he describes the attraction of animals (*paśukarṣaṇa*) with the words beginning "of the letters" (*varṇānām*), and so forth.

Human beings are called *varṇas* because they choose (*vṛ*) perfection. Among human beings, according to their class, the Brāhmaṇa is the most excellent among all classes; he is the "beast" (the pre-eminent one).
Among quadrupeds such as donkeys and the like, the elephant is preeminent;
therefore it is said: "The elephant is called the foremost among quadrupeds."
There is also a word *hasti* ending in the vowel *i*.
Among birds, the swan alone is victorious; among animals, the tortoise is supreme;
and among the gods, it is said that the movement of the mouth occurs in various forms. || 4 ||
"And among birds, the swan alone [is supreme].
He also mentions the taming of birds as it arises in the context of cultivation: the meaning is that among crows and other such birds, the swan alone is the best.

And he is a royal swan (*rājahaṃsa*), as indicated by the word "and" (*ca*). Among animals, he is one who has conquered the tortoise; that is, among aquatic animals, he is one who has conquered the tortoise.
The tortoise is the best, and he is renowned as Niraṅku;
this is what is called "the moving of the gods' mouths."
The goat, the buffalo, and the cock—these are the "mouth-movers" (*mukhacālana*), such as the goat and others, so called because they move their mouths.
To the question "Of whom is there mouth-moving?", he says: "They play (*divyanti*) in various forms, thus they are gods (*devāḥ*)."
The Dānavas and others. || 4 ||
These are designated as animals; they constitute the mandala for the accomplishment of siddhi:
the crow, the crane, the jackal, the twice-born (parrot), the great mantrin (peacock), the curlew, the sarasa crane, and the kadamba goose.
These are designated as "animals" (paśu) and constitute the mandala for the accomplishment of supernatural powers (siddhi).
These animals and this bird have been described by the Buddhas who are equal [to one another].
This maṇḍala is both the means for attaining spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*) and the [accomplishment] itself; such is its nature.
Regarding that, he describes the summoning of birds for the purpose of worship, beginning with the word "crow" (*kāka*). The *jambuka* is commonly known as the *puṇḍarī*.
The "great minister among the twice-born" is the parrot (*śuka*).

The *krauñca* is a particular kind of cry. The intention is that the crow, the crane, the jackal, the great minister among the twice-born, the *krauñca*, the *sārasa*, and the *kādambaka* are the most excellent.
It was stated previously that among these, the *haṃsa* is the most excellent.
In that regard, if some should maintain that by the word *haṃsa* a Kṣatriya or a particular type of yoga is intended, then this [present] explanation would not apply. || 5 ||
The accomplishment of eating, fire-offerings, and ritual offerings becomes available for one who desires it;
[this is achieved] with the milk of a black female dog, combined with black beans and rice. 6.
One should offer oblations into the mouth of the corpse with the mantra, free from hesitation;
the best of practitioners should perform the homa for one hundred and eight times.

He asks, "What is the use of these? and replies: "The consumption of food, fire-offerings, and the performance of bali-oblations. He asks, "What is achieved by this? and replies: "Success becomes available to one who desires it."

The accomplishment of that [rite] consists of the consumption, fire-oblations (*homa*), and ritual offerings (*bali*) by crows and other such birds, as well as by the *kādambaka* swans; it consists of the consumption, fire-oblations, and ritual offerings by crows, vultures, jackals, twice-born men (*dvija*), great mantra-reciters, *krauñca* cranes, *sārasa* cranes, and *kādambaka* swans.
*Kriyāsiddhi* is a complete compound word.
He describes the *sādhana* of the Great Preta, beginning with "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) and so forth. By means of the root-mantra of Sumbha—

Having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) with the mantra and having obtained the sign (*nimitta*), one should take an unbroken and non-putrid corpse to the cremation ground at midnight; there,
with black beans and rice grains broken into pieces smeared with the milk of a black female dog, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) into its mouth with that very same mantra.
One should perform this. He says exactly this: "The milk of a black bitch is to be offered by the best of practitioners," and so forth. (6–7)
Then the ghost rose up and said, "I am your servant.
He brought forth a sword from Pātāla, as well as the power to seize and subdue the planets.
It shows that he has previously performed service by virtue of his excellence: "Pātāla" refers to the accomplishment of Pātāla;
that is to say, the accomplishment of entering into a subterranean cavern (*bila*).
"Arise" refers to traveling through the air;
"and a sword" refers to the accomplishment of the sword; and by the word "or," the accomplishments of the wheel and so forth are included.
*Graha* means seizure;
*nigraha* means the crushing of the wicked. || 8 ||
Having bestowed a pill, collyrium, a treasure, an ointment for the feet, or an elixir—granting one such accomplishment—he then departs; it is not otherwise.
"Pills, collyrium, treasure-trove, foot-ointment, or elixir"—
the word "or" (*vā*) is used here as a conjunction (*samuccaye*).
The rest is easily understood.
Having bestowed one or another of these perfections, he departs; it cannot be otherwise, because of the fixed nature [of his vow]. || 9 ||
The lower and upper messengers are perfected in this tantra; of this there is no doubt.
Then there are the Goṣṭhopalikās and the remaining Śuṣkaśiras.
"The Siddhas who are the lower and upper messengers are present in this tantra; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, the lower Yoginīs are those situated on the earth, while the upper Yoginīs are those situated in the intermediate space.
The implication is that from this, success will follow.
Regarding the phrase "and cow-pen scrapings":
these refer to dried cow dung from a cow-pen.
"The remaining [are] dried skulls; 'therefrom' means for that purpose the rosary.
(10) The remaining [objects] are the cowrie shells (*kapardaka*). "Dried skulls" refers to the *riṣṭhaka* beads. "Therefrom" means for that purpose the rosary (*akṣasūtra*). (10)
One should make an unbreakable rosary from great conch-shell or from tortoise shell;
this very rosary bestows unsurpassed accomplishment. (11)
One should make a rosary from the bone of a tortoise;

this is mandatory for the accomplishment of a Vetāla. For the rites of pacification (śānti), nourishment (puṣṭi), subjugation (vaśya), and malevolent magic (abhicāra), as well as for the Putrañjīva rite and all other ritual actions mentioned in the *Catuṣpīṭha*, [the rosary] should be made of beads (gulikā).
It should be observed. || 11 ||
Four-armed and four-faced, or likewise having as many arms as desired, with a white body, most fierce, and indeed possessing the appearance of Bhairava. || 12 ||
Beholding Vajravārāhī, who bears her own color and weapons, and the Hero adorned with a garland of skulls and his body smeared with ashes. (13)
"Four-armed," and so forth:
in the sādhana of Vetāḍa, [one visualizes the deity] as four-armed, holding a vajra, a trident, a skull-cup, and a sword (or khaṭvāṅga).
The connection is that one should meditate [upon him].
The Blessed One has four faces—white, dark-blue, red, and yellow—toward the east, north, and so forth. As long as the lakṣa...
The meaning is that there is no restriction as to whether [the mantra] is placed in the mouth or on the arm;
furthermore, instruction from a teacher is required. Alternatively, it may simply be the four faces of Śukla (the White One).
The signs [are known] from instruction.
Therefore, it should be understood that this is the case elsewhere as well, due to instruction. "In that manner" means: just as there is instruction.
Beholding Vajravārāhī, who bears her characteristic color and weapons— that is,
she who holds the vajra, skull-cup, and so forth.
From this [it follows] her four-faced nature;
the Lord is white, and the Goddess is also white.
His body is adorned with mudrās and other ornaments; he is marked by matted locks and a crown, and holds a trident;
his face is slightly terrifying with bared fangs, and he is seated upon a great corpse.
Then, having understood this according to the rule, the yogi should meditate upon all the deities;
the practitioner should do so at all times.
For those distinguished by such qualities, success becomes a desirable woman. (15)
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, the procedure for the generation stage of the practice of the animal, the *paśu*, and the *vetāla*, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
Having understood this sequence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanākrama*), one should always cultivate the thirty-six deities— the meaning of "all deities"—
in three groups.

Regarding the state of having a hundred thousand arms, faces, and so forth: in all the right hands there is a vajra, and likewise in the left hands a trident, or else a khaṭvāṅga and a skull-cup; all the faces are white.
Everything else is to be understood through the sequence of the means of accomplishment. || 14-15 ||
Animals are birds;
beasts are donkeys and so forth;
a vetāla is a hungry ghost (preta).

The thirty-second [chapter] is that which prescribes the sequence for the generation of their means of accomplishment (*sādhana-utpatti-krama*); it is both that and a chapter (*paṭala*), thus "the thirty-second.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*.
The thirty-third chapter, on the ritual procedure for honoring the secret worship.
Beyond this, there is nothing; he is a practitioner in all yogas.
It should be performed according to one's ability with foods to be chewed, foods to be eaten, fish, meat, and so forth. (1)

Now, showing that worship and other rites should be performed preceded by respectful service (*satkāra*), he says "ataḥ" and so forth. The connection is as follows: "then, for the practitioner who performs worship and so on, [the result] becomes supreme or non-supreme according to how it is done.
This applies to all things to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

The *yogas* are those [states] attained; this is a locative case used in the sense of "on account of" (*nimitta-saptamī*). Demonstrating the offering of honor, he says: "edible," and so forth. Edible...
The "cow-slaying" and so forth [are the acts]. The "food" consists of curd, ghee, sugar-candy, sweetmeats (laḍḍuka), and the like.
Because there are many things to be eaten, "food" refers specifically to curd and the other such items.
Fish refers to the Rohita and others;
meats refer to those of the goat and so forth;
by the word "and others" (ādi), other edible items are also included as available.

These are the specific details. It should be understood that by means of these, the practitioner (sādhaka) will perform the worship (*pūjā*), as this is the subject at hand. Thus, the sense is that one who performs worship in this manner is an extraordinary practitioner. "According to one's capacity" (*yathāśaktitaḥ*).
The sense is that whatever power one possesses, that should be employed therein;
thus there is no transgression of one's capacity. || 1 ||
Even when [the usual offerings] are not available, one should diligently provide the five types of edible foods and so forth;
indeed, one should always perform an extensive variety of foods and drinks at night.

However, if the capacity to produce the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) is not present, then the five nectars— consisting of the five types of food and so forth— must be produced through meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*) and consumed with effort and according to the rules.
"But one should always do it at night. This means that during the day one may consume food and so forth and engage in [worldly] service, but at night one must do so according to the rule.
Because the word "tu" has that meaning. || 2 ||
And then the messenger should eat; indeed, the practitioner especially should do so, having placed her head upon his own body, honored as the non-duality of heroes.
And then the messenger (dūtī) should eat (adyāt). That which is eaten is "at" (i.e., food, such as what is to be chewed and so forth). She should eat; she should consume it.

"Having placed his head upon his own limb," means having taken the skull-cup in his own hand, he should then eat the food offerings. [He should perform] the worship together with the messenger (dūtī).
"One should perform" is the collective meaning.
Regarding "worshipped by the non-dual hero":
even the worship through meditative union (*samāpatti*) is performed by the hero together with her.
The meaning is "to be accomplished.
Regarding the reading *svotsaṅgam* found in some manuscripts:
in that case, having placed the source of the lotus-dharma upon his own lap by means of the Hero (Vīra).
It should be explained that what is to be accomplished is that which is worshipped by the non-dual heroes. || 3 ||
Whether it be one's mother, or a sister, or a daughter, or a female relative, or indeed a wife—
one should perform the rite for liberation from the bonds of bondage according to this prescribed method.

Whether she be a mother, a sister, a daughter, a female relative, or indeed a wife—these five are *yoginīs* because of their affection, like that toward a mother and so forth. Together with them, one should effect a liberation that is perfectly free from bondage. || 4 ||
Then the mantras will be perfected until the dissolution of the world;
having assumed the form of the teacher, the practitioner receives the worship.
"Therefore, mantras are perfected"—thus say the deities.
To the question "In what length of time?", he says: "until the dissolution of the summoned.
This means until there is a dissolution—that is, a transformation—of the summoned afflictions (*kleśa*).
He states that such hospitality toward the Yoginī should be performed,
beginning with the words "In the Ācārya," etc.:
"Having assumed such a form of my own within the Ācārya, I accept the worship."
Regarding the phrase "being one who accomplishes siddhi," the Blessed One said: "For when such a teacher is worshipped, Vajradhara is worshipped;
by worshipping him, all the Tathāgatas are worshipped"—this is the intended meaning. || 5 ||
The posture of the heroes and the mudrā are indeed required, without a doubt;
the practitioner, being well-composed, should perform singing, dancing, and so forth.
As long as all embodied beings wander in saṃsāra, overwhelmed by suffering and grief, so long do they not become knowers of yoga. (7)
Then the practitioner should worship the mudrā with his whole being;
when worshipped, they desire what is worthy of worship, but if treated with disrespect, they consume [the practitioner] with fire.
I take up the seat, the station, the mudrā, and the insignia of the heroes;
the song endowed with vajra-words;
and the dance beginning with the ālīḍha posture.
By this word: and thus the practitioner, well-composed and whose self is the yoga of the deity,
speaks of the majesty of the Śrī Heruka yoga,
beginning with "as long as," and so forth.
As long as they wander in *saṃsāra*, they do not possess the knowledge of the yoga of Śrī Heruka; this is because the particle *ca* has the sense of "as long as" (*tāvat*).
To the question, "And who are those who do not take delight therein?", he says: "all embodied beings (*dehinaḥ*) whatsoever. As many as...
The meaning is "all embodied beings indeed.
One should worship the *mudrā*, that is, the deity.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "When worshipped," and so forth. [Worship...]
Because he strives, he is "pūjya";
that is to say, he is a worshiper. || 6-8 ||
In the Yoga Tantras, human beings are primordially perfected Mahāmudrās;
they should be worshipped with great effort, and thereafter, O Hero, one should practice heroism.
The deity Mahāmudrā is primordially established and established by nature. To the question, "Why does the world not know her who is such as this? he says: "mānava" (the conceited person).

One who "blows toward" (vāti) or attains the afflictions such as pride is called *mānava*; the meaning is that he is ignorant because of his state of being proud (*mānavatva*). Likewise, she is to be honored and treated with respect according to the previously mentioned rule.
"Afterwards, one should practice the state of being a hero among heroes.
This means that having first abandoned conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), one should thereafter practice the non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatva*) of the hero's mind. || 9 ||
Having thus performed worship, the practitioner, rising from the netherworld (pātāla),
[attains] pacification, nourishment, subjugation, attraction, killing, driving away, and so forth.
For paralyzing, immobilizing, creating enmity, and likewise for subjugation, one should worship Karmasiddhi; thus, success is achieved without difficulty. 11.
In all rites whatsoever, there is no doubt for the practitioner. || 12 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, the procedure for the secret worship and offerings, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
Thus, first of all, there is worship.
Then, by means of that, one becomes an achiever of all siddhis, such as those of the netherworld (pātāla) and so forth. Regarding "peace" (śānti) and so on: this is easily understood. || 10–12 ||
Secret worship consists of honoring with food and so forth, while respect consists of reverence, prostration, and the like;
that which prescribes these two is the "chapter," and thus it is so called.
The thirty-third [chapter], the thirty-third.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 33.
The thirty-fourth chapter: the ritual procedure for the non-dual messenger (advayadūtī) and the fire-oblation of summoning.
Now follows the detailed ritual procedure known as the "Wheel" (cakra) of the Ḍākinījāla, by means of which that [practice] swiftly succeeds for the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
The word "atha" (now) indicates that immediately after the description of worship and honor,
one should understand that the detailed procedure known as the *Ḍākinījālacakra* will be explained.
The state of the *ḍākinīs* is *ḍākinya*; that itself is the "net" (*jāla*) because it binds through the letters beginning with *ka*, *kla*, and so forth, like a net.
That which explains its circle (*cakra*), i.e., its maṇḍala, is [the tantra]; it is the detailed procedure (*vidhi-vistara*) in which the ritual action (*karman*) occurs.
That is so. The "elaboration of the ritual" refers to the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *ḍākinīs* and so forth. To the question "What is that?", he says "In which," and so on.
"She" refers to Khaṇḍarohā.
It should be understood that [the goal] is accomplished. || 1 ||
One should join all the heroes and ḍākinīs with the lotuses;
likewise, one should deposit the station of the avadhūtī between the eyebrows.
Then, one should not offer anything else into the fire except through the mouth of Vīrocchuṣma;
likewise, five oblations should quickly be made with beef and blood.
In the twenty-four lotuses of the mandala of Sarvavīra, the ḍākinīs accompanied by the twenty-four heroes are to be installed.
Therefore, it says: "one should assign them."
"One should employ them"—
even with the reading "niyojitāḥ" (employed), the meaning is the same. Here, the word *puṣkara* denotes a leaf.
Therefore, the plural number is used. "One should place the seat of Avadhūtī between the eyebrows"—by this, the third eye of all the deities, beginning with Vīra, is indicated; for...
Between the eyebrows, at the forehead corresponding to the nose,
because it destroys evil, the *avadhūtī* is mind-only;
that is its state.
The third mark is the eye;
the forehead is also the station of the Hero.
By this, the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the deities is shown. Being thus constituted...
The yoginīs should perform the oblation;
one should not offer anything other than the two women through the mouth of Vīrocchuṣma.
[Vīrocchuṣma-mukha] means the mouth of Vīrocchuṣma.
One should offer oblations while characterized by a face possessed of wrath;
the intended meaning is that no other substance is to be used, but only beef.
The beginning with "gaviti" is easy to understand.
First, five oblations (āhuti) should be offered. || 2-3 ||
Then, while the sacrificial fire is blazing, one should offer nine oblations;
one shall behold the single-faced [deity] who faces all directions, appearing like an ocean of garlands of flames.
One should likewise worship the four-faced Vīreśa and Vīravīrālaya;
on the petals are the four female messengers (dūtīs), and there is the blissful non-duality of the Cakravīras.
"Then one should offer nine oblations into the blazing fire"—this is easily understood.
Having offered into the mouth of the fire, one then offers into the mouth of the deity; thus he says "into the flame," and so forth.
One should visualize a wheel in the center of the *kuṇḍa*; it faces in all directions. Because it has four doors, it is the four-faced Śrī Heruka.
The meaning is that one should behold the wheel, which is the abode of heroes, marked by heroes, and joined with yoginīs accompanied by heroes.
"And four messengers on the petals" means,
according to the sequence of the [lotus] petals:
on the petals starting from the east and so forth.
There are four ḍākinīs:

"The Ḍākinī, as well as Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī. The term *cakravīrā* (wheel-heroine) means that she abides by means of the experience of the non-dual true bliss residing within the three wheels.

It should be understood that the non-dual bliss exists in such a way because it is attained through the yoginīs situated in the three wheels who have entered into the state of the non-dual hero. || 4-5 ||
One should present Khaṇḍarohā externally according to the form of the injunction;
however, one should show her situated in her own form in the center of the wheel.
"One should place Khaṇḍarohā on the outside" means that one should place Khaṇḍarohā upon the petal situated at the back with her own forms.
"But one should show her seated in the middle of the wheel. Here, the first word "tu" (but) serves to indicate a distinction, while the second has the sense of "only" (eva).
One should display or meditate upon [the deities] in their own forms corresponding to the ritual action— such as white forms and so forth in rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and the like.
As for what was stated in the procedure for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), that "one should place Khaṇḍarohā on the outside," is intended to indicate her preeminence in all ritual actions.
It should be understood that one should employ that [mantra] for summoning and other such purposes. || 6 ||
This wheel, which bestows all accomplishments, has been pointed out to you;
one should likewise cause it to shine forth according to the specific ritual action.

"This is what has been pointed out to you regarding the wheel, which bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*). This assembly of deities pointed out in the wheel, which bestows all accomplishments, the practitioner seeks for you."

"According to the nature of the rite" (karmānurūpataḥ) means that this which has been stated— namely, that one should offer the full oblations (pūrṇāhuti) into the mouth of the deity who has been meditated upon as possessing a color corresponding to the rite— is to be understood.
And it is not only in the context of the fire-offering (homa) that [the color] corresponds to the rite.
There is beauty of form, but it exists elsewhere as well;
in the reading "the accomplisher of all siddhis," the practitioner (sādhaka) is specifically qualified. || 7 ||
O Hero, as it has been briefly explained in the Ocean of Knowledge (Vidyārṇava), one attains accomplishment through the non-dual yoga of the messenger; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, the Procedure for the Non-dual Messenger’s Fire Offering and Summoning, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
He explains how the multitude of deities is indicated by the *cakra* with the words "the ocean of vidyās," and so forth.
"By the hero" means that one should perform the oblation having entered into union with the heroine, who is Vajradhara’s messenger. (8)

The fire-offering (*homa*) characterized by the messenger of non-duality (*advayadūtī*) is that by which attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) is performed; therefore, it is called the chapter [dealing with] that. It is the thirty-fourth, the thirty-fourth.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 34.
The thirty-fifth chapter: The Procedure for Deceiving Death through Non-dual Action and Time.
Now, the most excellent and supreme rite, as characterized by its proper sequence, consists of worship whose essence is non-dual yoga, well-applied to each specific rite.
The word "atha" (now) indicates that this follows the explanation of the placement of the deities (*devatānyāsa*).
It should be understood that the "excellent rite" (*karmavara*) ensues,

In ritual practice, the recitation of mantras is the most excellent method because it accomplishes the desired objective; this is characterized by its sequential order.
As for "characterized by sequence":
it is understood as being marked by the proper succession, such as the sequence of fierce rites (*krūrakarma*) and so forth.

Regarding how the mantra is to be recited, he says: worship must be performed. Of what nature? It is that worship which is "joined with every ritual action," characterized by non-duality—the yoga or meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) consisting of the embrace of Vajravārāhī, which is its very self or essential nature. || 1 ||
Those mantras which bring about accomplishment are their divisions in due order;
one should cause that mantra, beginning with the letter and the messenger, to revolve with the speed of an arrow. (2)
"Those mantras which bring about renown are their divisions in due order. Those whose nature it is to effect the accomplishment of realization are such [mantras],

They should be understood as being divided according to their application in practices such as those for pacification (*śāntika*).
He states the division so as not to overstep the sequence, beginning with the word "caste" (*varṇa*) and so forth.
Those heroes of whom the female messengers (*dūtī*) are the first are called "the messengers and so forth" (*dūtyādayaḥ*).
Where the *varṇas* such as Khaṇḍakapālī and others,
as well as the *varṇas* such as the female messengers (*dūtī*) and so forth, are described, that is [the mantra]; it is the eight-syllable and other mantras of that Śrī Heruka.
It should be understood that he should mutter that mantra.
To the question "How? he says: "He should whirl with the speed of an arrow."
The term "śaravega" is formed by the elision of the third case ending;
that mantra should revolve all around with the speed of an arrow. || 2 ||
The mantras, joined with one another, are then separated by means of entry;
thereafter, the garland of seed-syllables is swallowed and established within the syllable *hūṃ*.
He says that very thing: "mutually," and so forth.

The meaning of the distinction regarding their entry is as follows: having entered inside through one's own mouth, they are emitted again via the vajra-path;

This is the significance of the different modes of entry.

In the rite for cruel purposes, the sequence is as follows: entering from one's own mouth into the mouth of the Goddess, then emerging through the path of the lotus, entering the thunderbolt (*vajra*), then reaching one's own mouth, and [re-entering] the mouth of the Goddess.
Describing the completion of this procedure, he says:
Regarding "then the seed-garland is swallowed":
it should be understood that one should visualize the mantra-garland with its syllables closely joined to one another. "Established within the syllable HŪṂ" means...
That [mantra] in which the person to be accomplished (sādhya) is established between two *hūṃ* syllables is thus described.
At the conclusion of the mantra to be recited—namely, *hūṃ devadattaṃ māraya hūṃ*—there is the interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) preceded by *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ* at the beginning of the position. (3)

But through cessation, it becomes attainable; it does not go to a single state, by means of the *sampuṭa* (the joined) through the state of being joined, and by the binding of the *vajra-śṛṅkhala* (the adamantine chain).
One should pierce with the vajra and then whirl the picchaka;
likewise, one should attract it as if with a hook, and similarly employ the mallet for agitation.
Therefore, he says: "But through cessation, it would be accomplished; it does not go to a single state.
The word "but" (tu) is for emphasis. [It means] through the cessation [brought about] by the two *hūṃ* syllables.
"By means of the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) through the state of being encased" refers to the rite of pacification (*śāntika*). *Oṃ devadattāya svāhā oṃ*.
Thus, as before, there is *vidarbhaṇa*, *saṃpuṭīvidarbhaṇa*, and *saṃpuṭībhāva*.
There is a confinement (*nirodha*) by means of two *oṃ* syllables at the beginning and the end.
"Vajra," and so forth.
The explanation of the phrase "established within the syllable HŪṂ" has been stated.
In the rite for the fierce [deities], one should pierce with the vajra known as the syllable HŪṂ.
The extraction of the *hūṃ* syllable from the beginning and end of the object to be accomplished constitutes its piercing.
To the question "By what means?", he says: "by the binding of the vajra-chain."

"Bound by the vajra-chain" means that for whom this is so, it is thus. "One should whirl the vajra like a peacock's tail feather" means that one should whirl the mantra; this is how it should be understood.
The swiftness of entry and exit through the mouth and other openings by means of mantra has been demonstrated.
In rites for the cruel, Khaṇḍarohā is black and holds a vajra in her hand; in rites for pacification, she is white and holds a khaṭvāṅga in her left hand.
"One should attract as if with a hook. When there is attraction, then: *jaḥ*, "attract Devadatta, *jaḥ*";
this is the piercing (*vidarbhaṇa*).

As before: by the word "hook" (aṅkuśa), the syllable *jaḥ* is meant. Reciting the root mantra, through the power of the mantra, he pierces the heart of the target with the red Khaṇḍarohā, who holds a hook in her hand, and draws [the target] forth.
Regarding "likewise the pestle for agitation": for the purpose of agitating armies and the like, the interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) is performed as *hūṃ* agitate Devadatta and so forth *hūṃ*.
And Khaṇḍarohā is joined with her own color.
The meaning of the word "likewise" (tathā) is "with pestle in hand" (muṣalahastā). || 4-5 ||
For eating, it is said to be a thunderbolt; for piercing, an arrow is joined to it;
and for the evasion of timely death, a khaṭvāṅga staff is joined to the body.
The skull-cup, serving as the vessel for the offering (arghapātra), is assigned to the mouth by means of the weapon-mantra (astra). || 7 ||
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the ritual procedure for deceiving death through the time of non-dual action, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 35.
Regarding eating—that is, consuming—Khaṇḍarohā herself, assuming her own form, [utters]:
"Phaṭ! Devadatta, eat! Phaṭ!
This is the *vidarbhaṇa* (the ritual piercing).
"In piercing, [the mantra] 'O Khaṇḍarohā, arrow in hand, phaṭ, pierce Devadatta, phaṭ' is the *vidarbhaṇa* (encasement).
And for the evasion of untimely death, the *khaṭvāṅga* (skull-topped staff) is joined to the body. Thus, for the evasion of untimely death, the *khaṭvāṅga* is on the left.
Dhāriṇī is Khaṇḍarohā.
The syllable HŪṂ is white, emitting thousands of streams of flowing nectar.
"HŪṂ! Revive Devadatta! HŪṂ! Thus [it is said].
Regarding the piercing (*vidarbhaṇa*):
in all ritual actions, the manifestation of the mantra is required; one should offer the *argha* oblation with a skull into the mouth of Khaṇḍarohā as she arrives.
Thus he says: "The skull is the *argha* vessel, [and] the mouth [is the recipient]."
The word "tu" has the sense of [emphasis].

Regarding "astraniyojitam": the meaning is that one should meditate upon Khaṇḍarohā as performing the application of weapons, beginning with the hook (aṅkuśa), upon the limbs of the person to be accomplished, immediately after the offering of the guest-water (argha). || 6-7 ||

"Non-dual action" refers to that by which, through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and the deception of death at its appointed time are performed; thus, this chapter is so named.
It is the thirty-fifth, the thirty-fifth.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. || 35 ||
The thirty-sixth chapter: The Ritual for the Attraction of the Worship of Reality.
Now, the great worship of mudrās is proclaimed as the application of mantras;
for these mudrās and worships bring about swift accomplishment, without a doubt. (1)
"Then" (atha) means immediately after the non-dual activity.
"Mudrā" refers to the worship of the external mudrā.
To the question "Of what kind is it?", he says: "of the mantra."
The mudrā proclaimed as the "mantra-deposition" (mantranyāsa) is so called because it is performed by means of the deposition of the three-syllabled [mantra]; that is its worship.
And the mantra consists of three syllables. For these [three] bring about swift accomplishment; for (hi), because (yasmāt). || 1 ||
Having joined the mantra to the two liṅgas, the non-duality of the ḍākinīs and the heroes; likewise, the practitioner of mantra should perform the union of the ḍākinīs with their heart-mantras. (2)
The wise one should churn the Yoginī as desired with his purified body;
having realized the non-duality of the hero-worship, he should perform the ritual activity with diligence. (3)
He states the conjunction with the mantra, beginning with "mantra" and so forth.
The connection is as follows: having joined the three-syllable mantra, one should churn the Yoginī.
"Two signs" means the sign of the two, wisdom and method. He says this very thing: "The ḍākinīs and heroes..."
"Non-dual" (advaya) means that which possesses both the ḍākinī and the hero; this is the sense of its "liṅga.

Having produced the vajra and the lotus with the syllable *hūṃ*, and the vajra-jewel with the syllable *oṃ*, and the filaments of the lotus with the syllable *āḥ*, and having placed the three syllables upon the body and so forth, one should churn the yoginīs.
"The pure body according to one's desire":
thus is the pure body. The worship of the non-dual absorption has been explained.
Having understood and performed the worship of the heroes (vīrapūjā) consisting of fish, meat,
and so forth, one should diligently perform rites such as those for pacification (śāntika) with full concentration. || 2-3 ||
Having analyzed it according to his own will, the practitioner should apply even the contrary [mantra];
he should bring about the state of action for the purposes of restraint and favor.
Having analyzed— that is, having separated— the rites such as *śāntika* and so forth, which are otherwise contrary to one another and distinct, one should apply them.
He states that very same point by means of the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) in the passage beginning with "nigraha" and so on.
The objects of restraint and favor are the purposes; [the word "in" (teṣu) denotes] the locative case in the sense of cause (nimitta). || 4 ||
Separated according to the divisions of reality and joined within the pathways of the channels,
one should accomplish the purpose of the practice, both external and internal.
By this, one shall quickly accomplish [the subjugation] of gods, asuras, and humans alike.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the Ritual for Attracting through the Worship of Reality, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 36.
He provides the explanation for what was indicated by the phrase "mutually joined" (*anyonyaghaṭitā*) and so forth, beginning with "pierced" (*bheditā*):
the mantras previously mentioned are joined in sequence within the pathways of the channels (*nāḍī*) and the pathways of the verses (*padya*).
Because of their fundamental nature;
that is, by way of the distinction of reality and the distinction of the expansion of ritual action (*karmaprasara*).
"One should accomplish for the sake of application" means that one should accomplish rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) for the purpose of providing an illustration.
By this, success is attained; nowhere else is success found.
One should accomplish everything by undertaking this practice. || 5-6 ||
For the sake of accomplishing the expansion of the activities of the principles (tattvas), worship is the means of attracting them;
it is that by which this is prescribed, and thus it is called a "chapter" (paṭala).
The thirty-sixth [chapter], the thirty-sixth section.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 36.
The thirty-seventh chapter: The Ritual Procedure for Mastery over the Inner Self.
Now I shall proclaim another [practice], the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) by which one is overcome by the [divine] form.
The mantras and the *ḍākinīs*, when mutually entwined and joined together in one place, [achieve this].
Now, with the words "atha" and so forth, he begins to explain the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
The word "atha" indicates immediate succession to the ritual actions accomplished by recitation (*japa*).
The term "anyatamam" refers to the means.
I shall explain by analyzing right practice; I shall fully proclaim it.
"Vigrahākrāntasādhaka" means the means (upāya) that accomplishes those sentient beings who have entered into that body (*vigraha*); this is the meaning. This—
"Dāha" means that the mantras and the ḍākinīs, which are mutually entwined, are joined together in one place.
The meaning is that by combining these three—the root mantra, the king of vidyās, and the ḍākinī mantra—one should accomplish the medicinal elixir (bhaiṣajya). || 1 ||
Having consumed the food that has been vomited, one should cause it to be ejected at the end of the recitation;
then, after a full seven nights have passed, one should employ it in eating and other such activities.
By this, they come under one's control for as long as life lasts; there is no doubt.
Having drunk the ghee of a tawny cow, one should vomit it up at the conclusion of the recitation.
Then, one should smear one's own face with that [substance];
if [the person] is constantly angry, they will be brought under control simply by the sight [of it]. || 4 ||
Having anointed [the body] with sesame oil mixed with rice flour,
the mantra-practitioner, having fashioned a *śaṃkulikā*, should employ it for consumption.
He says this very thing: "Having eaten," and so forth;
"one should vomit by means of the end of the recitation. Having washed what was eaten and regurgitated, once again—
Having consumed that, one should vomit it up.
Having mixed it with unrefined camphor, one should recite the three mantras at the three junctions of the day for seven nights.
Then, by giving it in food and other such things, it will come to pass as described.
Having drunk Kapilā-ghee—the ghee of a tawny cow—over which the mantra has been recited seven times, one should vomit;
with that [vomit], one should anoint oneself and the face.
"Then," it says.
Immediately after the oil massage:
"having massaged," and so forth;
thereafter, sesame oil should be applied to the massaged limb.
The word *tu* is used for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Regarding the phrase "combined with rice-flour":
having prepared a *śaṅkulikā* made of rice-flour and cooked it in that oil, one should offer it in this manner by means of eating it.
The word "tu" has the sense of "only.
In every case, it should be understood that there is the recitation of mantras. (2-5)
If one does not release the ritual action, [the deity] remains perpetually under control for as long as one lives;
having eaten black sesame seeds mixed with *rājikā* mustard and then vomited them out, [one should perform the rite]. (6)
One should grind kuṣṭha, apāmārga, karaja, udara, and kīṭaka with one's own blood and then saturate them with semen.
One should employ food, drink, collyrium, garments, and ointments;
by this means, there is no doubt that subjugation will last for as long as one lives.
If karma does not release one, and if one were not liberated,
then having eaten black sesame seeds mixed with *rājikā* mustard and vomited them up, [one would still be bound].
"Kuṣṭha, combined with apāmārga, karaja, udara, and kīṭaka.
Here, the word "ca" (and) is used for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*) in the ritual application.
In the case of *turviśeṣa*: having eaten black sesame seeds together with *rājikā* (black mustard), one should induce vomiting.
The *kuṣṭha* [root] should be prepared after it has emerged from seven water-drinking sessions.
*Karaja* means a fingernail.
*Udarakīṭaka* refers to a small insect that has emerged from the belly.
*Khāna* means food.
There is elision of [the nasal] in the word *gātra*.
An oblation of beef, with the deity smeared with its blood, brings [the target] under control at that very moment; if he does not come, he dies.
Having visualized his flesh before him, the wise practitioner should perform the fire offering (*homa*).
At the conclusion of the *homa*, having offered the ritual oblation (*bali*), he may instantly attract the three worlds.
Success shall be achieved within seven nights. || 10 ||
"Anointed with blood for the sake of the oblation by means of an offering of beef.
This means that the offerings of beef are smeared with its blood for the purpose of the *homa*.
Through the *homa* performed with beef anointed with cow's blood, the practitioner gains knowledge of the deity to be accomplished and brings them under control.
Alternatively, "deity" refers to a worldly deity, and "meat" refers specifically to beef;
therefore, he says "of that."
"In front" means: either in front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*) of Śrī Heruka, or before its image, or at its mouth; there, to the east and west, is the *kuṇḍa* for all rites (*sārvakarmika*).
"Success shall be attained within seven nights";
that is, success comes from performing oblations at the three junctions of the day for seven nights. || 9-10 ||
The characteristic of the conduct of the samaya is difficult to find in the three worlds;
it must always be concealed with effort by oneself through secret mantras. (11)
One of meager fortune does not obtain the hidden meaning, nor does one succeed;
it is obtained by practitioners of little merit only when I am pleased. (12)
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, the procedure for the section on internal subjugation, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

"Difficult to obtain" refers to the rite of subjugation (*vaśyavidhāna*). Since it is characterized by yogins through the practices of the *samaya*, it is the "characteristic of the *samaya*-practice" rite of subjugation.
"Unfortunate" means having little merit from previous lives.
Regarding the phrase "by those of little merit": it is not obtained by these practitioners who possess only small present merit; however, it is obtained again by me when I am pleased. (11-12)

The rite of subjugation (*vaśya-karma*) performed even upon one who is already under control is that by which the "Section on Subjugation" (*vaśyādhikāra*)—the method of homa involving medicinal substances and so forth—is governed;
that chapter (*paṭala*) by which it is prescribed is the thirty-seventh (*saptatriṃśattama*).
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the *Śrī-Ḍākinīvajrapañjara-vivṛti* (The Commentary on the Glorious *Hakrasaṃvara*). 37.
The thirty-eighth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Secret Abodes of the Yoginīs and the Haunts of the Heroes.

Then follow the secret signs (*chommaka*) of the ḍākinīs, the characteristics of the body, and likewise the classification of the limbs of the heroes; whatever is to be accomplished is already accomplished therein.
Since this has been declared in the Tantra to be entirely secret, he says "therefore," and so forth.
The *chommakas* are the secret signs mentioned in the text, such as "Ḍā" for "man," and so on.
In the specific case of Turviśeṣa:

the Ḍākinīs, such as Pracaṇḍā and others, [provide] the body, hands, and so forth; for the purpose of giving the *chommaka* (secret signs), its characteristic consists of the class of marks, scents, and so on belonging to the Ḍākinī family.
The breaking of the limbs of a hero, such as the face, mouth, arms, and so forth; likewise, [the breaking of] "and so on"—this must be concealed. || 1 ||
Vīreśvara neither writes it nor recites it before anyone;
he should conceal it in every way, for the practice of the Left (vāmācāra) is well-guarded. 2.

It should also be understood that the yogin Vīreśvara neither writes nor speaks of the *chommaka* (secret signs) and so forth, nor of the piercing of the limbs of the heroes (*vīrāṅgabhedana*). "In the presence of someone" means in the presence of those belonging to other tantras and the like.
"One should not recite" refers to the tantra;
it is well-guarded as the "left-hand practice."
The secret signs (*chommaka*) and so forth have been well concealed by those practitioners of the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara* who follow the left-hand path (*vāmācāra*).
If a mantra-practitioner recites the secret-characteristic ḍākinīs out of negligence,
I do not see even a thousand ḍākinīs of his in any way.
That evil-minded one is not to be eaten. || 3 ||

If the mantra-practitioner recites the *Guhyalakṣaṇa-ḍākinīs* out of negligence— that is, if the *ḍākinī* residing in the book recites, writes, or speaks due to negligence, which is a lack of attention to her own duties— [the following occurs].
"I do not see that" means that I do not see [the attainment of] success (*siddhi*) and so forth.
Furthermore, he says "and other things as well": "A thousand *ḍākinīs* are to be devoured in many ways."
The meaning is that this occurs for him. The word "no" indicates a shake of the head [in negation].
Why? He says: "He is evil-natured," and so forth. That...

The suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*), meaning "one who is very wicked" (*sudurātmaka*). "Self" (*ātman*) refers to the distinguished mind (*viśiṣṭaṃ citta*). || 3 ||
He is a destroyer of the sacred bond, one of evil conduct, and a slayer of Brahmins—of this there is no doubt.
This wicked-souled fool is a sinner in his behavior and has been utterly deceived.
The *samayas* are the mantras, mudrās, and established doctrines; the *brahmans* are the Buddhas.
One who practices only evil is a "practitioner of evil" (*pāpācāra*). Therefore, one whose conduct is wicked and whose disposition is unrighteous is a "wicked practitioner" (*durācāra*).
"Deluded" means utterly foolish;
"deceived" because of separation from what is desired; "this one" refers to the author of the recitation and so forth. || 4 ||
I am not his protector when he is being devoured by the yoginīs;
in the midst of the guhyakas, that practitioner is merely a sacrificial animal.

And I am not the protector of that evil-minded one of wicked form as he is being devoured by the *yoginīs*. Why is this so? He says: they conceal, cover, and protect, thus they are *guhyakās*, the *yoginīs*. The particle *tu* has the sense of "also. Of those who protect—
Even among them, he is like a sacrificial animal, specifically a goat, because he is to be slain due to his great transgression;
such is the practitioner.
Therefore, the word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction. || 5 ||
That betrayer of his guru and violator of the samaya is fallen from the world of the Buddhas;
whereas he who protects the tantra of Śrī Heruka, whose appearance is formidable, [is saved]. (6)
"Fallen," and so forth.
"The Buddha-world" refers to the appearance of a Buddha in the world;
he would thus become fallen even from that.
This is the state of being; and that consists of treachery toward the Guru and treachery toward the *samaya*.
Furthermore, as for him who protects—that is, guards—the *tantra* of the venerable Heruka’s terrible vision—
Because it generates fear in those who have not realized the truth. || 6 ||
I shall show favor to that person of auspicious countenance along with the ḍākinīs;
the gurus will grant their approval, and the practitioners will keep it secret. || 7 ||
I am its benefactor; "benefaction" (anugraha) means a particular kind of affection. [The form] "ḍākinī" is derived by the elision of the third case ending.
He is one who favors others in such a way that their faces become bright and auspicious;
they give their consent.
Even the teachers approve of him;
they conceal him and hide him. Upon seeing him, other practitioners embrace him.
Alternatively, the meaning is that "concealment" (gūhana) refers to establishing among the virtuous people of the world that "this is the casting aside of his [the opponent's] position. || 7 ||
He is always beloved by the yoginīs, and for him there is no doubt regarding the attainment of siddhi;
the practitioner attains heroism and becomes the sovereign of the sky-goers in the three worlds.
The practitioner who desires the state of a hero becomes honored everywhere;
yoga proceeds for him, and he attains the oral tradition.
"One who desires heroism" means one who longs for the state of being a hero; for such a person,
yoga proceeds.
The yoga of continuous application proceeds as meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
He finds and receives from the presence of the guru the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) and the approval regarding the forms of the objects of knowledge belonging to perfected disciples. (8–9)
But having seen the heroic Ācārya who observes the vow of Śrī Heruka, the practitioner, rejoicing at every sight, [should act] with this mantra. (10)
"Vīra" [is so called] because of being fearless in the course of worldly life.
"One who maintains the vow of Śrī Heruka" refers to one who [follows] what is taught in his own scripture.
Because he is a protector;
the connection is that another practitioner should rejoice upon seeing his heroism.
"Having seen, having seen" means repeatedly.

"By this mantra" means that the practitioner, characterized by the yoga of Śrī Heruka, should rejoice at the mere sight of others who are likewise characterized [by it]. This is the intended meaning. || 10 ||
One should recite the hero who is supreme through the root mantra seven times, interspersed with the *praṇava* and the syllable *hūṃ*. || 11 ||
Having bowed with effort to those [deities] who are worshipped by all the Buddhas and others, one will undoubtedly always sport with the Great Hero. 12.
The connection is as follows: while reciting the root mantra as stated, one should bow down to those who observe the vow of Śrī Heruka and rejoice with effort.
To the question "What then? he says: "Worshipped by all the Buddhas and others."

There should be worship of Vajradhara and the others. Regarding that, as for how one should prostrate, he says: because that yogin is engaged in the play of the Great Hero Śrī Heruka, this [prostration] occurs for those who behold him as a yogin. (11–12)
Vārāhī resides in their hearts, established in non-duality with the Heroine-Yoginī;
therefore, by the sight of that merit of that noble-born living being, [he attains liberation]. 13.
Regarding the question "What [happens] for those who remember?", he says: "Of them," and so forth.
Those in whose hearts the heroes reside—namely, those who observe the vow of Śrī Heruka—are called "those in whose hearts the heroes reside" (*hṛdisthavīrāḥ*).
The singular genitive case is used in the sense of the plural nominative.
In the phrase "yoginyam advayasthitam," the substitution of *am* for the plural ending occurs according to the rules of etymological derivation (*nirukta*).
Therefore, this is the meaning:
from what source do such beings arise?
Because they are [the result] of those yogis—
Thus, the goddesses abide in a non-dual form.
Therefore, because of this, for beings of noble birth,
it is due to their meritorious vision.
How is it so for him?
Because, through the sight of his merit as one who maintains the vow of Śrī Heruka, living beings experience auspicious births. || 13 ||
On riverbanks and seashores, on mountains and at crossroads, at ponds, wells, lotus-pools, deserted dwellings, and gateways. (14)
Thus, with blood-red eyes, the ḍākinīs are stationed everywhere, as well as in the Mahābhairava cremation ground, in the netherworld (pātāla), and likewise in the sky (khecarī). || 15 ||
Together with those many terrifying and mighty Vetālas,
the great hero sports at his pleasure.
In hollows, caves, and secret places, the hidden female yoginī sports with the practitioner in those various locations and regions. (17)
