Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Secret Abode of the Heroes, the Region where the Yoginīs are to be Accomplished," in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
He states the place of play with the words beginning "river" and so forth:
"with bloodshot eyes," because of their passion upon seeing one who observes the vow of Śrī Heruka.
The word "ca" (and) expresses joy.
"Kuhara" means a cave; "gahvara" means the interior of a mountain.
In the secret, dense forest;
that place where hidden human yoginīs reside is the "Gūḍhamānuṣyayoginīsthāna" (the abode of hidden human yoginīs).
This is an adjective qualifying all [the items] beginning with rivers. || 14–17 ||
The abodes of the Yoginīs themselves are prescribed as the secret dwelling places of the heroes; because of this, this chapter is so designated. It is the thirty-eighth, the *aṣṭatriṃśattama*.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 38.
The thirty-ninth chapter on the ritual of the loud laughter of the Vision [of the Goddess].
Now, the great adept-yogi reveals the eightfold laughter-mantra to him and bestows it; of this there is no doubt. (1)
The word "atha" (now) indicates that immediately after the locations of the Yoginīs, [the practice] proceeds sequentially through laughter.

In whatever manner it becomes eightfold, thus the great accomplished master (*mahāsiddhayogī*)— the practitioner of Śrī Heruka— is [established] in the great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*), namely, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā.

And the mantra here is: *kili kili cili cili sili sili dhili dhili*; this is the remainder of the mantra of the King of Vidyās, by which there is eightfold laughter. Also, with the mantra of the Goddess, *hā hā he he ho ho hūṃ hūṃ*, there is eightfold laughter.
The passage beginning with "tataḥ" and so forth is easy to understand. || 1 ||
With a terrible and loud sound, the fearsome ḍākinīs,
upon hearing it, tremble before that hero and flee in all directions.
If the hero does not fear, he is taken by those ḍākinīs together with them, grasping him by the left hand, and led to their own city. || 3 ||
He says that one must not fear even when surrounded by yoginīs who are terrifying: "The [yoginīs] flee from that hero who is afraid.
The word "ca" (and) means "because. "From that" means from the surrounding.
"The hero does not fear."

If the hero does not fear, then he is seized by them by the left hand and led to their own city; thus, this is the dual purpose, which he expresses as: "Then, having been seized by the left hand, he is led to their own city by them."
"With the ḍākinīs" (ḍākinīsārddham) is [an example of] the elision of the third case ending. || 2-3 ||
One who desires the power of Śrī Heruka is led to the state of Khecarī;
delighting there eternally, one shall go to Sukhāvatī. || 4 ||
Neither old age nor death exists anywhere for the practitioner whose very form is mantra. || 5 ||
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual of the Terrifying Laughter of Vision, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
"By one desiring the power of Śrī Heruka" means by one who longs for union with Śrī Heruka; "the state of Khecarī" is Sukhāvatī.
This very place is explained as "one's own city."
Aging and death do not exist everywhere because those two are born of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The sense is that when that [construction] is abandoned, they too are abandoned.
To the question "Why is conceptual construction itself abandoned?", he says: "The practitioner is the embodiment of mantra. *Mantra*...
The direct realization of the true nature of all phenomena; the sense is that [the yogin] consists of that very essence. (4–5)
"Vision" (*darśana*) is the perception of the *ḍākinīs*, and "loud laughter" (*aṭṭahāsa*); that by which these two are performed is the chapter (*paṭala*), and thus it is so called.
It is the thirty-ninth (*ūnacatvāriṃśattama*). Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 39.
The fortieth chapter: The procedure for practicing the great mudrā that subjugates by means of the five colors.
Thereafter, I shall fully explain that by which one may bring a mortal under control;
by this, a hero established in the ritual of mantra-yoga attains success within a month.
Now he teaches the chapter on the fire-offering (*homa*) for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), beginning with the words "Then," and so forth;
for once sentient beings have been subjugated, they can be directed toward one's own teaching.
Thereafter, I shall explain it.

To the question "What is that?", he says: "by which one may bring a mortal under control. The meaning is: that *homa* by which one may bring a being who is not already submissive (*avaśam*) under one's control (*vaśam*).
And as to how long it takes for that to be accomplished, he says: "It is accomplished in a month.
Of what nature is the hero? He is one who abides by the ritual procedure of mantra-yoga. [This refers to] mantra and so forth—
The meaning is "that which was previously [stated]. || 1 ||
Flesh combined with fish-meat and *unmattaka* [liquor], even in every circumstance, brings the Lord of Heroes to the practitioner within seven days. (2)
If one devoted to the night-homa performs it three times a day with exactly one hundred and eight oblations, he bestows the great siddhi.
Within seven days, one shall bring under control the king together with his army by means of half [the portion], the heroic minister by half of that, and the [other] minister by half of that again.

He explains by whose application [the practice] is accomplished: "meat" and "fishes" as previously mentioned. It should be understood that with meat there is the external *homa*, and with those fishes there is the internal one.
Even in every state, the Lord of Heroes, Śrī Heruka, though possessing four arms and so forth,
[is attained] within seven days.
Having performed the offering of one hundred and eight oblations three times a day for three months, then, by means of the homa performed for seven days, the objective is accomplished.
It bestows accomplishment upon the practitioner.
Regarding the phrase "devoted to the night-homa": "night" (*niśā*) is a conventional term for wisdom (*prajñā*). Wisdom—
The sense is that one should perform the oblation while being disciplined (*yukta*).
He states this very point with the words beginning with "a hundred," etc., where *sarvatantra* means "in all cases" (*sarvatra*) as a collective conjunction. By half [of the verse].
"By fifty-four oblations.
"By half of that," meaning by twenty-seven.
The connection is that one should bring the minister, who handles matters such as peace and war, under control. (2.4)
For the vassal kings, one should perform oblations according to the sequence of thirty-two fire-offerings;
for a Brāhmaṇa, however, one should offer twenty oblations over the course of seven days.
In this manner, one should offer oblations seven times for a Kṣatriya and five for a Vaiśya;
for a Śūdra there should be three, and for one of the lowest caste (antyaja), one should offer only once.
Seated upon a single seat, the heroic practitioner, following the lineage tradition, shall attract all sentient beings by means of the power of the mantra. (7)
In the case of neighboring kings and others, thirty-two oblations should be offered in the evening for the sake of those who practice yoga and so forth.
The phrase "one should perform the homa according to the sequence of oblations" establishes that the oblations are to be offered according to the sequence of the letters.
He says this very thing with the words "twenty," and so forth:
one should offer twenty oblations for a Brāhmaṇa,
but only three for a Śūdra.
There are three oblations;
one should offer one for the outcaste.
"One [should] offer once" means one should give a single oblation;
this is for the sake of outcasts (caṇḍāla) and others. "Resorting to a single seat" means...
Taking refuge in Śrī Heruka. || 5-7 ||
Acting thus, the mortal hero who fulfills his desires according to the prescribed rule and practices the yoga of the deity shall attain an auspicious aeon.
The practitioner will be pleasing to the ḍākinīs; there is no doubt about this. || 9 ||
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, titled "The Procedure for Practicing the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) for Subjugation through the Five Colors. || 40 ||
Showing that a person may be devoid of observances, vows, and the like, he says: "But at will," and so forth.
One enjoys forms, sounds, and other objects of desire at will, according to the prescribed rules—that is, according to the rules for the yoga of the deity.
The intention is that one who practices the five strands of sensual pleasure should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
To the question "What then?", he says: "He shall obtain"—the ellipsis being "the accomplishment of subjugation" (vaśīkaraṇasiddhi). || 8–9 ||
The subjugation of the five colors is performed, preceded by which the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā is prescribed; because this is the chapter [dealing with that], it is so called.
It is the fortieth [chapter].
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 40.
The forty-first chapter: The ritual procedure for the arrangement of the twenty-four-syllable maṇḍala.
Now follows the most excellent and supreme rite, by which practitioners come to know [the methods for] subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, killing, expulsion, and so forth.
Yawning, paralysis, delusion, and indeed pinning; the seizing away of speech, as well as muteness, deafness, and blindness. (2)
Causing impotence, as well as the transformation of form—one who practices these twelve great rites should always accomplish them. (3)
Success comes for the practitioner by mere remembrance; of this there is no doubt.
Among all the most excellent [sites], the Ḍākinīs are all-pervading, beginning with the sacred seats (pīṭha). || 4 ||

Regarding the question of what kind of accomplishment of action (*karmasiddhi*) belongs to a yogin who has attained power, the word "atha" (now) introduces the response. Thereupon the Blessed One said: "The supreme action," meaning the most excellent.
It should be understood that this is so because it brings about the desired object with preeminence.
To the question "How so?", he says: "by which practitioners know.
This means that the knowledge of the practitioner is supreme. To the question "Why is that?", he says: "subjugation," and so forth.
Now, "I shall explain the excellent ritual" (*atha karmavaraṃ vakṣye*);
this reading found in some versions is easily understood.
[It concerns] subjugation and attraction (*vaśyākarṣaṇa*).
Subjugation, attraction, killing, and expulsion— these twelve are the extensions of ritual action (*karmaprasara*).
Through the mere recollection or thought of these great rites, their accomplishment arises for the practitioner.
He states the locations of the twenty-four Yoginīs: "In all the most excellent [sites]," meaning in the preeminent *pīṭhas* and so forth.
The term "pīṭhādi" (the seats and so forth) [is used] by eliding the locative case ending; "sarvavyāpinī" (all-pervading) [is used] by eliding the nominative plural ending.
The word "tu" (but/however) [indicates] that there are exactly twenty-four ḍākinīs in the seats and so forth.
It qualifies [the subject]. || 1-4 ||
Those who are born in various regions, endowed with knowledge within their own wombs, are called ḍākinīs; they are the mistresses of the vajra-maṇḍala. (5)
In Kulatā, in a secluded place, and likewise in the city of Sindhū,
in Suvarṇadvīpa, and in Saurāṣṭra, she is Gṛhadevatā.
In the city of the Pretas, in the region of Himavat, in Kāñcī, in the country of Lampāka, as well as in Kaliṅga, Kośala, Triśakuni, and Roḍraka; || 7 ||
In Kāmarūpa, Mālava, Devīkoṭṭa, and Rāmeśvara;
at the Godāvarī and the Urvaḍā, as well as in Oḍḍiyāna and Jālandhara. || 8 ||
The daughters of Pullīra, Malaya, and the others pervade the non-dual hero;
they are all capable of assuming any form at will for the sake of quelling the speed of the mind.
"In their own wombs" means in their own lineages. "The mistresses of the Vajra-maṇḍala" refers to the consorts of the Śrī Heruka maṇḍala.
By the words "in Kulatā," and so forth, he indicates the locations—having first mentioned them by the general term "pīṭhas" and so on, they are then specified as "in Kulatā," and so forth.
When [the practice] is being performed, the cremation grounds and so forth should be understood as extending up to the sacred seats (*pīṭha*).
This is for the purpose of instruction.
[The list begins with] Pullīramalaya and so on—
The *pīṭhas* and so forth are to be understood by means of these words;
[the term] "house-deity" (*gṛhadevatā*) is due to the elision of the locative case,
and "triśakuni" is used in the sense of the locative.
The word "first" (*prathamā*) has the same meaning as the word "likewise" (*tathā*).
To the question of where else these Vajramaṇḍala leaders are located, it is stated:
"in Kulatā," and so forth.

Regarding these regions such as Arbuda and so forth, he says: those of which Oḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Pullīra, and Malaya are the first are "Oḍiyāna-Jālandhara-Pullīra-Malaya and so forth," namely Arbuda and the others ending with Kulatā.
The underlying intention is that, having taken Pullīra-Malaya as the starting point, they exist in Jālandhara, Oḍiyāna, Arbuda, and so on; this is for the purpose of instruction.
This is the instruction on the sequence of manifestation.
By this, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Yoginīs in the mandala and in the body at Pullīramalaya and other locations has been explained.
[She is] the Mother (*putriṇī*), the Virgin (*kanyā*), who pervades the non-duality of the Heroes (*vīra*).

Because the maidens (kanyāḥ) always remain in that very state, their character is pervaded by non-duality with the heroes such as Khaṇḍakapālī and others; thus [the term] is formed, with the elision of the case-ending.
Puṃ, Jāṃ, Oṃ, Aṃ, Goṃ, Rāṃ.
*Ḍaṃ māṃ kāṃ oṃ trīṃ koṃ kaṃ laṃ kāṃ hiṃ preṃ gṛṃ sāṃ suṃ naṃ siṃ maṃ kuṃ*.
These twenty-four syllables, which constitute the mantra, are concealed.
From these—along with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the bindu, and the *nāda*—as follows:

When [the goddesses] have arisen in sequence and reside within the body at Pullīramalaya and so forth, those born from the mantras such as "oṃ kara kara pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ" and so on are to be meditated upon.
[They are called] "those who take form at will."
Their forms are dependent upon mere desire.
To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "for the cessation of the mind's impulse.
When the mind is engaged in a particular purpose, once that is accomplished, [the impulse ceases].
The cessation of the movement of the mind. || 5-9 ||
The six Yoginīs are in Kulatā; the six Mothers are in the Maru country;
Lāmā is in the Sindhu country; and the Kulanāyikās are in the city.
In Lampāka and Saurāṣṭra, the family deities reside;
in Pretapurī, there is Mahākanyā, the Ḍākinī who assumes various forms. (11)
It is said that she dwells with her daughter on the Himālaya and in Kāñcī;
in the region of Pañcāla she is the household deity, and in Kaliṅga she is the observer of vows. (12)
In Kośala, the Piśitāśanas; in Pretapurī, the Vajraḍākinīs; and in Sthūleśvara and Triśakuni, those born from the Kula of Khaṇḍarohā. (13)
In Pullīramalaya and on the Golden Mountain (Kanakādri), there were twenty-one thousand women born of the Caṇḍāla caste. || 14 ||
He says "the six yoginīs," etc., to explain that those of the same class who wander in the outer regions are being set forth.
Among those residing within the body or within the mandalas at Pullīramalaya and so forth, Pracaṇḍā and the others are to be known in their respective order;
however, in the outer regions, those of the same class may be arranged in whatever way is appropriate.
Vajravārāhī, Yāminī, and the others are the six Mothers; they possess the forms of the seven Mothers in the region of Maru. They belong to the lineage of Lāmā and are the leaders of the families.
"Born from the family of Śrī Heruka;
in Lampāka and Saurāṣṭra, they are the family deities.
This means that they should be worshipped in the form of the family deities.
In the city of the pretas, there is the great maiden Ḍākinī Saharūpiṇī;
she is a ḍākinī in the form of a maiden, belonging to the class of Rūpiṇīs. [She resides] on the Himālaya.
And in Kāñcī, there are those known as Sabālikās;
that is, those belonging to the class of Sabālikās.
In the region of Pañcāla, there are household deities (gṛhadevatā).
In Devatā and Kaliṅga, they are observers of vows;
in Kośala, they are flesh-eaters and consumers of great meat; and in Pretapurī, they are Vajraḍākinīs.
The Yoginīs born in Pretapurī possess non-dual knowledge;
those born from the Kula of Khaṇḍarohā reside in Sthūleśvara and other such places.
"At Pullīramalaya, on the Golden Mountain"—
here, the mention of "twenty-one thousand women of the lowest castes" is for the purpose of indicating their great number. (10–14)
Indeed, however many other yoginīs of Śrī Heruka there may be among the remaining [deities], they are the mistresses of his maṇḍala in the Great Yoga of Śrī Heruka. 15.
"Indeed, as many as there are among the others" means that in other regions as well, they are of such a kind; "yāvantyo" is equivalent to "yāvatyaḥ."
"Yoginīs of Śrī Heruka" [is formed] by eliding the first plural ending; thus,
there are thirty-six yoginīs who are the mandala-deities of Śrī Heruka.
The Great Churner is the nature of wisdom and means; or rather, Śrī Heruka is endowed with that means.

The meaning is that among those [goddesses] who are associated with him whose form is wisdom (*prajñā*), the leader of the mandala, Vajravārāhī, has entered into union. The "great churning" is the emanation (*nirmāṇa*) which is indivisible;
for their emanation is to be accomplished by Śrī Heruka.
Some say she is the leader of the Śrī Heruka Mahāmudrā Maṇḍala. (15)
The three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, are pervaded by the twenty-four ḍākinīs;
for this is the commitment (samaya) of the ḍākinīs, which has been fashioned and meditated upon. 16.
"Twenty-four" means that the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, which is the very nature of body, speech, and mind, is pervaded by twenty-four. Why is this so?
He says: "For this is the pledge (*samaya*) of the *ḍākinīs*."
This is the instruction on the *samaya*.
To the question "How much is this? he says:
"It is emanated."
Because its measure (*māna*) has emerged as limited (*mita*), that [meditation] is so described.
To the question, "Is this the direct fruit of these [meditations]? he says: "And that is cultivated."
The meaning is that he has attained sovereign power. || 16 ||

Whatever [practice] such as meditation may exist on the surface of the earth during the Pūrṇā [day], one should always follow the left-hand path (vāmācāra), remain naked, and be concentrated at night. || 17 ||

"Whatever there may be, such as meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and so forth, on the surface of the earth in [the state of] Fullness (*pūrṇā*)," means that whatever practices such as meditative absorption exist,
which are connected with mantras, mudrās, and so forth, those belong to the *ḍākinīs* alone.
"Mahī" means when the ground is full, complete, and its very nature is the surface;
"nagna" means uncovered.
"At night" refers to equanimity. || 17 ||
The heroic yoginīs and all the heroes born of heroes are pleased;
worship of the self-arisen ones should be performed with the offering of the dance of mudrās.
All tasks, without exception, are accomplished through the worship of Vāmā. || 18 ||
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, the procedure for the placement of the twenty-four-syllable maṇḍala, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
To the question "What is the result of that?", he says: "All," and so forth.
Those who arise from the Hero, Śrī Heruka, are the "arisen from the Hero" (vīrasambhavāḥ), namely the heroes such as Khaṇḍakapāla and the others.
And the Yoginīs, beginning with Pracaṇḍā, are pleased.
Mudrā is the union with the deity; by means of that, there is the offering of dance.
It is not, however, by way of being ordinary.
Therefore, worship should always be performed with the self-arisen *bodhicitta* conjoined with *rajas*.
Thus has been described the purity of worship, because the worship of the left is superior. || 18 ||

The twenty-four secret syllables beginning with *pu* constitute the maṇḍala; it is that by which the placement (*nyāsa*) of the assembly of that many yoginīs is prescribed, and thus this chapter is so named. This is the forty-first [chapter].
The fortieth [chapter].
Thus ends the forty-first chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 41.
The forty-second chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Illusion of the Form of the Laughter-Mantra Yoginī.
Then the hero, having drunk the flower-water, should recollect this mantra;
likewise, the practitioner should perform a dance there together with the mudrā.
One should perform the consumption of meat at night, consecrated by the mantra.
By drinking and likewise giving this curd-whey (mastu) in this manner, it brings about happiness. || 2 ||
Having been touched, the woman of noble family laughs; by means of truth, she becomes a celibate practitioner.
At the conclusion of the sādhana, through the mudrās of laughter, she then becomes one who possesses pride in her gaze.
Explaining the laughter indicated in the thirty-ninth chapter, he speaks this chapter on its mantra and so forth, beginning with "Then" (*tataḥ*).
Since this laughter cannot occur without the mantra and so forth, the hero is one endowed with the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*).
This mantra consists of eight words.
Or one should recollect or recite the seven-syllable mantra. Having done what?
Having drunk the flower-water, which is the bodhicitta mixed with pollen,
one should then perform a dance with the vajra-step together with the consort, the Prajñā.
The connection is that one should consume meat at night; of what nature? Triple-constrained (*triyantrita*).
It is constrained by the three, beginning with the body.
Nevertheless, he asks "by what? and replies "by this. By the word "this," the address is referred to.
He states the mantra: "May it be a bringer of happiness.
*Oṃ astu sukhāvahaṃ hūṃ*—this is the mantra.
In some places, it is "oṃ sukhāvaha hūṃ.
Having consecrated the five nectars and so forth with this very [mantra], they should be employed.
He says that one should give it to others as well: "Having drunk and likewise having given.
Having touched [the substance] for those who have taken the vow (*samayin*), and having become joyful, one should laugh after giving it in accordance with the mantra.

Therefore, he says: "He should laugh. In the reading "having asked," it should be construed as: having asked, "Are you well? he should laugh. "Of noble lineage" (*mahākulī*) and "of great vows" (*mahāvrati*) mean one who is engaged in the practice (*caryāyogi*).
"By truth is she a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacāriṇī).
It should be understood that truth is Brahman and austerity is Brahman; and austerity is what is spoken of here.

The external mudrā, being thus constituted, should perform laughter. Having done what? It says: "the object to be accomplished" (sādhya), and so forth. One who accomplishes is the "object to be accomplished," namely, the practitioner (sādhaka).
At the conclusion of tasting those five nectars, having seen [the consort] characterized by the mudrā of laughter,
one should perform laughter.
Of what nature is she?
"Proud of views" (dṛṣṭigarvā): she is so called because she possesses pride through that view—that is, through its perception. Such is the consciousness that comes to be.
"By this" means by the [mantras] beginning with *kili kilī* and those beginning with *hāhā*. Laughter (*hasanam*) is "laughter" (*hāsyam*); it is established by the suffix *ṇyat*.

The connection is that the former practitioner should laugh by means of tasting the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). And since she is his external mudrā, it should be applied in the same way; thus it is established that there is laughter for both wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*).
This is shown by the words beginning with "by truth" (*satyena*).
Some say that another yoginī, seeing the practitioner in such a state, might laugh. (1–3)
Indeed, by means of this, one should produce laughter both by night and by day;
likewise, O Hero, hear now as it truly is the formative action (rūpakarma) which is the trunk (śuṇḍa). || 4 ||
Then there was dancing, the shedding of tears out of devotion, as well as self-exertion,
the leaping over the thunderbolt, and likewise worship while naked.
This is the sequence of the group of mudrās for all the Vāmeśvarīs:
exhaling, impelling, laughing, and the wonderful dance of erotic passion.
Whatever one should perform before the Viśva, one should recollect the mudrās and mantras;
the eightfold laughter—hā hā, he he—is most dear to the Sovereign of the Universe.

"At night" refers to the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*), whose nature is the subsiding of the relish for conceptualizations regarding external objects; "by day" refers to the innate (*sahaja*) bliss, whose nature is pure self-consciousness alone.
The word "and" (*ca*) signifies the conjunction of these two—bliss (*ānanda*) and supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).
In that way, it indicates the meaning of suchness (*tathatā*), which is the thorough knowledge of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-parijñāna*).
The sense is that whatever is performed within innate awakening (*sahaja-avabodha*) attains the state of reality (*tattva-daśā*). [The word] *bahi-*...
The meaning is quite clear.
Having seen that yogin, the yoginīs residing in the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and other locations display unprecedented forms and actions; thus he says "rūpa" and so forth.
The action (karma) or activity of form—that is, of one's own essential nature (svarūpa)—is secret (guhya), because it is revealed only in such a manner.
Just as it was established by the heroic Tathāgatas, he says that very thing: "Dance," and so forth.
First there is the dance, and then it occurs through the falling of tears from the eyes; thus it is without grammatical case-endings (*nirvibhaktika*).
The performance [of the ritual] is done with devotion;
personal exertion is rising up by oneself;
and from the word "likewise" (tathā), [one should offer] the arghya water and so forth.
In the reading "with devotion, there is the bristling of the hair," this refers to horripilation born of affection (*sneha*).
He describes the practitioner’s activity contained within that [state] with the words beginning "of the vajra," etc. [The word] *laṅgha*—
The meaning is "the arising of the vajra," which is the supreme state (*namatiśaya*).
In the reading *alaṅghanam*, it means that [the practitioner] leaps entirely, either as "I" or as "prior."
It is precisely for the sake of supreme delight (*ratiśaya*).
In the reading *ālambana*, it means "attaining" (*prāpaṇa*), which is the action [of attaining]; and by the Yoginī, there is the attainment of the Vajra. Therefore...
He said: "In that same way, there is worship even by the naked. This means by virtue of being unrestrained;
[this applies] to all the Vāmeśvarīs, the Yoginīs.
For this very reason, it is for yogins.
The word "tu" (but/then) indicates a distinction:
this sequence of the host of mudrās, as well as the vajra-leap and so forth, [is for them].
By means of the exhalations (*recaka*) and so forth,
one should specifically perform the visualization before oneself, in the presence of the yoginīs who performed the preliminary rites; [this involves] the mudrās and mantras.
The mantra of the laughter-mudrā.
He states that very [mantra]: "hā hā he he," and so forth.
"hā hā he he" constitutes the eightfold laughter.
The connection is that one should recollect the *hāsa-mudrā*.
By the word "others" (*apareṣām*), the inclusion of "ho ho hūṃ hūṃ" is intended,
because of the statement that words ending in the plural number, such as these, serve as indicators of a group (*gaṇa*).
The latter half of this mantra is also taken up, beginning with "kili kilī" and so forth,
ending with "the supreme beloved of Viśveśvarī."

These letters are exceedingly dear to the Yoginī. According to the reading "the specific practices (*viśeṣacaryāḥ*) are supremely dear," this refers to the specific practices consisting of ritual actions such as dancing and so forth. (4–7)
For in their presence, there arises a cry of "Alas! accompanied by weeping and tears;
through that very [practice], she becomes dear to them when properly joined with meditation and mantra.
The yoginīs of the heroes experience pleasure along with horripilation and other signs;
those who are conceived as "left" (vāmā) perform the leaping over the vajra. 9.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, the procedure for the laughter-mantra and the form of the Yoginīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
Then they utter cries ending in "Hā!
Hā! Therefore it is said: "For here, in his presence, there is the cry of 'Hā! Hā!'". It is further stated that they constantly shed tears of weeping: "He causes the shedding of tears of weeping."
Along with that very shedding of tears, even the cry of "Alas! Alas!
would become dear to them.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because they are well-joined with meditation and mantra."
The sense is that these yoginīs, being well-joined and restrained through meditation and mantra, will become joyful upon seeing one of their own kind;
thus, for both the yoginīs and the yogins, there arises mutual joy, mutual horripilation, and so forth.
He says that the crossing over by means of the vajra occurs at the tip of the cough:
"of the vajra," and so forth.
Those who are conceived as the left-handed yoginīs—
It should be understood that they are indicated by such phrases as "in front of them" and so forth, because they are perceived through the observation of conventions and the like. || 8-9 ||

The laughter-mantra and the illusion of the Yoginī-form are prescribed therein; because it is that by which this is established, it is called a "chapter" (*paṭala*). It is the forty-second, the forty-fourth.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 42.
The thirty-third chapter: The Ritual Manual for the Accomplishment of the Upahṛdaya Rite.
Now I shall describe the visualization of the heroic non-dual man;
for one who knows the rules regarding the distinctions of places, meditative cultivation is always most dear.
Now follow the gazing at the Yoginīs and the naked worship.
He speaks the chapter on the ritual procedure for the seven-syllable mantra, beginning with "atha" and so forth.
"Atha" means immediately after the explanation of the laughter and other [expressions].
The connection is that he will explain the "observation" (avalokanā) and so forth.
"Man" (nara) is used because he is the supreme among men. "Having known" refers to knowing the disposition (āśaya) of those to be trained (vineya).
Because the existence of that which is supported depends upon the support. || 1 ||
Whether at a crossroads, in a house, at a site of heroes, or on a mountain, the ḍākinīs behold their place of assembly even from afar. || 2 ||
By the words "at a crossroads," etc., he states the different locations— the sense being that meditation should be performed right here.
Or "in the house" means, first of all, in the house itself.
He speaks of "beholding" in the passage beginning with "beholding," and so forth.
They abide for the sake of the *samaya* (the pledge), that is, for the sake of the meaning of the *samaya* and so on. || 2 ||
The ritual application of the Nagnapūjana-mudrā is now described further: having cast aside another garment, one should desire the mudrā and touch her with it. (3)

"The ritual application of the *nagnapūjanamudrā* is explained hereafter"—thus concludes the instruction on naked worship (*nagnapūjā*). Regarding the ritual action, he says "having cast off," and so forth: having cast off other garments or skins and the like, the naked one, having put them on, should desire the *mudrā*.
"One should touch with that" means that by means of that action, one should become happy. || 3 ||
In this very manner, acting as the principal agent, one should cause all the rites to be performed;
likewise, perform the binding of the directions with the root mantras and the other four [mantras].
"Thus" means that nakedness and the wearing of skins are drawn forth.
"All actions" refers to eating and so forth.
The root mantra is eight—
Pada: [Regarding the slaying of one who performs cruel deeds by means of assault, there is another four-footed *sumbha* mantra.
The instruction is that these two should be recited upon seeing the Yoginī.
The binding of the directions (*digbandha*) and so forth should be performed by way of projection (*ākṣepa*) at the time of meditation and other such practices. Therefore, he says:
"The binding of the directions with four [mantras] in that manner.
There is an alternative reading: "Performing the binding of the directions in that manner."
Regarding the "turnings of the directional binding" (*digbandhāvartana*):
it should be explained that one performs these turnings of the directional binding by means of the mantra itself.
Thus, [the word] "perform" (*kuru*) [is used].

All rites such as worship and so forth [should be performed] with the root mantras; likewise, "perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) with the other four" is the alternative reading. In this case, it should be construed as: "perform all rites with the root mantras, and perform the binding of the directions with the other four four-line [mantras]."

The term *digbandha* [is used] with the elision of the second case ending. There are two instances of the word *tathā*; it should be explained as meaning "in such and such a manner" according to the distinction of types. || 4 ||
Even by the hosts of gods in heaven, she could not be seen during her worship;
having cast upward a handful of flowers, she became a sky-farer, completely filling the space above.
No flower fallen there from the [offered] leaf is seen upon the ground;
one may thereby bring under control a thousand sky-faring goddesses (khecarīs) residing therein.
The Gopī said: "In worship, it would not be seen even by the hosts of gods in heaven.
She spoke of the power of the seven-syllable mantra: "Having thrown a full handful of flowers upward, one becomes a sky-walker (khecarī)."

The meaning is that one should raise up the full handful of flowers (*kusumāñjali*) over which the seven-syllable mantra has been recited; and by that, he becomes a *khecarī*, a *khecara* situated in the intermediate space (*antarīkṣa*). This refers to the *añjali*.
The feminine gender is used due to the usage of the *ṛṣi* [Vedic/authoritative source].
Therefore, he says "not there," and so forth;
for it is seen right there that the flower does not fall.
On earth... "A thousand," and so forth, is easily understood. || 5-6 ||
Having also drawn forth Vāgīśa and Mātṛkā, he knows them in their proper order,
as well as the divine, divine narratives, and likewise the movement of the luminaries.
In subterranean villages, forests, and cities, at crossroads, under solitary trees, in the houses of heroes, on mountain peaks, or likewise in the sky; || 8 ||

He knows Vāgīśa Bṛhaspati and his mother Vāṇī; he knows the divine account, that which occurs in heaven. "Divine account" refers to the stories of the celestial Yoginīs. He knows the movement of the luminaries, the planets. Regarding "Pātāla": [he knows it].
He knows what occurred in the seven netherworlds (pātālas).
"In a village," and so forth; that is, in Nandigrāma and other such places.
In the forest, in the great forest;
in cities such as Vardhamāna and others;
and in the hero’s house, which is the abode of the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapāla) and other spirits.
In the sky, that is, in the atmosphere;
on the peak, that is, on the mountain peak. || 7-8 ||
They remember the *hṛdaya* and *upahṛdaya*, yet they are not seen by gods or humans;
therefore, practitioners always remain in these places.
Those who remember and recite the seven-syllable Heart and Sub-Heart mantras in these locations are not seen by gods or humans.
The meaning is that in these places, the accomplishment of invisibility (*adṛśyasiddhi*) arises from that recitation.
Therefore, the conclusion is that practitioners always reside in these places; the sense is that this mantra is to be recited in these very locations. || 9 ||
Having meditated upon the seven-syllabled mantra at the top of a red-colored tree, one may cause even mountains that have been broken to be restored; otherwise, they remain as such.
Having placed [the mantra] upon his own body, he should lie on the ground on a seat of darbha grass;
he should mutter the seven-syllabled mantra one hundred and eight times.
In a dream, he reveals everything that is desired by the mind—whether it be an untimely death, something lost, or whatever other matter may have occurred. (12)
By means of mantra-recitation upon a sword, a thumb, water, a lamp, or a mirror,
the practitioner of mantra, through constant self-yoga, should cause Prasena to descend.
"Consisting of seven syllables" means that he whose constituent syllables consist of the number seven is thus described;
having meditated upon him at the tip of a tree.
One should bend the tree;
[it is] unbroken and undivided.
Thus, the state of being bound by desire is shown.
"Bhūdharān" means rocky mountains. "Ātmakāya" means for the sake of one's own purpose;
the reading is "ātmakāma."
This is easy to understand.
Regarding "in one's own body": having placed the six syllables in the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and the syllable *phaṭ* in the mind, one should lie down upon a seat of *darbha* grass.
The remainder is easily understood. The mantra declares that the lifespan shall last for this many years; or [it refers to] Śrī Heruka.
"Slain by death" means that he has gone from the presence of death; "vanished" means having become invisible. From the region—
The phrase "all" is a summary that includes other effects situated within the interval.
She refers to the deity. Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over a sword and so forth, one should cause the light of the Prasena to descend. || 10–13 ||
Having meditated thus and having recited [the mantra] seven times, one should reveal the auspicious and the inauspicious;
then the hero, having applied the seven-syllable mantra according to its divisions. (14)
Having reflected upon the diseased person, one should recite the mantra a thousand times while focused on the center of the sun;
[in an instant, one should visualize a consciousness the size of a thumb].
One should show the one afflicted by disease as being like the form of a crystal. 15.
By the mere sight [of it], there will undoubtedly be the destruction of disease;
the sick person shall become free from illness, like the autumnal moon.
One should show a sword or similar object to a girl or a young woman;

those two will declare whether it is auspicious or inauspicious. Now, with the words beginning "atha," he speaks of the pacification of disease: having directly inscribed the seven-syllable mantra within the sun [disk] using yellow orpiment or other substances.

Having written it or meditated upon it, one should visualize the afflicted person in its center and recite [the mantra] one thousand times; this is done by means of separation and interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*). It is like the appearance of crystal because of its purity.
One should show that person afflicted by disease; "one should see" means one should meditate upon it. In the alternative reading *sphaṭikākṣarasadṛśam*, it means syllables as white as crystal.
One whose mantras are similar and auspicious is such [a practitioner];
one should visualize such a mantra and show it to the hand of the person afflicted by disease.
The accusative case is to be explained as having the sense of the dative.
Regarding the phrase "from the moment, [he is] the size of a thumb":
one should meditate upon consciousness in his heart, equal in measure to a thumb and like pure crystal.

Of what nature is it? It is that from which all various diseases have departed; thus, one should meditate upon this body and consciousness as being liberated from all diseases and recite the mantra—this is the collective meaning of verses 14–16.
Having thus placed the wheel in the left hand in the center of the moon,
which resembles crystal and syllables, one who has been afflicted by all diseases is liberated once it is so placed.
He states another yoga, beginning with "the moon" (śaśi), and so forth.
That which has the left hand is the "left-hand wheel" (vāmahastacakraka).
Having visualized the lunar disc in the left hand, one should contemplate a nine-square wheel there, with the syllable *Oṃ* in its center.
In the east is Hrīḥ; in the south, Ha; in the west, Hṛ; in the north, Hlaṃ.
Again, HŪṂ in the center;
PHAṬ in each of the four corners. This is the seven-syllable mantra.
Excluding the letter *ṭa*, there are seven syllables;
some say it is the syllable *oṃ*.
Therefore, he says: "the crystal-syllable..."
"Kāśam" means that the wheel is such because it possesses *kāśa*, which is light (*prakāśa*), due to the seven syllables being white like crystal through their distribution (*saṃvibhāga*).
Furthermore, it is such because all diseases (*sarvavyādhi*) are deposited (*vinyasta*) therein.
One should meditate on the left hand [of the deity] as being the wheel of the neutral objects of attainment; such is the oral instruction. || 17 ||
Fever, possession by spirits and the like, epilepsy, colic, leprosy, and likewise all diseases born of poison—there is no doubt that these are all [cured]. (18)
"Jvaretyādi":
the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*),
because it is from [this medicine] that the disease of those bitten by venomous creatures and so forth is broken.
"Diseases such as those caused by the poison of a snake-bite within a wheel" (cakrāntardaṣṭaviṣādi): by the word "etc. (ādi), poisons from stationary sources and so forth are included.
The particle "tu" is used for emphasis.
Since all disturbances have departed from it, that is the "all-disease" [sarvavyādhi]. || 18 ||
Having meditated on the syllable within the lunar disc, [the enemies] flee in the ten directions.
At night, one should indeed grind cow-flesh with the three sweets in the secret place.
Having learned the seven-syllable mantra, one should perform eight thousand oblations;
on the following day, the practitioner of the mantra shall obtain a thousand palas of gold.
By performing ten thousand oblations, one shall obtain Surāṣṭra;
or else, one may contemplate the King of Mantras anywhere at all.
He is born right there at that very moment; of this there is no doubt.
Through the white [syllable] peace is produced, while through the black [syllable] one may cause death in an instant.
By means of red [sindūra], one becomes a subduer and immediate attraction occurs;
by means of yellow, there is the overcoming of all—this is the certainty of the scripture. (23)
By means of yellow [meditation], one certainly gains prowess over ships, machines, elephants, and armies;
by the mere thought of white, one is surely liberated from death.
Even when seized by hundreds of great serpents, he quickly awakens from their fangs;
likewise, even when rendered unconscious by poison, he regains consciousness upon seeing it. (25)
One seized by fever, planetary spirits, or epilepsy will become terrified upon seeing [the practitioner's] hand;
moreover, a person should always perform mental recitation while clenching their fist in battle.
For as long as the fist is not released, everything indeed succeeds;
for even an enemy with raised weapon is [held at bay] as long as the fist remains clenched.
Even if one so desires, it is simply not possible to cast away one's weapons;
or rather, in all matters, it is indeed accomplished in this very way.
Regarding "the syllable on the moon-disk":
as before, having seen and meditated upon the left hand with the seven syllables placed upon the moon-disk,
one should show it to one afflicted by disease, or one should wipe away [the affliction] with it.
"They flee in the ten directions"— the rays of those syllables are the ten directions, such as the east and so forth, whose nature is the flowing nectar.

"Vidravanti" means they pervade. The sense is that one should display the left hand with its syllables (*akṣara*) having such a nature, and by means of it, one should wipe away [the impurity]. He states the fire-oblation (*homa*) beginning with "cow-flesh," and so forth.
The "three sweets" are jaggery, honey, and sugar.
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "the king of mantras":
he states that where one contemplates [this mantra] for the sake of pacification and so forth, there pacification and the like arise; thus, at that time, it arises therein—of this there is no doubt.

Regarding "doubt," he states the recitation: "with white," and so forth, up to "one should immediately attract. Having seen [the deity] as red in color, one should [hold] the left hand with the seven-syllable [mantra].
With the words "Or else," and so forth,
he demonstrates the signs of accomplishment (*siddhiliṅga*), showing that for one who recites the mantra, everything is accomplished in this very manner. (19–28)
With leaves, flowers, fruits, betel, and likewise with food—this is the first [type of] bodily union; the second is that which pertains to one's power (śaktika). || 29 ||
The third is indeed by means of speech, and the fourth is not perceived,
even upon the earth girdled by the ocean and covered with trees.
By means of this king of mantras, accomplishment here is certain;
within the three realms of existence, both moving and unmoving, it is indeed possible to bring about what is beneficial and what is harmful. (31)
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, the procedure for the accomplishment of rites through the *upahṛdaya*, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 43.

"With vessels" means with useful items; "with various betel-leaves" refers to the maintenance of the body. "The second [type of person] is powerful according to his capacity"—the sense is that even non-human beings become his servants.
The third [type] is from speech alone;
the meaning is that it is the accomplishment of speech.
The meaning is that the king of mantras has been contemplated.
As it is said: "Mantra, mantra is declared to be the utterance that impels the reality."
The yogi is the one who bestows curses or favors through speech, body, and mind. || 29–31 ||

The *hṛdayopahṛda* refers to the ritual action; that by which the task to be accomplished—such as the rite of casting flowers (*kusumapātana*) and so forth—is performed is called a *paṭala*, and thus it is so designated. This is the forty-third [chapter]. The forty-fourth.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. || 43 ||
The forty-fourth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Seven-Syllable Mantra of the Six Yoginīs.
Now, having thoroughly mastered the messenger (dūtī) by means of those joined with the seven syllables, whatever rite one undertakes there is swiftly accomplished in that very instant.
Having performed the placement of the six Yoginīs according to the rite of the seven syllables, one should fashion the wheel situated in the hand according to that same procedure.
Having meditated upon the one who bears form, the King of Mantras, accompanied by the exhortation from the left,
reveals his hand to him while being uttered from his own mouth.
Now, regarding "atha": the expansion of the ritual activities of the mantras of the six Yoginīs is introduced.
That expansion of ritual activity is that wherein the messenger (dūtī) is accomplished and becomes manifest.
Having done what is it introduced? He says: "having commenced the ritual action" (*karma samārabhya*).
It should be understood that the expansion of ritual action is introduced after performing the acts of attraction and so forth.

By what means? He says: "having accomplished [them] through those joined with seven syllables. The mantra of the six Yoginīs is to be distributed and accomplished—that is, to be realized—by means of oneself.
Its "conjunctions" (saṃyutāni) are the meditations on their combinations.
The ritual action is stated as "kara" and so forth.
*Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ hreṃ huṃ hūṃ phaṭ* is the seven-syllable mantra.
[It refers to] the six yoginīs.
The connection is that one should attract the target after having placed those seven syllables and six yoginīs in the middle of the hand. To explain the placement, he says "six," and so forth:
the wheel situated in the configuration of six spokes, wherein the attraction occurs, is that [wheel] of six—
The word *saṃsthitam* (situated) is an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇam*).
Therefore, it refers to a specific [position].
The word *vāma* (left) is a modifier of the middle of the hand. Six—
One should attract him by showing one's hand in such a way that the wheel becomes stabilized;
therefore, it is said: "to whomsoever one shows the hand."
Having done what, and to whom does he show his hand? He says: having meditated upon the *cakra* (wheel), which bears the form of that which is to be drawn forth.

Again, having done what? He says: having uttered with the mouth "the King of Mantras," with the elision of the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyālope*). [The word] *ṣaḍ*— (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be part of a commentary on a tantric ritual manual. The translation reflects the technical grammatical analysis and ritual context.)
Having uttered the seven-syllable [mantra] related to the Yoginī with the mouth— this is specified because it is to be meditated upon—
he asks what kind of king of mantras it is, and says: "endowed with the impulsion."
Having visualized a six-spoked wheel in the left hand, one should place the syllable *oṃ* in its center.
On the five spokes, one should arrange the six syllables: *hāṃ hrīṃ hreṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
By means of the net of rays [emanating] from those [syllables], which take the form of hooks—
Having visualized the target being led away, one should show the hand marked with the wheel to him;
reciting the mantra accompanied by the command, "Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ hreṃ hūṃ phaṭ, attract Devadatta! while manifesting the hand visibly, one attracts him—thus it is said.
The meaning of inheritance. 1-3.
One should certainly draw [the target] using red sandalwood, black mustard, the dust from the foot of the person to be accomplished, and likewise salt. (4)
Having unified [the substances] and examined them, one should then churn them with both hands;
at night, one should offer oblations to the Yoginī in a Caṇḍāla fire according to the prescribed rule.

Or one should offer the powder into the funeral pyre fire; the person to be acted upon will become submissive. Having begun this practice, one should likewise recite [the mantra] up to one hundred times.
By that [mantra], the one who is to be accomplished is certainly drawn forth;
for when this application is perfected, one may bring wealth and men under one's control.
I do not speak otherwise; having taken the dust from his feet and mixing it with iron filings, it should be wrapped in a cloth from a cremation ground.
Having recited [the mantra] seven times at a crossroads, one should dig eight finger-breadths into the earth;
there, one should conceal that powder together with the name of the enemy.
If one should mutter [the mantra] with cow’s milk, he will be defeated;
however, by using that same powder with effort, there shall be a restoration once again.
Moreover, by taking that powder, success is indeed attained; there is no doubt.
Having added the five intoxicants, it should be wrapped in a cloth from a cremation ground.
One should write the name of the enemy there and perform the recitation one hundred times;
by concealing that in a cremation ground, the target will become insane.
Having carefully uprooted it and bathed it with cow’s milk, it will undoubtedly attain success; once released, it returns to its original state. || 13 ||
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, concerning the ritual procedure for the seven-syllable [mantra] of the six yoginīs. 44.

Having ground red sandalwood and other substances with both hands while reciting the mantra, the yogi should offer them as an oblation into the funeral pyre fire or the fire of a *caṇḍāla*, likewise accompanied by the injunction,
according to the prescribed rule.
The ritual procedure (*vidhi*) consists of the preparation of red sandalwood and other materials; that in which an eminent yogin performs this application is the fire offering (*havana*),
by virtue of its being based upon Śrī Heruka.
Those very same substances, such as red sandalwood and so forth, having been ground into powder, together with the dust from the feet [of the preceptor],
and accompanied by the name of the enemy— this is what is enjoined.
The meaning is that restoration is achieved by means of pure cow's milk;
the remainder is easily understood. || 4-13 ||
The six Yoginīs consist of the nature of seven syllables; that chapter in which their activities, such as summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*) and so forth, are prescribed is thus [described].
It is the forty-fourth.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. || 44 ||
The forty-fifth chapter: The Ritual for the Summoning of the Accomplishment of Action and Speech of the Six Yoginīs.
Now follows the supreme and most excellent ritual for achieving the accomplishment of speech.
Having collected one hundred and eight red *karavīra* flowers,
one should cause them to be consecrated by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times over cow’s milk.

Now, following the mantra-activity expansion consisting of the seven syllables of the *Ṣaḍyoginī-kavaca* mantra, he speaks the chapter on the mantra-activity expansion consisting of the remaining six syllables, beginning with "atha" and so forth.
"Atha" means after the explanation of the mantra-activity expansion consisting of the seven syllables of the *Ṣaḍyoginī-kavaca* mantra;
it should be understood that the "excellent rite" (*karmavara*) pertains to the six-syllable mantra.
*Oṃ vaṃ yoṃ moṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is the mantra; its function is to accomplish that [mantra’s] attainment.
The accomplishment through speech is direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). This—
[Vāha] says: "Karavīra," and so forth.
One hundred and eight flowers of the red *karavīra*, [to be offered] with cow's milk, with diligence.
Through the consecration by means of ritual action, one should perform [the rite] with one hundred and eight recitations. || 1 ||
One should strike the top of the linga with a flower consecrated by reciting [the mantra] once;
one should do this day after day for seven days, remaining well-composed.
Then, on the eleventh day, flowers should be taken;
having gone to a great river, one should cause each one to float away.
Then, with each flower consecrated by reciting [the mantra] once, he should strike the top of the *liṅga*.
He, the yogin of the deity, being well-composed, should do this for seven days.
"Then, on the eleventh day" means after seven days; the particle *tu* has the sense of "indeed" (*evārthe*).
Up until the eleventh day, those four days should not be included;
however, during those days, the mantra must also be recited there at the three junctions of the day (trisandhyam).
Therefore, "tu" signifies a special distinction regarding the eleventh day.
"Let it be properly grasped each day"— meaning let it be grasped after having correctly observed it without error— "let it be tied," this refers to the general action;
and the instruction is that the thread for tying should be made from the bark of the *karavīra* tree.
He states the distinction: "But the flowers... The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "eva" (only/itself).
The meaning is: "those very same flowers."
The great river is free from drying up;
"tu" is used for conjunction (*samuccaya*), for the sense of "but" (*vai-stadātva*), or for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*);
it certainly (*vai*) never [dries up]. 2–3.
One should employ all of those by reciting [the mantra] once over them in successive order;
however, in the case of a river, one should cast the final flower upstream against the current.
Having taken that [liquid] mixed with water, one should drink it without touching it with the teeth;
thus the practitioner attains perfection of speech, as revealed in the Guhyatantra.
He explains how the procession is conducted: "all of them in successive order.
At the time of striking, one should perform the placement of the first and subsequent flowers in rows, having understood the sequence.

Likewise, some say it consists of the binding (*granthana*) and the subsequent recitation (*pravāhaṇa*), as well as the sequence of the time of binding (*granthanakālānupūrvī*). Others say it is the "final flower" (*paścimapuṣpa*) of the time of striking (*tāḍanakāla*) and the "final flower" of the time of binding (*granthanakāla*).
It flows against the current (*pratistrotaṃ prapāti*). That which, having transcended the force of the current, moves upstream through the power of mantra—that is it.
The remainder is easily understood.
He for whom there is the accomplishment of speech is such a practitioner;
the meaning is that this is a chapter extracted from the Guhyatantra. || 4-5 ||

Having bound the *yoginī-yoga-mudrā*, the practitioner of mantra, facing the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, [visualizing it] as residing within the very belly of that person to be accomplished.
The wise man, with his mind fixed upon that [deity], should move the little finger at the three junctions of the day;
even a slayer of a Brahmin shall bring Indra and others under his control within seven days.
Having fashioned an image of the person to be acted upon with the powder of red sandalwood, its limbs smeared with the three pungent spices (trikaṭuka) and anointed with beeswax; || 8 ||
Having pierced her at the secret place with a copper needle,
the wise practitioner should heat her for seven days with smokeless charcoal of khadira wood.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred times, the king, along with his vassals and domestic priest,
shall then swiftly summon the inner apartments together with their retinue.
One should have the king, together with his retinue, inscribed upon birch bark;
one should write their names, interlaced [with mantras], using the lac-dye and yellow pigment of a *preta*.
Facing whom one should recite [the mantra], one should heat [that person] with a fire of *khadira* wood for the sake of attaining success in a cemetery, heating until the wax has melted.
When the king, that universal monarch, is being heated,
he draws forth the dust from the feet and red sandalwood of the one to be accomplished (sādhya).

Having assumed the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka) of the Yoginī-yoga-mudrā and having performed the vajra-bind, one should join the tips of the two middle fingers with the tips of the two thumbs, and then raise the two index fingers and join their tips together; thus some call it the Yoginī-yoga-mudrā.
Even when the reading is "yonimudrā" in certain places, it is this very same mudrā.
Immediately following this, it should be understood that there is recitation (*japa*). To explain how one should recite, he says "of the object to be accomplished" (*sādhyasya*), and so forth.
One should take the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*) as the six-syllable garland of the six Yoginīs, together with the *vidarbha* [intercalation], situated within the yantra.
Having placed [the mantra] inside the belly of an effigy of the target made from dust from the target's feet and so forth, one should move it and recite [the mantra].
How should one recite it? He says: facing toward the effigy of the target.

Remaining with that mantra in mind at the three junctions of the day, one shall bring Indra and the other gods under control by reciting it seven times for eight weeks, totaling one hundred and eight repetitions each time.
Ending in seven hundred and fifty-six. One should attract by means of those endings in "hundred" (śatānta).
"Then" refers to the totality.
The remainder is easily understood. || 6-13 ||
The practitioner, having gathered together the ashes discarded in a cremation ground,
should diligently heat them with smokeless embers of Khadira wood.
Having rubbed that dust with both hands, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Having performed the oblation until success is attained, one should indeed take up the dust itself.
Having restrained the breath, one should certainly bury that distracted [person] there;
she will become unconscious, deprived of consciousness, and afflicted.
And she was utterly deluded. || 16 ||

One should bury the dust of that [person], namely the ash from a funeral pyre, or the dust from a heated effigy, or dried [ash]. "The dust of the *homa*" refers to the smoke-dust of the fire sacrifice.
The remainder is easily understood. || 14–16 ||
Arriving with the speed of the wind, she falls upon the practitioner;
the wise one should then cause her to act as either a *paśu* or a *dūtī*, or he should divide her [between them]. 17.
Then indeed one should perform the rite and the seizing of the messenger (dūtī);
having taken a fresh Karavīra creeper measuring the length of an arm.
Having inscribed the mantra for whichever ritual the practitioner intends to perform, he should cast that creeper even into a blazing fire of thought. || 19 ||
Having quickly seized it from there, before it has been consumed by fire,
one should brandish it while recollecting Yama and having empowered it seven times with the mantra.

With the words "the animal," etc., he states another ritual application— one should cause a man or a woman to perform the rite desired by oneself. For that very reason follows the taking of a messenger (dūtī) and the subjugation of the messenger.
"Moist, the length of an arm" means: moist and measuring one arm's length. Having taken a *karavīra* creeper, upon which [the name] has been inscribed with the mantra.
"By means of interweaving whose name"— the meaning is that one should write that very mantra;
"but for one who performs the rite," however.
In the case of a reversal for a man or a woman, [one should act] with the Aparākṣara mantra of the Ṣaḍyoginīkavaca.
"He" refers to the man; "she" refers to the woman. (17–20)
At that very moment, she comes to the excellent woman in her own form with the speed of the wind;
the practitioner, during the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism, should recite [the mantra] one hundred times over a red karavīra flower.
A flower smeared with gorocana and placed in water, having been taken down into a great river and held in water reaching up to the navel; || 22 ||
Placed within the hollow of the palms and consecrated a thousand times with the mantra,
one should drink it along with water held in both hands until they are full.
Therefore, he says: "or in an excellent woman, in her own form.
Regarding "in an excellent woman," this means *varastrīm*. He states another application for the accomplishment of speech (*vāk-siddhi*): "the red flower of the *karavīra*," and so forth.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times under the Puṣya asterism,
it should be taken up. Then, that flower, smeared with *gorocanā* and placed together with water and *madana*, should be applied.

In that regard, one should perform the recitation one hundred and eight times. Then, having entered water reaching to the navel in a great river, one should recite it one thousand times with both hands.

Immediately after the thousand recitations, the water— which is full and contains unbroken *kesara* flowers and so forth— is placed by the *uttarasādhaka* into the cupped hands (*añjali*) of the *sādhaka*. Thus [it is said].
Where that flower, having been placed within the hollowed palms of the superior practitioner, is held with both of one's own hands. || 21-13 ||
Then success shall be his; the practitioner shall indeed achieve mastery over speech.
He will certainly attract a king or a queen by means of his mind alone. (24)
He swiftly brings gods, asuras, and humans under his control;
when enraged, he can kill with his mere word and even perform their eradication.
The practitioner restrains [all things] with his speech, saying "It is even so";
he can paralyze a river, a cart, a machine, or even the ocean by mere words alone.
By means of speech, one creates all things— elephants, horses, clouds, men, or even birds— whatever is desired by the mind.

He states the purpose of the accomplishment of speech (*vāksiddhi*) with the words beginning "the king," etc.: "One may kill a king by means of speech when enraged, and likewise effect his expulsion."
The eradication of the unequal, his eradication;
and elephants, horses, and likewise clouds— those elephants, horses, and clouds.
"Wherever there is a desire in the mind," [it means that] one performs the drawing [of the breath] and so forth toward whatever the mind desires. || 24–27 ||
Now, for the practice of attraction which causes the enchantment of all women:
having taken a red flower, one should gather [it] from the *karavīra* tree. (28)
Having empowered it with the mantra recited seven times, one should place it within the vagina;
having enclosed that flower, one should apply it to the secret place. || 29 ||
The practitioner, possessing the yoga of non-dual knowledge, should recite the mantra one hundred and one times;
then the adept should take one flower from among those situated within the womb.
Whomever one strikes with a flower, that person shall instantly become submissive—
distraught, deprived of consciousness, and entirely under the other's control in all the joints of their limbs.
And he quickly brings [the object] under his control if the conviction is firm;
this is the accomplishment of conviction, which unfailingly effects subjugation. (32)
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, the ritual procedure for the attraction [of beings] through the accomplishment of action and speech of the six yoginīs. || 45 ||
With the words "attraction" (*ākarṣaṇa*) and so forth, he states another application; that is easy to understand.
Regarding the phrase "if the cognition (*pratyaya*) ceases": cognition exists in that which possesses consciousness, but not in wood, stone, and the like. (28–32)
The mantra consists of the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) of the six yoginīs and another six-syllable mantra;
its ritual application is the "activity of the six yoginīs" (*ṣaḍyoginīkarma*).

That which effects the summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*) through the perfection of speech—that is, through the accomplishment of speech—is the chapter (*paṭala*) by which this is accomplished, and thus it is so designated.
The forty-fifth [chapter], the forty-fifth.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 45.
The forty-sixth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Five *Ha*-Syllables.
Now, the five *ha*-syllables accomplish all rites;
by the mere knowledge of which, swift accomplishment proceeds.
Now he states the ritual function of the five *hakāra*s, beginning with "atha" and so forth:
"Now the ritual procedure of the five *hakāra*s is set forth.
Regarding the phrase "of the five *hakāra*s":
The function of the five *hakāra*s is the task to be accomplished; or rather, it is the yogi who is the accomplisher of that expansion of the syllable *ha*. || 1 ||
One should crush the two hands with the five *ha*-sounds: *hā*, *hī*, *hai*, *hau*, and *haḥ*.
Even by means of the mouth of one who is thus impelled, blood flows forth at that very moment, and one shall kill the enemy.
One should rub one's own blood contained in a skull-cup with the blood from the ring finger until it dries up;
then the target will perish. || 3 ||
If, being angry and with bloodshot eyes, one recites the mantra with a blazing intensity,
one quickly kills the king along with his army, forces, and vehicles.
He states the five *hakāras*: *hā*, *hī*, *hai*, *hau*, *haḥ*—this is the pentad of *hakāras*.
Without the sixth vowel, the *hakāra* is distinguished by the remaining five vowels from the extraction of the six *vīra*-armour mantras (*ṣaḍvīrakavaca*).
The connection is that one should rub the two hands joined with five *bāṇas* by means of the five *hakāras*.
Therefore, he says: "the five *hakāras*."
Regarding "the two hands," this refers to the five *ha*-hand gestures;
having visualized a five-spoked wheel in the two hands, or having actually drawn it there, one places the five syllables upon it.
The collective meaning is that one should erase those two after either reflecting upon them or having written them down.
Since the word "five" refers to individual instances, when the letter *u* is also included, there are six *ha*s: *hā*, *hī*, *hū*, *hai*, *hau*, and *haḥ*.
Some say that the mantra consists of five *ha* syllables and is six-syllabled;
others say it is blood even from the mouth.

Having pierced the five vessels with a needle-like tip, one should visualize the blood being drawn out and residing within the skull; by doing so, he kills the enemy at that very moment. He states another application: "The blood of a dog," and so forth.
The ring finger is childless;
its blood, which is the menstrual flow, becomes dried up.
The meaning is that one becomes heated.
This should be performed by merely reciting the five *ha* syllables,
if [the opponent] is angry.
With these and other words, he describes the accomplishment of recitation (*japa*): having smeared both palms with poison, *rājikā*, and so forth,

and having written the five *ha*-syllables upon them as before using yellow orpiment, crystal, and the like with a pen made from a crow’s wing-feather, and having likewise visualized them through meditation, one should rub the dust from the feet of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) with both hands in a fire of *khadira* charcoal embers and offer [it] as an oblation (*juhuyāt*) according to the section on names.
The previous [rite]. By that very mantra, the enemy then vomits blood from the mouth and dies; so say some. (2–4)
One should offer oblations to the cat, the mongoose, the dog, the crow, the crane, the jackal, and the ḍākinī;
for these bring swift accomplishment in this tantra, without a doubt. (5)
He states the application of the *homa* offering, beginning with "mārjāra" and so forth.
"Ibhya" means a lord;
"jambuka" is used because it is an archaic (Vedic) form.
With the flesh of these [beings],
one should perform a fire offering preceded by an oblation to the ḍākinīs;
thus, one should practice that fire offering of the ḍākinī-oblation.
One should offer a bali-oblation to the ḍākinīs. The meaning is that one should perform the homa with their flesh, preceded by the ritual interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) with this mantra;
it brings about swift accomplishment.
These, namely the cats and so forth, bring about the attainment of sovereignty and other such powers. || 5 ||

Having made a rope from the hair of rabbits and other such animals and having consecrated it one thousand times with mantras, whoever one binds around their neck becomes exactly like that [animal]. || 6 ||

Having consecrated one’s hand a thousand times with mantras and joined each syllable with *karavīra* flowers, one should touch a pregnant woman; she transfers the fetus. When [the mantra] is released, there is liberation.
Whomever one threatens, that person dies; [whomsoever one wills,] one brings back to life again. || 7 ||
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual Procedures for the Five *Ha*-Syllables, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
"Of the rabbit and so forth":
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of the jackal and others is intended. "With the hand" (sahasta) is a form without a case ending; [it means] "the hand."

Having performed the consecration (*abhimantrya*) one thousand times, one should touch a pregnant woman with that [substance] along with *karavīra* flowers. To the question "What by that?", he says: "The fetus," and so forth.
"Joining each syllable individually."
The meaning is that after five hundred thousand recitations (*jāpa*), there follows the application of ritual action (*karmayoga*). Regarding "liberation upon release":
when her body is released by the hand, the liberation consists of the discharge of the fetus. (6–7)
In the applications of the mantras of the armor of the six yoginīs, there is the yoga of Vajravārāhī;

elsewhere, there is the yoga of Śrī Heruka. Because the accomplishment of the crushing of the hands through the activity of the five *hakāras* is prescribed therein, this chapter is so named. [Forty-six]...
The hundredth [is] the forty-sixth.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 46.
The seventy-fifth chapter: The Procedure for All Rituals of the Mantra of All Buddha-Ḍākinīs.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which is in the heart of all ḍākinīs;
by its mere utterance, there arises the fruit of all accomplishments.
Now he explains the expansion of the ritual activities of the *vajravārāhī-upahṛdaya* mantra, beginning with "atha ata" and so forth.
"Atha" (now) means immediately after the explanation of the expansion of the fivefold rituals of the letter *ha*.
The connection is: "I shall explain the *sarvaḍākinī* in its heart. *Sarva-ḍākinī* refers to the heart-mantra of Vajravārāhī;
"in its heart" means in the heart [of that mantra].
This means the near-heart mantra (upahṛdaya-mantra) of Vajravārāhī:
Oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā. Therefore, I shall now fully explain it.
Since the arising of the fruit of all accomplishments occurs [thereby], he says "by this" and so forth:
"I shall fully explain the arising of the fruit of all accomplishments by means of this recited [mantra]. Of that...
Because the *upahṛdaya* (subsidiary heart-mantra) is yet to be explained, one might ask: "How is it that 'all ḍākinīs' constitute its heart? [The answer is:
because of the expansion of its ritual activity (*karmaprasara*).
Because it is cultivated with certainty. || 1 ||
Then, by reciting the great vidyā-mantra of the ḍākinī, one brings all castes under one's control;
by constant recitation, one produces great prosperity.

Having prepared a stake made of human bone, consecrated one hundred and eight times with the six-limbed mantra, and burying it at someone's door, that person’s lineage is destroyed. If one buries it in a field, a cow-pen, or a place where buffaloes, elephants, or horses are kept, it destroys those [animals].
Destruction occurs. || 2 ||
The word *tataḥ* means "because of the fruit. It is "that" (*sā*) which is both the *ḍākinī-mahāvidyā* and that which is being recited; thus, it is [referred to] as such.
The term *ṣaḍaṅgulā* is without a case-ending.
"Extinction of the lineage" means that even his births are completely cut off; such is the sense. || 2 ||
Now, one who desires to bring a king or a royal minister under control should, being wise, fashion an image out of clay at the palace gate and place it eight finger-breadths high.
On the first day, he should offer three citron fruits mixed with flowers.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations, and [the target] becomes submissive.
By this very mantra, one performs attraction, paralysis, withering, delusion, crushing, the taking away of speech, blindness, muteness, and dismissal. || 3 ||
"An image made of clay":
in its heart, one should place its name written on birch bark or similar material, pierced by that mantra; one should conceal it at the king's gate.
"Eight finger-breadths" means that one should dig down to that depth and conceal it;
beyond that, [it is] for the mother—
Three *luṅga* flowers are to be offered;
thereafter, one should offer those same flowers another sixteen thousand times. || 3 ||

Now, for one who desires to turn a man into a woman: one should collect the flowers of a dead man, the fruits of the *kākāṇḍī* plant, and the skin, nails, and so forth from the feet of a hungry person; these should be made into equal portions.
One should grind them with the blood of a rabbit. [Eleventh...]
One should prepare a pill and dry it in the shade.
Thus, having tied it on one's hand on an auspicious day, on the twelfth day, whoever has the powder placed upon their head becomes a woman. || 4 ||

Now, if one wishes to turn a man into a dog, one should place *puṣpaloha* on the head of a mongoose and recite the mantra eight thousand times over seven nights. On the eighth day, having mixed it with saffron and empowered it one hundred and eight times, one should offer the powder as an oblation. Whomever one places that ash upon the head becomes a dog.
For the purpose of bringing [the object] back, one should perform a great worship of the Ḍākinī at night or during the twilight and offer a bali; thereupon, it becomes natural. || 5 ||
One who desires to turn a substance into a non-substance should offer one hundred and eight oblations of golden fruits; the substance becomes a non-substance.
One should offer oblations of *harītakī* [myrobalan]; it returns to its natural state. Now, one who desires to cause madness [should offer] the dwelling of a great bird (*mahāśakuni*).
One should offer oblations on the seventh day; then there will be an end to consumption.

For the purpose of bringing [something] back, one should offer husks; thus it is pacified. Having collected the hair of a cat during a lunar eclipse, if one offers oblations with a mantra while uttering the name of someone, that person—having taken the ashes—[of whomsoever...]
If he causes it to be placed on his head, he becomes a cat;
if he wins again, he returns to his natural state. || 6 ||
Having consecrated a cord made of crow-tendons with a mantra, if one ties it around someone's neck, that person becomes a crow. In this same way,
one assumes the form of a crow, a pigeon, a peacock, a parrot, an owl, a hawk, or a vulture.
Having made a rope from cowhair and empowered it one hundred and eight times with mantras, if one binds it around the neck of anyone, that person becomes a cow—
of whichever sentient being [it may be].
Having taken a cord of sinew and consecrated it with mantras, he ties it around his neck; he becomes exactly like that [creature].
Having made a cord from the [sinew] of any four-footed animal whatsoever and having consecrated it with mantras, he ties it around his neck; he assumes the form of that [animal].
For one who is liberated, there is liberation. Having consecrated grain with mantras,
one should cast it into the house of a great lord of wealth.
Having consecrated oneself with the remainder, one attracts all wealth within seven nights. || 7 ||
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, the chapter on the ritual procedures for all activities of the mantra of all the Buddhas and Ḍākinīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
Kākāṇḍī fruits are mahākāla fruits. A hungry crow. Puṣpaloha is iron.
*Kīṭa* is *dhuttūraka*.
*Mahāśakuni* is *pecaka*.
"Kākasnāyu" means the tendon of a crow. "By the remainder" refers to what follows.
This is what is meant:
