Immediately after throwing the grain, by sprinkling oneself with water consecrated with that mantra, one who has performed the recitation for seven nights attracts wealth. || 4-7 ||

That by which the mantra-activities of all the Buddha-Ḍākinīs are performed is called a "chapter" (paṭala); this is the forty-seventh (saptacālīśatima). Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 47.
The eightieth chapter, the ritual procedure for the secret maṇḍala which is the abode of all heroes and ḍākinīs.
Now I shall further proclaim another auspicious [teaching] concerning all ḍākinīs:
the heart-mantra of all yoginīs, which accomplishes all desired aims. (1)
The word "atha" (now) indicates that this follows the explanation of the expansion of the ritual application of the *upahṛdaya* mantra.
I shall now fully proclaim another mantra, which is the *hṛdaya*. Therefore, he says: "Sarvaḍākinī... and so forth.
That wherein all the *ḍākinīs* reside is thus the heart.

Regarding the phrase "that which is auspicious" (*yacchubham*): it is used in the sense of "because," meaning because it is auspicious, and because from it the *ḍākinīs* are born, and by whose recitation they become manifest. Of all [beings]...
Because he accomplishes all desired aims for sentient beings, the yogi becomes one who accomplishes all desired aims. || 1 ||
By the mere remembrance of whom even the three worlds tremble, and by the mere constant recollection of whom perfect accomplishment is attained in due course. (2)
By the mere recollection of whom even the three worlds tremble,
and by the mere recollection of whom even the three worlds tremble, and from whom perfect accomplishment and complete enlightenment arise.
It occurs in sequence;
"I shall fully declare that heart-mantra"—this is how it should be construed. || 2 ||
Hā svā ṭpha hūṃ hūṃ yenīrṇavajrava yenīkiḍāddhaburvasa oṃ. || 3 ||
He states that heart-mantra: *hā svā* and so forth.
The mantra is concealed.
*Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajra-*
When describing [the mantra], one should recite: *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. || 3 ||
This mantra is perfected through recitation; it is auspicious and performs all rites.
It belongs to the ḍākinīs and yoginīs, as well as to Khaṇḍarohā and Lāmā. (4)
This mantra is accomplished through recitation alone;
it is devoid of [the need for] writing and so forth.
Consequently, all the previously mentioned rites [are effective].
Those whose nature it is to perform [all actions] are the yogins who perform all deeds;
they are auspicious and pure.
Thus, "the performer of all deeds is auspicious."
In the reading, this is an adjective qualifying the mantra.
To the question "Whose mantra is this?", he says: "Of the ḍākinīs" means of Ḍākinī; "of the yoginīs" means of Rūpiṇī.
The word "tu" (but/and) is used for conjunction.
"Khaṇḍarohā, Lāmaya, and likewise"— that is, Khaṇḍarohā and Lāmaya.
The meaning is "also. || 4 ||
Thus, this mantra is proclaimed for all the yoginīs,
whether they be in the netherworld (pātāla), in heaven (svarga), or likewise again in the mortal world (martya).
Whatever action is performed, [it is auspicious and brings about all accomplishments]; this mantra, which accomplishes all attainments, shall bring all of that to fruition. || 6 ||
There is nothing superior to this in the three worlds, because it is the unsurpassed instruction on divine means. (7)
"Likewise for all" means for all [deities] such as Vajravārāhī and the others. "Such a mantra" refers to a mantra of this kind.
He explains the state of performing all activities by saying "pātāla" and so forth.
"Vartate" means it is known throughout the three worlds. All—
It is the accomplisher of success;
the meaning is that there is no other means of accomplishment superior to this. Why? Because this mantra accomplishes everything.
Thus he says: "The unsurpassed," and so forth.
"This" refers to the heart.
It is called "divine means" because it bestows divine methods.
A regional section. || 5-7 ||
I shall describe the abode of all ḍākinīs concisely, and not in detail:
having depicted a divine mountain where various flowers and fruits arise. (8)
Above that, one should constantly meditate upon the Ḍākinīs,
the Lāmās, the Yoginīs, Khaṇḍarohā, and indeed the heroes among heroes.
Pointing out the *yoginī-nyāsa* that was previously mentioned, he says "all," and so forth.

Although one should have said "having meditated upon" (*bhāvayitvā*), the fact that "having written" (*likhitvā*) is stated indicates that even by writing it down in this manner, one achieves the same accomplishment.
"Mount" refers to Sumeru. "One should constantly meditate upon it" means that one should constantly [visualize] the peaked palace (*kūṭāgāra*) as a continuous stream.
"So be it. Above the gabled pavilion (kūṭāgāra), the ḍākinīs and others are to be visualized according to the sequence of the sādhana. Therefore, he says "the ḍākinīs," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of the heroes":
It should be understood that the twenty-four yoginīs, beginning with Pracaṇḍā, are to be visualized together with the heroes (vīras), beginning with Khaṇḍakapālī;
this is because of the plural number used in the phrase "the ḍākinīs," and so forth.
The same applies to Kākāsyā and the others.
It should be understood that one should likewise meditate upon Vīra and Śrī Heruka. (8–9)
"Hā hā he he" is the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* of the twenty-four heroes;
likewise [it belongs to] Vajrasattva, Vairocana, and Padmanarteśvara. (10)
Śrī Vajraheruka, Ākāśagarbha, and Hayagrīva;
Ratnavajra, Mahābala, Virūpākṣa, and likewise Bhairava. (11)
Vajrabhadra, Subhadra, and indeed Vajrahūṃkāra;
Mahāvīra, Vajrajaṭila, Aṅkuri, and Vajradehaka. || 12 ||
Vajraprabha, Amitābha, Surāvairin, and Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin;
Kaṅkāla, Mahākaṅkāla, and Khaṇḍakapālin as the first.
The entire world, in its totality, is pervaded by the twenty-four heroes;
likewise, the ḍākinīs and yoginīs of the heroes, such as Pracaṇḍā and the others. (14)

The practitioner should visualize [the deities] as residing in the wheels (cakras) in all ritual activities; desiring accomplishment, he should remain well-composed and constantly contemplate himself as being of the nature of the wheel. || 15 ||
Asking what these heroes are like and how many they are, he says: "Hā hā he he," and so forth.
This means the twenty-four heroes characterized by laughter.

"One should visualize the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*"—this is the explanation following the previous summary. He states the detailed explanation by means of the sequence of the heroes, beginning with "Vajrasattva" and so forth;
the word "should visualize" (*bhāvayet*) is to be connected everywhere [in the subsequent verses].
The second [verse] begins with "by Khaṇḍakapālin" (khaṇḍakapālinā).
Regarding the word "etc. (ādi): it refers to that which stands at the beginning;
by that which stands at the beginning, Khaṇḍa-...
The meaning is that one should meditate upon Mahākaṅkāla and the others together with Kapālin.
He states the conclusion by way of number: "of the twenty-four heroes."
The entire maṇḍala and the body [are formed] by twenty-four heroes. Therefore, he says "the world" (*jagat*), because this term denotes the body. Khaṇḍakapālī, Mahākaṅkāla, Kaṅkāla, Vika...
Ṭadaṃṣṭrin, Surāvairin, Amitābha, Vajraprabha, Vajradeha, Aṅkurika, Vajrajaṭila, Mahāvīra,
Vajrahūṃkāra, Subhadra, Vajrabhadra, Bhairava, and Virūpākṣa.
Mahābala, Ratnavajra, Hayagrīva, Ākāśagarbha, Śrīheruka, Padmanarteśvara, Vairocana, and Vajrasattva—
by these eight [Khaṇḍakapālas]...
The mind-wheel is black, [comprised] of the deities from Kapāla up to Vajradeha, who are black;
the speech-wheel is red, [comprised] of the deities from Aṅkura up to Virūpākṣa, who are red; and the body-wheel is white, [comprised] of the deities from Mahābala up to Vajrasattva, who are white.
According to the opinion of the Ācāryas, these may have either two arms or four arms.
[The locations for the mantras are: the head, the topknot (*śikhā*), the right ear, the back of the head, the left ear, the middle of the eyebrows, and the eye.

In the two armpits, the two shoulders, the pair of breasts, the navel, the nose, the mouth, the throat, the heart, the penis, the lingam, the anus, the thighs, the shanks, the toes, the soles of the feet,
the heels, the big toes, and the two knees, one should meditate upon Khaṇḍakapāla and the others, joined with Pracaṇḍā and the rest. Thus, by these...
The pervasion of the body. He states the summary meaning of the *piṇḍārtha*: "Of the heroes, the heroes are the ḍākinīs;
they themselves are the yoginīs. And these...
"Pracaṇḍā and the others are to be seen as residing in the wheel";
by this, the pervasion of the wheel is indicated.
To the question "By whom [is this performed] in all rites, such as those for pacification and so forth?", he says: "by the practitioner" (*sādhaka*).
If one is a practitioner, then it is performed by him; thus he says this.
Concluding [the section], he says: "One should constantly meditate on the nature of the wheel.
The meaning is that one should meditate on that which consists of the assembly of heroes and heroines as being of the nature of the wheel. (10–15)
One should recite the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* according to the previously mentioned procedure;
it is the great wheel, the locus of all accomplishments, and likewise the abode of all attainments. (16)
He speaks of the conclusion of the worship with the words "by that which was previously mentioned," and so forth;
the meaning is: by means of the outer, secret, mental, and essential-nature worships.
He states the object of worship with the words "the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*."
"The Great Wheel" and "Possessing Great Accomplishment" are synonyms; such is the discourse on alternative designations. || 16 ||
The well-spoken words of ten million Buddhas and indeed ten million Heroes, each surrounded by a retinue numbering ten million Yoginīs. (17)
He states the opinion of the Tathāgatas of the past and so forth as follows: "The well-spoken," and so on.
This tantra is the well-spoken word of ten million Buddhas.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the agent;
thus, "even the ten million of heroes" (vīrāṇāṃ koṭim eva) means by means of the very ten million of yoginīs.
He states their multiplicity: "But each individual Yoginī is surrounded by a retinue numbering ten million.
This means that each Yoginī is encircled by Yoginīs numbering one crore (ten million). || 17 ||
The Yoginīs, the Ḍākinīs, Khaṇḍarohā, Rupiṇī, Lāmā and the others, who bring about all accomplishments, are auspicious. (18)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, the ritual procedure for the secret maṇḍala which is the abode of all heroes and ḍākinīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

These are the twelve, beginning with the Ḍākinīs, and the twenty-four, beginning with Pracaṇḍā, as well as Vajravārāhī. He refers to these very ones with the words "yoginī" and so forth; by the word "likewise" (tathā), all of them are included.
To the question "Why are these to be worshipped?", he says: "They bring about all accomplishments and are auspicious. (18)
The heart-mantra of Vajravārāhī, which is the abode of all ḍākinīs, and her secret maṇḍala— since these two are prescribed therein, it is called a "chapter" (paṭala).
The forty-eighth [chapter], the forty-fourth.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 48.
The forty-ninth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for Transforming Form to be Accomplished in Seven Lifetimes.
Now, I shall explain another ritual concerning livestock according to the prescribed rule, by the mere knowledge of which swift accomplishment proceeds.

The mantra-practitioner, having fashioned sacrificial animals out of rice flour in the proper sequence—namely, a donkey, a human, a tortoise, a camel, a jackal, a horse, and so forth—[should proceed]. (2)
In this regard, Viśvavarāha and these others are indeed remembered as sacrificial animals (paśus).
From among them, I shall declare the ritual procedure and how their characteristics should be.
Now, clarifying the process of becoming Śrī Heruka, he says "atha" and so forth.
"Atha" means immediately after the explanation of the heart-mantra of Vajravārāhī and the rest; he says "paśukarma" (the act of the beast).

"Animal rite" (paśukarma) refers to a ritual involving animals, characterized by the attainment [of results] over seven lifetimes. "Made of rice flour" means that *śāli* is a specific type of grain that ripens in the winter.
The animal whose modification (*vikāra*) consists of ground rice flour is described as such;
he speaks of the animal with the words beginning "donkey" (*khara*), and so forth.
"In that place" refers to seven births.
The *viśvavarāha* is a specific type of deer with various colors. It is to be consecrated along with the donkeys and other animals.
The meaning is that one among these [is meant];
and by means of these, the action has already been clarified.
The birth as a donkey and so forth, as a human, a camel, or a goat, is observed for up to seven births;
and that occurs through these very [actions].
Regarding the phrase "from these," etc.: I shall explain how that karma and its characteristics come to be from these seven human births.
It is to be applied. || 1-3 ||
Those who have been born once, twice, thrice, four times, five times, or even six or seven times—these are undoubtedly beasts. (4)
He whose speech is melodious, who gazes with unblinking eyes, who speaks the truth, who is pleasant to behold, and who is always devoted to the true Dharma; || 5 ||
For one whose body is always fragrant finds birth as his own self;
endowed with these characteristics, he is born from seven previous births.
By merely tasting it, one shall assume a divine form;
likewise for whoever applies it as a tilaka, whether by smelling it or merely touching it.
He becomes an accomplished one immediately; he may assume any form at will.
Having taken the *rocanā* (yellow pigment) from his heart, it should be held by the wise man.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "Those who have one birth, two births, three, four, five, or even six or seven births—they are indeed *paśus* (bound souls), of this there is no doubt. Because of their scriptural origin (*ārṣatvāt*) and because they share the characteristics of bound souls (*paśu-sādharmyāt*), they are called *paśus*.
He states the characteristic:
"fragrant," and so forth.
He states the function: "by that," and so forth.

The meaning is that upon merely smelling it or touching it, one becomes a possessor of a divine form. Whoever applies this *tilaka* immediately becomes a perfected being (*siddha*); he assumes whatever form he desires. He [assumes] his own desired—
"Rūpadharo hyasau" is an alternative reading.
He states by whom the *tilaka* should be made: "with *rocanā*, etc. [The word] "having taken" (*gṛhītvā*) is understood through the modification of the case ending from "of you two" (*vām*). (4–8)
Having recited the heart-mantra, one should apply a tilaka to him;
and whatever being’s form one desires to assume, [one should do so].
By means of a tilaka made from that respective substance, one becomes that very form; of this there is no doubt.
Having taken the juice of the vṛkṣaparṇī plant along with yellow pigment (rocanā) and mercury (budha), [one should apply it].
Having applied a tilaka on the forehead, one becomes identical in form to him, without a doubt;
indeed, one should bind the hair of a sacrificial animal upon the hand and the head.

Alternatively, if one mixes the five parts of a tree and likewise combines them with its hair, and binds it upon the hand or the head, one will undoubtedly become identical in form to that [tree]. || 12 ||
Furthermore, a man who practices yoga and recites mantras is certainly not incapable of blocking the path to accomplishments such as the subduing of thorns, afflictions, and propitiations. (13)

Regarding the phrase "with the heart-mantra": he explains what constitutes the nature of their own desired form for Śrī Heruka and Vajravārāhī by saying "of whom," and so forth. "At the hand-top" means at the base of the arm.
By the word *kara* (hand), the hand together with the arm is meant.

Regarding "its five limbs": for whichever animal or tree one desires [to visualize], its five limbs—Vairocana and the others—as well as its leaves, flowers, and so forth, are to be joined through practice.
"Sitajāpī" means one who meditates while reciting; it does not mean one who is incapable, but rather one who is indeed capable. "Mokṣe mokṣaḥ" means liberation within liberation.
To the question, "Why does one not remain even here in the form of an animal and so forth?", he says: "Alas," and so on.
This means the state of being an animal (*tiryaggati*). (9–13)
Or by means of an elephant, horse, donkey, tortoise, camel, boar, or jackal;
or by a crow, owl, and so forth, a vulture, a curlew, a hawk, or a crane. (14)
He shall indeed become handsome, ugly, or possess a divine form; he will be a great heroic yogin capable of assuming any form at will—of this there is no doubt. (15)
There is no accomplishment higher than this to be found in the three worlds. || 16 ||
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, the chapter on the ritual for transforming the form to be accomplished through seven births. 49.
To whom does he assume these forms? He says: "Of elephants, horses," and so forth.
The instrumental case is used in the sense of the genitive;
the meaning is that he assumes the form of these.
And "graceful" (abhirūpa) means "possessing" (dhārī).
[There is also an explanation of these:
in this ritual action, with elephants and so forth as the sacrificial offering—
And enjoyment should be practiced;
from that, one obtains beauty and other such qualities.
Here too, there is the operation of both hearts.
"There is nothing beyond this":
this refers to the power established through seven births, which is naturally established (*prakṛtisiddha*). || 14–16 ||

That by which the transformation of form—namely, the state of having the form of an animal and so forth—is prescribed as something to be accomplished through seven births, that is such a chapter; it is the forty-ninth, the forty-ninth [chapter]. Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 49.
The fiftieth chapter: The Procedure for Designating the Ground for the Vaśya-homa Altar and Other Matters.
Now I shall explain the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa), by which the certain subjugation (vaśya) arises; through this correct ritual, swift accomplishment is brought about.
"Now" (*atha*) means: immediately after the description of the transformation of form accomplished through seven births;
I shall explain the ritual procedure for the fire offering (*homa*) of the eightfold laughter-mantra beginning with "hā hā he he."
The meaning is: that by means of which, through the offering of cow-flesh according to the prescribed rite, the swift accomplishment of the subjugating ritual proceeds. || 1 ||
Having soaked beef with liquor, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the left hand;
even a Buddha comes under one's control, let alone insignificant mortals.
By offering spittle, a tooth-stick, and likewise the dust from one's own body into the fire along with liquor bearing one's own name, one may bring the three worlds under one's control.
By means of this oblation made with dust, blood, vomit from one who has eaten, and human hair,
there shall be an immediate summoning.
Alternatively, the wise practitioner may perform the fire-oblation with hair vomited from his own body;
by employing the nimba tree, he shall immediately achieve enmity [between his targets]. || 5 ||
Being composed, one should offer oblations of pungent oil in a fire of *dhatura* flowers while reciting the name [of the target], using crow feathers; this brings about immediate expulsion and death.
He states the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the words beginning with "cow" (*go*) and so forth.
*Niṣṭhīvana* is phlegm discharged from the throat.
*Śvakeśāḥ* means the hair of a dog.
"Immediate attraction" means: *sat* is that which moves, goes, and comes—the seed-syllable *yaṃ*. That very syllable performs the act of attracting.
The method by which that [victim] is drawn forth is as follows:

seeing the victim, who resides upon a wind-mandala generated from the syllable *yaṃ*, approaching, one should perform the fire offering (*homa*) with the blood of a menstruating woman and other substances; this is the summary.
"Śvakāya" means the body of a dog.
"Sadyas" means that which perishes instantly; thus, it refers to the expulsion and killing of one who is living [at that very moment]. (2-6)
Whether waking, sleeping, rising, eating, or even engaged in sexual union, the practitioner of mantra should always recite at all times; for him, no obstacle shall arise.
One should offer one hundred oblations with the meat of a Jambūka;
by doing so, within just three months, the poverty of his family shall be destroyed.
If someone, the practitioner, should perform a fire offering with human flesh mixed with wine one hundred and eight times for three watches of the night. (9)
For one who has practiced on all the stages without exception, the Ḍākinī, being pleased and brought under control within six months, will bestow a kingdom upon him; of this there is no doubt.
One should meditate upon all the deities and perform the fire-oblation for two watches;
by that very means, one shall attain the state of a sky-walker (khecarī) with one's own body. || 11 ||
One should offer as oblation the flesh of a jackal, both internally and externally;
quickly, that which sets all accomplishments in motion shall come into his hand. (12)
He states the fruit for one who recites constantly: "while awake" means being alert;
"asleep" means lying down in bed; "engaged" means performing an activity.
Having sat down while asleep, he rises, saying, "Arise.
He is called *mithuna* because he possesses the pair (*mithuna*). It is called *māra* because his mind possesses the *māras*, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.
Because of the statement, "The mind itself is the Great Māra," there is a variant reading:
"The practitioner of mantras should recite at Mahākāla; there is no fixed time. In that context, for the purpose of recitation, it is perfectly [appropriate].
The sense is that one should not observe the time [of death].
And the laughter-mantra is: *oṃ hā hā he he ho ho haṃ haṃ phaṭ svāhā*. And: *oṃ kili kili sili sili cili cili dhili dhili phaṭ svāhā*.
And: "A hundred oblations.
One should constantly offer a hundred oblations made of *arka* bark and so forth three times [per day]. One should meditate—
One should offer oblations to all the deities for two watches (six hours).
At that time, the meditation on the deities should be accompanied by the meat and wine of all [beings],
specifically with the meat and wine of the jackal.
The jackal’s meat is decayed;
it is to be offered to the deities,
both internally and externally.
Thus, because of its utility: one who desires to perform oblations in the fire of the sacrificial pit [should use it], for it is that which sets all accomplishments in motion. (7–12)
One should perform the recitation of the mantra at night and cause the enemy kingdoms to fall;
by doing this every day, one will become a king oneself.
There is nothing superior to this found anywhere in the three worlds;
thus, the yogi, assuming various forms, may die at his own will.
By performing one hundred thousand oblations with wood of the *bilva*, the *palāśa*, and likewise the *udumbara* tree, one quickly becomes a lord of great wealth. || 15 ||
One desiring royal power should offer beef mixed with liquor;
for once one has attained Yogeśvarī, who indeed could remain in poverty? (16)
The recitation of mantra;
here, "recitation" refers to meditation performed with mantra, which is the service of mantra.
Regarding the phrase "alone at night," he says: "the royal [practices]."
One should cause [it] to fall. He states the reasoning: "For who indeed, having attained the Mistress of Yogis (yogīśvarī), would remain in poverty?
The mantra of laughter (hāsa-mantra) is that in which the deities are the mistresses (īśā) of the yogīs.
Poverty itself is the state of being poor. || 13-16 ||
They are accomplished with ease by means of the jackal-homa;
by performing the jackal-homa, one quickly becomes equal to the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada). || 17 ||
Even one who lacks vows, conduct, and purity shall attain success once possessed [by the deity].
[One should avoid] excessive quantities of kushmāṇḍa, mung beans, black gram, and chickpeas. || 18 ||
By binding the mouth with honey, *madhucchardis*, black mustard, and house-tamāla leaves, the yogi becomes able to act according to his own will, wherever he may be situated. (19)

"According to one's pleasure" means that there is no fixed rule; by the phrase "one who does not observe vows," etc., it indicates precisely this state of being according to one's pleasure. "Possessed" means authorized by the deity.
Through a dream, there is the vision of omens: long life from seeing *dūrvā* grass; vomiting honey from eating the remains of honey;
and smoke from hanging over a *tāla* leaf held in the house.
All that [is accomplished] for him in whose single part of the house the recited mantra is concealed; it becomes exactly as described. || 17-19 ||
Now I shall further explain the Yoginīs of the sacred sites (bhūmipīṭha) and so forth, who are the limbs and sub-limbs of Śrī Heruka, consisting of both the stable and the mobile. (20)
The *pīṭha* is on the stage of *pramuditā*, and likewise the *upapīṭha* is *vimalā*;
*prabhākarī* should be known as the *kṣetra*, and *arciṣmatī* as the *upakṣetra*.
Chandoha is Abhimukhī, and Upacchandoha is Sudurjayā;
Dūraṅgamā is in Melāpaka, and Acalā is in Upamelaka.
Sādhumati is the cremation ground, and Dharmamegha is the Upaśmaśānaka;
having consecrated Śrī Heruka, these are the internal stages.
"Now" (*atha*) means immediately after the description of all the applications. "I shall proclaim another"—if one asks what that is, he says: "the ground" (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the phrase "the yoginīs of the pīṭhas and so forth":
those for which the pīṭha is the first are the "pīṭhas and so forth," namely the locations such as the upapīṭhas; these are indeed the stages (bhūmis).
The seats and so forth; [this is] due to the elision of the second case ending. "Yoginī" refers to the yoginīs.
"Aṅgāṅga" means limb upon limb.
The limb consists of the hands and so forth;
its sub-limb consists of the joints and so forth;
the head consists of the neck and shoulders.
The powers are sensation and so forth;
the limbs and sub-limbs of Śrī Heruka consist of the elements such as earth and the aggregates such as the physical body.
The connection is: "I shall proclaim that which constitutes the means for every limb.
*Upapīṭha* is simply *papīṭha*, due to the elision of the letter *u*.
Having understood and ascertained Śrī Heruka,
he states that these stages (bhūmis) are to be deposited upon his limbs: "These are the internal stages."
The meaning is that these are the internal stages. || 20–23 ||
On the stage of the ten perfections, let the Yoginī speak in the tongues of barbarians;
whether in heaven, among mortals, or in the netherworld, she is the stable and immovable essence within the body of the Hero.
In Pullīra and the other [sites], as previously described, resides the Great Yoga of Śrī Heruka, the Lord who is the master of all desires, existing both externally and internally. (25)
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides,
it exists pervading everything, being heard of everywhere in the world.
Then, one should accomplish success with a mind joined in meditation;
this secret reality has been proclaimed for the benefit of practitioners. (27)
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, the procedure for the instruction on the grounds of the sacrificial fire-offering (homapīṭha) and so forth, for subjugation, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
Regarding the phrase "on the stage of the ten perfections":

the ten stages beginning with *pramuditā* (the Joyous) are the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*), namely: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, aspiration, power, skillful means, and gnosis.
"Let the Mlecchas speak"— this refers to the language of the Yoginīs. By the words "In heaven," etc., the three wheels [are indicated].
One should understand that having mastered the great yoga of Śrī Heruka, one should accomplish siddhi; this is how it should be applied.

Some maintain that the qualifiers beginning with "from all [sides]" refer specifically to this [yoga] by means of the lion’s sport mudrā (*siṃhavikrīḍitāmudrā*). In that context, the hand is the vajra, and the foot is the anus. (24–27)

The "Instruction on the Grounds for the Oblation for Subjugation and the Sacred Seats" (*vaśyahomapīṭhādibhūminirdeśa*) refers to that text by which the oblation for subjugation (*vaśyahoma*) and the grounds of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth are pointed out.
It is a "prescription" (*vidhi*) because it prescribes the reality of the meaning (*arthatattva*) through various methods;
a chapter (*paṭala*) is one whose nature consists of such a prescription.
The fiftieth, the fiftieth.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 50.
[The Summary of the Cultivation, etc. The Fifty-first Chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the tradition that is very difficult to obtain;
it was spoken by me in the Tantra using the secret code-language of the heroes (*vīrasaṅketabhāṣita*), and it must be kept hidden.
Now he speaks the chapter on the summary of the meaning of cultivation and so forth, beginning with "atha" (now) and so on.
"Atha" (now) marks the conclusion of the teaching. "Ataḥ" (therefore) means:
because nothing whatsoever is accomplished without the manifestation of the deity.
Therefore, the connection is: "I shall now declare the tradition.
Tradition (āmnāya) is the lineage of instruction from authoritative persons (āpta).

"Sudurlabham" means that tradition (*āmnāya*) in which those who possess excellent understanding are difficult to find. It is to be kept secret for the purpose of eliminating the faults of those who would cause harm.
"By me alone. He asks "Why?
and says: "In the *tantra*.
That by which things are extended (*tantryante*) and refined (*saṃskriyante*) is thus [called a *tantra*].
That which is called the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara; "spoken by convention" means it was spoken through symbolic terminology;
it was spoken by the heroes, that is, the Tathāgatas, by means of conventional symbols.
The sense is that the convention (*saṅketa*) here is entirely unprecedented.
Consequently, one need not suspect the existence of correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*), for a word does not convey meaning in isolation. Why?

In that case, it is accompanied by convention (saṅketa), and since that convention was established even by the heroes (vīras), it is rightly called "the speech of the heroes' convention" (vīrasaṅketabhāṣita). || 1 ||

Having first performed the emptiness of the causes and so forth, one should recite "Ālikāli" while wearing the lower garment, the five mudrās, and so on, with the consort as the limb of wisdom and the lattice of stakes. (2)
Then, what is the intended meaning even of the word "saṅketa"?
It is the clothing, namely the tiger skin and the elephant skin.
"Pañcamudrādi" means [the five mudrās] and so forth.

The five mudrās—namely the necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*), crest-jewel (*cūḍaka*), armlet (*keyūra*), earring (*kuṇḍala*), and sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*)—are present upon him; thus he is adorned with a necklace, a garland of heads, a girdle, and so forth.
[He embraces] the limb of wisdom (*prajñāṅga*) with the vajra and the vajra-bell.
One should perform the ritual of staking; this is the staking. The cage is made of vajra;
because this is an illustration, it includes the vajra-fortress and so forth. (2)
From the initial emergence of the sound (nāda) up to the yoga of withdrawal,
one attains the bliss of nourishment by nectar and the consecration by hand.
One should protect [the deity] with the Great Armor (Mahākavaca) and perform worship with the Universal Mantra (Sarvamantra).
This fourteenth reality has been explained in brief.
Regarding "the flow, the resonance, and so forth":
"flow" (pravṛtti) is the purification of the aggregate of form and the other aggregates; "resonance" (nāda) is the [essence of] the drop (bindu). The former—
It has the form of a line.
Here, the letter *ma* should be understood as not being separated from the top of the syllable *hūṃ*;
furthermore, it should be known as having the very nature of a bindu (dot).
*Nāda* and *makāra* are *nādamau*. Those [syllables] such as the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and so forth, which have those two as their beginning, are "those beginning with *nāda*" (*nādamādīni*).
And *pravṛtti*...
And "the *nāda*s and so forth" refers to the *nāda*s of activity and so forth;
"up to the point of the yoga of withdrawal" means that withdrawal is preceded by emanation.
Because it is focused upon that,
there is the fulfillment of the nourishment by the nectars;
that is, the accomplishment of the nourishment by the five nectars.

The lower garment, the five seals and so forth, the ritual stake, the cage, the utterance of Ālikāli, the cause and so forth, the engagement in emptiness, the resonance (nāda), the drop (bindu), the yoga of withdrawal, and the bliss of nourishment by the nectar.
The fourteen principles have been stated primarily as: hand-worship, consecration, the great armor-protection, and mantra-adoration; thus he says: "This is the fourteenth principle.
Four and ten.
That which has such parts is "of that nature.
The subject matter of the treatise is concise;
therefore, he says: "in brief" (saṃkṣepeṇa). || 3-4 ||
The best of men who practices this, having purified himself from all evils,
attains the stage of the Tathāgatas in birth after birth.
Born into the Tathāgata family, he becomes a righteous king;
yet, as before, he is deficient in all auspicious marks due to his past sins.
By this, he who practices, acts, or— in other words—
learns from this very [teaching],
he [is freed from] all evil.

"His self becomes purified"— because of the constant connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat*, [the meaning is as follows]: he whose all sins, such as the five immediate transgressions (*pañcānantarya*), are purified, and whose self— that is, his mind— is thus, because of the placement of the suffix *niṣṭhā* at the end of the compound, is a yogi of such a kind.
"Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons; having reached the necessary conditions and the [proper] time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. Thus it is said.

Without the fruit of karma, there is no destruction; even by means [of purification], there is only purification. There is no means whatsoever for its destruction, according to the statement: "They do not perish without having borne fruit."
Because the word *khalu* has the sense of certainty,
the fruit itself is indeed the means for its destruction.
Furthermore, even another means, which is of the very nature of karma, [is sublated] by that former one.
If the fruit characterized by the destruction of karma were produced, then because it would lack the capacity to produce any further fruit, there would be total annihilation.

If it is argued that such a specific means, while producing its destruction, simultaneously produces a nature of supreme, untainted great bliss— just as a lamp, while dispelling darkness, produces light— then [we reply]:
For it does not remove darkness;
rather, it simply illuminates.
When that [object] is illuminated by itself, darkness departs. This is the means—

How could its majesty not be accepted, such that it would be rendered fruitless? Thus, [the statement] "actions do not [bear fruit] for one who does not know the means," and so forth, is not contradicted;
and one attains the stage of the Tathāgatas.
One attains the stage of Tathāgata-knowledge, which consists in the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
If this were not the case because there is no reaching the ultimate limit of the excellence of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prakarṣa-paryanta*), then what would [be the consequence]?
To this he says: "Born in the family of the Tathāgatas in birth after birth.
One whose lineage is the Tathāgata is born from such a progenitor.
Furthermore, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used here with the suffix *lopa*.
[The phrase] "in birth after birth" means in a divine birth or in a human birth; [the construction] "he becomes a righteous king" is like the examples from Sumati, Kośala, and others.
He says "Just as... and so forth to explain what would happen if even one who is extremely wicked were somehow to practice the fourteen principles (*tattva*):
"Just as [the purification] of body, speech, and mind... and so on.

He whose evil karma—performed through activity, accumulated, and bound to the beginning, middle, and end—is such that he is "one whose previous and subsequent [karma] is evil"; for him, "of one whose previous and subsequent [karma] is evil," the genitive case is used in the sense of the nominative.
And he who is devoid of all the characteristics of a person (puruṣalakṣaṇa). || 5–6 ||
He who constantly meditates upon this [goddess] becomes the lord of all desires on earth,
like a vessel filled with ghee placed in the midst of a fire.
Just as clarified butter melts when heated and disappears from two vessels over time, so too does evil perish through the name "Śrī Heruka. (8)

Now, whoever meditates upon this Śrī Heruka, who consists of the fourteen principles (tattvas), becomes the lord of all desires on earth. When the mass of his sins has been rendered powerless, the fruit of action arises solely from meditation.
Or else, as in the case of prior sins and so forth—
When destruction has been brought about upon the earth through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one becomes a lord of all desires.
To explain how former sinful karma is destroyed by meditating upon Śrī Heruka— who possesses the form of arms, faces, and so forth— he says "ghṛta," etc.

Just as a vessel filled with clarified butter is placed in the midst of a fire, he asks: "What would happen in this case?"—[the answer being] that the clarified butter melts as it flows. If that is so...
In the vessel, the substance characterized as water, flowing like clarified butter, flows— that is, it attains fluidity—
and becomes mixed with the water; such is the meaning.
To the question "What then?", he says: "Time perishes.

Having reached a long period of time (*kālaṃ*), the water perishes. He explains that as long as the water does not perish, the clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) does not perish; this is the inherent power of the substance. [Regarding] the vessels—
Since fire is also a receptacle for vessels, it too is called a "vessel" (bhāṇḍa). Likewise, he says this very thing— that karma is exhausted— by stating that "evil perishes."
It is called "sin" (*pāpa*) because it causes beings who are attached to cast them into the ocean of *saṃsāra*; this is common karma.

However, when the fire of the knowledge of emptiness and the vessel of the form of Śrī Heruka are cultivated, the karma characterized by attachment to the apprehended object and so forth—which was deposited within the aggregates and so on—is destroyed, and thus the aggregates and so forth become faultless.
And yet, because of an attachment to emptiness, that very thing becomes faulty, as it lacks the performance of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) as it truly is. Thus it has been said:
"O Vajragarbha of great compassion, beings are liberated by means of existence itself."
"Beings are bound by existence and are liberated through its thorough understanding.
Thus, one whose afflictions are destroyed and whose course is ended does not attain supreme enlightenment;
yet one whose afflictions are rampant is unable to accomplish even his own welfare.
"Thus, by you who have exerted firm vigor in order to attain awakening, the afflictions were not utterly consumed, but were reduced to the lightness of a mere blade of grass. And:
"Regarding *Śrīheruka*: the syllable *Śrī* is non-dual gnosis; *He* is the emptiness of causes and so forth."
The array devoid of the letter *ru* is not established anywhere as "ka."
Thus, it consists of wisdom and means.
From its name, that is, from the name itself; for this very reason, the word *iti* has the sense of the genitive case. Bending (*namana*).
The state of being dependent upon the power [of another] is called *nāma*. || 7-8 ||
Whether through meditation, mere contemplation, recitation, study, or writing,
one obtains the enjoyment of heaven or else becomes a universal monarch.
At the time of death, however, the yogi beholds Śrī Heruka and the other heroes and yoginīs, their hands busy with various flowers and bearing various banners and streamers. (10)
Amidst the sounds of various musical instruments and the offerings of diverse songs, that which is called death leads the faint-hearted to the state of a sky-farer. 11.
To the question "When [does this occur]?", he says: "In meditation" (*dhyāne*).
Meditation is reflection (*cintā*).
Recitation is general; self-study is one-pointed.
Anxiety is writing;
it is the state of being a universal monarch for oneself,
even when the yoga of Śrī Heruka and the Yoginīs has not been accomplished.
If death should occur while the recitation and so forth have not been completed, he says "cittī" and so on to address what happens then: "yogī" refers to a person who is a yogi;
"śrīherukādivīrayoginī" refers to the heroes and yoginīs beginning with Śrī Heruka.

Due to the elision of the third-person plural ending, [the word] "nānā" (various) is used. Because they preside over the musical instruments and so forth, the ritual activities of Śrī Heruka and the others are perceived even slightly. (9–11)

Thus, the great tantra of the illustrious Cakrasaṃvara—which is difficult to find on earth even for gods and great heroic yoginīs—is [attained] by one who, having understood it, [acts] without devotion. (12)
The torment of suffering shall be his constant and perpetual state;
[he shall wear] a wooden staff, a crest-jewel, armlets, earrings, and the sacred thread. || 13 ||
With the sounds of the girdles and small bells upon the garlands of skulls adorning his neck,
he was like a swarm of bees around the filaments of the mountain peak, which is like a lotus.
He says this very thing with the words "In this way," and so forth.
The God is Śrī Heruka;
the Great Heroes are Khaṇḍakapālī and the others.
The yoginīs, such as Vajravārāhī and others,
are difficult to perceive with the fleshly eye.
Having understood the great tantra, the glorious Cakrasaṃvara—
Even having understood [the truth], if through lack of devotion one remains without devotion,
poverty arises for him; therefore, he is likewise tormented by sufferings.
The passage beginning with "necklace" (*kaṇṭhikā*) and so forth shows the conclusion of the teaching.
The term "necklace, crest-jewel, and armlet" (*kaṇṭhikā-cūḍa-keyūram*) is singular because it is a collective compound (*samāhāra*).

The phrase beginning with "at the throat" and so forth is the conclusion of the ornaments (*bhūṣaṇa*), as it was before. The phrase "in the filaments at the summit of the mountain" is the conclusion of the locations (*sthāna*).
"And *ālikālyam*" refers to the synthesis of the five aspects; that is, the meaning of *āli* and *kāli*. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the remaining aspects. (12–14)
Having approached the Lord of Gaurī, who is embraced by the limbs of Vajra-ghaṇṭā, and who is joined by a host of twenty-four heroes and yoginīs; || 15 ||
"Gaurī" is in the instrumental case in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*).
This is the withdrawal of the seat.
"Embraced by the vajra and bell" refers to the hand-symbols (*cihna*).
This is the summary of the base [section].
These two signs are indicative of other signs as well.
"Half of twenty-four" refers to Kākāsyā and the others.
Twelve is half of twenty-four.
The yoginīs joined with the vīras are the twenty-four vīrayoginīs; their groups [are as follows].
The hosts of heroic yoginīs; the short vowel [in "vīra-"] is due to Vedic usage. "United" (saṃyukta) refers to the summary of the thirty-six yoginīs. || 15 ||
One should meditate upon the supreme state of the Great King Śrī Heruka, who possesses the yoga of the assembly of all heroes and yoginīs. 16.
All were satisfied and became non-dual, acting as the agents of emanation and reabsorption;
beings possessed of various inclinations were awakened by various modes of conduct. || 17 ||

"Wherein the Great King Śrī Heruka [resides]" is the summary of the Lord (*nāyaka*), expressed as "the Great King Śrī Heruka. "The place" (*pada*) is the substantive (*viśeṣya*). This is the summary of the entire maṇḍala in the form of the support and the supported.
Having spoken in brief, [he now speaks] again in extreme brevity:
He says "sarva" and so forth.
In the sense of "all heroes," this is the singular genitive case. [It refers to] the yoginīs.
Thus, "with retinue" (saparṣat) means he exists together with a retinue. "Possessing yoga" refers to one who is united with Vajravārāhī, who is the churner.
The short vowel [in *madhya*] is due to Vedic usage (*ārṣatvāt*).
In the reading *madhyayogavān*, it means one who possesses the intermediate bliss free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
"Now, therefore, the secret," and so forth.
Having heard the teaching ending with the words "possessing the yoga of churning," all the previously mentioned heroes and heroines were satisfied because they had attained the essence of the Dharma;
through their satisfaction, they became twofold, that is, doubled.
Emanation is radiance; withdrawal is the contraction of those things that have been radiated.
The heroes and yoginīs listen to the Dharma for the sake of the supreme goal.
For the sake of those to be converted by Śrī Heruka, the Blessed One, having been requested by Vajravārāhī, manifested such an assembly engaged in listening to the Dharma and taught the Dharma.
To the question, "Why indeed is there such devotion to Śrī Heruka? he says, "Various," and so forth.
They are those who ascertain various meanings. Their *caryās*—that is, their modes of conduct—are of various forms, characterized by such states as being householders and so forth.
"Awakened by various *caryās*" means they have been led to realization. This...
"Perform [it]!"—thus they were made firm. || 16-17 ||

If, through the teaching of the profound Dharma, there should arise faith in those to be trained by various methods, it has been taught by means of diverse skillful means for the sake of those disciples who follow various paths. (18)
One should not utter reproach; one should remember the inconceivable nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
For this is not my domain, nor do I know the true nature of phenomena.

To the question "Why is it so?", he says: "It has been taught through various means for disciples of diverse dispositions, so that through the instruction of the profound Dharma, there may arise resolute faith."

If there were any kind of inclination (adhimukti) among those to be trained through the methods of the Śrāvakas and others, then the inclination was taught by means of various expedients and various kinds of paths.
With what intention was such a statement made? He says:
Regarding the phrase "by means of the teaching of the profound Dharma":

the "teaching of the profound Dharma" refers to the instruction (*nirdeśa*) or exposition (*deśanā*) of the profound Dharma, which consists of the non-duality of wisdom and skillful means; by that cause, liberation has been taught through various methods.

The meaning is that whatever conviction in the Dharma [he possesses] was taught to him. One should not raise the objection, "For what purpose is there a diversity of convictions? because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is to be remembered as inconceivable; or alternatively, [it is for the sake of guiding those with various dispositions].
They have been taught through various means and in the forms of various deities;
the intended meaning is that sentient beings themselves are presented in the form of deities.

While it is appropriate to have such conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in the Mantra Mahāyāna—which consists of wisdom and skillful means—because one may act according to one's own inclination, nevertheless, even so...
If one asks, "What would happen if it were so?", he says: "Profound," and so forth.

The limb of wisdom (*prajñāṅga*) has the nature of profound emptiness (*gambhīra-śūnyatā*). The limb of skillful means (*upāyāṅga*) consists of the Dharma [manifested] in the forms of arms, faces, and so on.
That which is both profound and a phenomenon (dharma) is "profound dharma" (gambhīradharma).
That unsurpassed tantra called the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*, by means of which it is taught, is the "instruction on the profound dharma" (gambhīradharmanirdeśa).
In this case, if there were no conviction on the part of those to be trained, then no rejection of them should be made.
To the question, "What indeed should be done? he says: "They should be remembered."
Regarding the phrase "the nature of inconceivable phenomena" (*cintyadharmatā*):

the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of inconceivable phenomena—that is, of meditative cultivations (*bhāvanā*)—is to be recollected and taught. The intended meaning is that the very form of meditative cultivations is always inconceivable.
"In these phenomena, such as the aggregates and so forth, there is no object of mine in the form of something to be grasped or the like.
He asks, "For what reason? and says, "By which," and so forth.
"I do not know the nature of the reality, suchness, or emptiness, in the form of a phenomenon (*dharma*)."
Because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself;
as it has been said: "For the mind does not know the mind.
Cognition devoid of the grasped object and so forth is *cittamātra* (mind-only), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). As it has been stated:

"Other than consciousness, no such thing as emptiness exists that is distinct from it; for the distinctness of a separation is considered to be its non-distinctness [from what it is separated from]. (18–19)
Those great-souled ones, the perfectly awakened Buddhas and their sons as well, know this:
it remains established whether Buddhas arise or do not arise. (20)
The true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is always inconceivable and devoid of decrease or increase; having reflected thus, one should not disparage any worldly beings. (21)
He states who it is that knows them: "they know," and so forth.
They are the perfectly awakened ones (*samyagbuddha*), those possessing perfect awakening; they are the great-souled ones (*mahātman*), those of vast intellect.
Those Buddhas are the fathers of whom; those sons of theirs are the Bodhisattvas, because, having become Bodhisattvas, they become Buddhas.
Or, they are the sons of those Buddhas—“their sons”—because they are born from them.
The self of the Buddhas is the Dharma; because they awaken to the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the Buddhas will fully awaken to it,
and the Bodhisattvas likewise awaken to it.
Designation is purified by millions [of eons] through awakening; they know the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
To the question of when this *dharmatā* might arise, he says:
"From arising," and so forth.
The meaning is that they remain bound and persist even in the absence of the arising of Buddhas, or even in the ordinary state prior to such arising.
This is expressed by the word "always."

Because it remains eternally established in the form of a continuous flow of its own nature (*prakṛti-pravāha-prabandha*), it is inconceivable (*acintya*). Why? Because it is impossible to conceive of it as being "increasing" over such a vast duration of time.
Having weighed them thus as being devoid of decrease and increase, and having equalized the enlightened and the unenlightened, all worldly beings are not to be censured. || 20-21 ||

For their course is inconceivable, and the Buddha’s drama is inconceivable; through the various divisions of the secret yoga of the Sūtras and Kriyā-tantras, they possess a nature that introduces sentient beings, as if delighting in this or that [method]. // 22 //

Thus ends the fifty-first [chapter] of the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*, the King of Mahāyoginī Tantras, the *Uttaratantra* known as the *Śrīheruka*, which falls within the one hundred thousand [verse] *Mahātantrarāja* of the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*; it is the king of all scriptures, the supreme among the supreme, the unvanquished by the omniscience attained through the recitation of the great hero Śrīheruka, and the primary accomplishment.
The chapter is completed. || 51 ||
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; thus proclaims the Great Śramaṇa.
This is the religious gift of one who follows the most excellent Mahāyāna.

The establishment of the destinies even for those worldly beings is inconceivable; why is this so? He says: "The Buddha-play is inconceivable. The Buddhas themselves are established in various forms, and thus it is called a play.
He says this very thing with the words "sūtra" and so forth:
*sūtra* refers to the *sūtrānta*;
*kriyate* refers to the *kriyātantra*.
"Abhi" means "towards" (abhimukha);
the genitive case is used in the sense of the first [case].
"Caryā" means conduct (*caryā*).

The tantra is the Yoga-tantra, the Guhya-tantra; the word "tu" (but/rather) is used for conjunction; "sattvāvatāra" is [to be understood] with the elision of the fourth case ending; [it means] liberation.
The removal of the bonds of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The word "tu" is used in the sense of "but," for the purpose of leading inconceivable beings who are divided by all [their various] differences.
[This is] the leading of beings.
And it is inconceivable. "The perfectly awakened ones (sambuddhāḥ) bring them forth" connects with what precedes.
And in each respective case, such as in the mundane world and so forth, the perfectly awakened ones are like those who delight, being as if they themselves were delighted.
The meaning is that the equality of the *rata* (delight) is inconceivable. Now, "sūtra" refers to the discourses (*sūtrāntas*),
and "kriyā" refers to the analytical exposition (*vibhāṣā*).
The Abhidharma is the Madhyamaka;
the Yogaguhyam is the Yogācāra.
This is indicated by the passage beginning with: "Now, therefore, I shall explain the secret."
The secret has been promised.
The Blessed One taught it through the passage beginning with “by the medium and supreme breath,” and so forth.
As for the agent, expressed by the word “all” (*sarve*), she is described by the passage beginning with “all are satisfied” (*sarve tuṣṭāḥ*) up to “delighting therein” (*tatra tatra ratā*).

The Blessed One himself has shown that by this much [of the text], she has established the satisfaction of those to be trained and so forth; thus, the connection is that the fifty-first chapter—characterized by such qualifiers as "the Great King of Tantras" and so on—is completed. || 22 ||

In that regard, concerning the term *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, he says "Mahā... and so forth, demonstrating the specific nominative-case qualifiers distinguished by the implied word "therein" (*tatra*): "And it is great because by means of this one extends and nourishes the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*)."

And as for the *tattantra*, it is that which shines forth where the supreme, untainted great bliss (*paramānāsrava-mahāsukha*) resides; thus it would be characterized by such attributes as "the Great Tantra King" (*mahātantrarāja*).
It consists of one hundred thousand [verses] and is equal to space (*khasama*); because it contains within it the "falling" or "emerging" from its midst, it is called *lakṣāntaḥ-pāti*.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), there is an inclusion of the meanings from other tantras.
This has been explained in successive order.
Like a king, he is a king—of all.

Because he stands above all treatises and systems and because he is their illuminator, the Blessed One possesses the nature of the Moon. For this reason as well, the Moon is stated to be the subject matter [the illumination].
Śrī Heruka together with Vārāhī; the "Great Ones" refers to the thirty-six Mahāyoginīs, such as the Ḍākinīs and others;
and the twenty-four heroes, such as Khaṇḍakapāla and others.
The mantras are perfected through recitation.
The omniscience [consists of] the knowledge of the characteristics and so forth of the yoginīs, as well as direct perception and other forms of knowledge.
Aparājita is Śaṅkara accompanied by Durgā.
The "primordial accomplishments" (ādibhūtāḥ siddhayaḥ) refer to the accomplishments beginning with *gha*.
It is called such a tantra because it proclaims the accomplishment known as the "Unconquered Sword," which was mastered by the Great Hero Śrī Heruka through recitation and grants all-knowing wisdom.
By the word "and" (ca), the purification of the stages and so forth is indicated.
It is called "the transcendent" (uttara) because by means of it, one transcends the ocean of existence (bhava).
The suffix *ac* is applied after the root *pac* and others; thus,
*tantraṃ* means the accumulation of merit and wisdom.
*Cakra* means the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).

The *śrīcakra* is the glorious wheel; because it restrains the minds of sentient beings from the wrong path, it is called *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*. Since it denotes Śrī Heruka, the tantra is also referred to by that same name.
The term *mahāyoginītantrarāja* is a compound word (*nirvibhaktika-pada*) consisting of "the great" (*mahaḥ*) and "that king of Yoginī-tantras" (*tad yoginītantrarājam*).
This is because of the abundance of instructions from the Yoginīs.
In the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, the great king of tantras contained within a hundred thousand [verses], the sovereign of all scriptures,
the supreme (*uttara*) tantra named *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*, which is the ultimate of all-knowing ones accomplished by the recitation of the great hero Śrī Heruka.
In the *Mahāyoginītantrarāja*, the fifty-first [chapter]—meaning the fifty-first—is correctly obtained and completed.

The collection of words beginning with "the great king of tantras" (*mahātantrarāja*) and ending with "the king of the Mahāyoginītantra" (*mahāyoginītantrarāja*) consists of nominal forms (subantas). The word "completed" (*samāpta*) is to be joined at the end of the title *Śrīherukābhidhāna* across all fifty-one chapters.
Just as the words of the Guru’s commentary were recorded by me from memory,
so too do these words of mine come forth through the grasping of their meaning.
Even when this matter of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted has been ascertained through valid means of knowledge,
doubt does not cease without the instruction of a guru.
Like a garland, I bear upon my head the command of my guru— which is delightful in its various expressions and dispels the delusion of wandering— along with all that is connected to it.
Through the perception that the world is a vibration of one's own mind,
let it be contemplated that one's own mind alone is apprehended;
for here, there exists no mandala other than one's own mind.
Without the planets, quickly [attain] the mandala of existence.
Meditate upon the state of Śrī, the state of the deity,
from which you shall go to a stainless, stable station;
for without the cessation of worldly existence there is no tranquility, and without tranquility [there is no liberation].
Existence is the non-differentiation within pure manifestation.
She was like a beloved toward the principles that have now arisen from the lotus-born Śrī Cakrasaṃvara, which are mines of the nectar-like essence of secret instructions.
Those whose minds and intellects are pure through merit carry forth faith.
Indeed, having observed other eminent poets who composed extensive works, my intellect also took delight in accomplishing that same purpose;
for when the occasion is right, even one who is capable dances and sings.
Due to such eagerness, would even an unworthy person not go there?
Having elucidated the world of the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara* with clear terminology, like the sun illuminating the universe,
may people carry forth those virtues through whatever merit I have thereby acquired.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 51.
The *Śrīcakrasaṃvarapañjikā* composed by the learned master Bhavabhaṭṭa is hereby completed.
Just as a lamp situated inside a jar does not shine outside,
but once that jar is broken, the flame of the lamp shines forth thereafter.
For one's own body is indeed the jar, and the lamp is indeed the reality;
when these are joined by the mouth of the Guru, the wisdom of the Buddha becomes manifest.
He perceives the sky as arisen from the sky, the space of space;
in this very way, this practice has been demonstrated by the Guru from his own mouth.
